12359.name: unkown_apt_group
12359.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]This intrusion set, likely associated with the Russian Federation, is an unknown APT group. It is also known as backdoordiplomacy, cloudcomputating, backdip, and quarian, and shows overlaps with groups like lotus panda. Its infrastructure includes domains like 1tutor.ru, conversesuisse.net, and cntula.ru. Key techniques involve using legitimate web services for command and control (T1102.001 Dead Drop Resolver, T1102.002 Bidirectional Communication) and data exfiltration (T1567), as well as spearphishing via third-party services (T1566.003) and lateral movement via remote services (T1021). Its motivation is believed to be cyber espionage.[/profile]

12361.name: T1567
12361.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]T1567, Exfiltration Over Web Service, is an exfiltration tactic used on platforms including Windows, Linux, and macOS. It involves adversaries using legitimate external web services, such as text storage sites like pastebin[.]com, to transfer stolen data, often leveraging the services' pre-existing network permissions and SSL/TLS encryption for cover. This technique is distinct from exfiltration to code repositories and has been associated with groups like APT28 and BlackByte.[/profile]

12362.name: T1071
12362.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]The entity is the MITRE ATT&CK technique T1071: Application Layer Protocol, used for Command and Control. It operates on platforms including Windows, Linux, macOS, ESXi, and Network Devices. Adversaries use standard OSI application layer protocols like HTTP, DNS, SMB, SSH, or RDP to blend their malicious communications with normal network traffic, embedding commands and data within the legitimate protocol streams to avoid detection and network filtering. This technique is distinct from using custom C2 protocols (T1094).[profile]

12363.name: T1518
12363.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]T1518 (Software Discovery) is a Discovery tactic technique applicable to Windows, Linux, macOS, IaaS, and ESXi platforms. It involves adversaries enumerating installed software and versions to assess the environment, identify security measures, locate vulnerable software for potential exploitation, and discover widely deployed tools like software deployment utilities that could facilitate lateral movement or broader infection. Associated threat groups include SideWinder, MuddyWater, and Volt Typhoon.

12364.name: T1021
12364.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]T1021 (Remote Services) is a Lateral Movement technique applicable to Windows, Linux, macOS, IaaS, and ESXi platforms. Adversaries use valid accounts to log into services that accept remote connections, such as SSH, RDP, VNC, and telnet, to perform actions as the logged-on user across the network. This includes accessing enterprise domain machines, SaaS/IaaS services, and management platforms like VMware vCenter. Legitimate remote management tools, such as Apple Remote Desktop (which uses VNC and SSH), can also be abused for this purpose, and the technique can be leveraged in conjunction with privilege escalation methods like SID-History Injection.

12365.name: T1036
12365.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]T1036 (Masquerading) is a Defense Evasion technique used on Windows, Linux, macOS, ESXi, and Container platforms. It involves manipulating the name, location, or metadata of malicious files or processes to appear legitimate, such as by renaming system utilities or giving malicious shortcuts the names of benign programs to evade detection.

12366.name: T1219
12366.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]T1219, known as Remote Access Tools, is a command-and-control technique targeting Windows, Linux, and macOS. It involves abusing legitimate remote access or management software—such as graphical desktop support tools or command-line remote administration clients—to establish interactive command and control channels, often inheriting the permissions of the user or software. This can provide adversaries with persistent, redundant access, and the tools' installation routines may create services for persistence. It has been used by groups like Carbanak, MuddyWater, and FIN7.[/profile]

12407.name: T1105
12407.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Ingress Tool Transfer (T1105) is a Command and Control tactic applicable to Windows, Linux, macOS, ESXi, and Network Devices. Adversaries transfer tools or files from an external system into a compromised environment, often through the command and control channel or alternate protocols like FTP. Common utilities for this include `copy`, `certutil`, `PowerShell` commands like `IEX(New-Object Net.WebClient).downloadString()`, `curl`, `scp`, `wget`, and package managers like `yum` or `winget`. Files may also be transferred via web services or cloud storage sync features (e.g., Dropbox). This technique is distinct from internal Lateral Tool Transfer (T1570) and is associated with numerous threat groups, including APT29, Lazarus Group, and Volt Typhoon.[/profile]

12408.name: T1012
12408.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Query Registry is technique T1012 under the Discovery tactic, targeting Windows platforms. It involves adversaries interacting with the Windows Registry to gather system, configuration, and software information, often using utilities like Reg.exe. This data is used during automated discovery to inform follow-on actions. A specific example is querying the registry key `HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Nls\Language` to infer the system language. The technique is associated with numerous threat groups including APT41, Lazarus Group, and Volt Typhoon.[/profile]

12409.name: T1027
12409.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]T1027, Obfuscated Files or Information, is a Defense Evasion technique used on Windows, Linux, macOS, ESXi, and Network Devices. It involves making files or executables difficult to analyze or discover by encrypting, encoding, compressing, or archiving their contents. Adversaries may also split payloads into benign-seeming files, encode portions of files to hide strings, or use obfuscated scripts. This behavior is commonly employed by numerous threat groups, including APT41, Sandworm Team, and Kimsuky, to evade signature-based detection during initial access or later stages of an attack.

12410.name: T1059
12410.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]T1059, known as Command and Scripting Interpreter, is an Execution tactic technique applicable across Windows, Linux, macOS, and other platforms. It involves abusing built-in or cross-platform interpreters like PowerShell, Unix Shell, Python, JavaScript, and Visual Basic to execute arbitrary commands. Adversaries embed scripts in initial access payloads or leverage remote services for execution, with exploitation linked to vulnerabilities such as CVE-2022-30190. Associated threat groups include APT37, FIN7, and OilRig.

12412.name: T1102.002
12412.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]The entity is MITRE ATT&CK technique T1102.002, named Bidirectional Communication, under the Command and Control tactic. It operates on Windows, Linux, macOS, and ESXi platforms. This technique involves adversaries using legitimate external web services like social media or popular websites to send commands to and receive output from a compromised system over that same service channel, such as by posting comments or updating documents, to blend with normal traffic and leverage inherent SSL/TLS encryption. Related groups include APT28, Lazarus Group, and FIN7. Associated vulnerabilities include CVE-2023-46805.

12413.name: T1102.001
12413.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]T1102.001, known as Dead Drop Resolver, is a command-and-control technique used on Windows, Linux, macOS, and ESXi platforms. It involves adversaries using legitimate external web services like social media or popular sites to host obfuscated or encoded information, such as domains or IP addresses, that point to additional C2 infrastructure. This method provides cover by blending with normal traffic, leverages SSL/TLS for protection, and enhances operational resiliency by allowing dynamic changes to back-end infrastructure, as seen in campaigns by groups like APT41 and Kimsuky.

12414.name: T1566.003
12414.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]T1566.003 - Spearphishing via Service is an Initial Access technique for macOS, Linux, and Windows. It involves sending targeted phishing messages through third-party services like social media or personal webmail to bypass enterprise email security. Adversaries build rapport with targets using fake accounts, then deliver malicious links or attachments via these less-secure channels, often under the guise of job opportunities or expected communications. Associated groups include FIN6, Lazarus Group, and APT29.

12415.name: T1059.005
12415.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]This entity is MITRE ATT&CK technique T1059.005, named Visual Basic, under the Execution tactic for Windows, Linux, and macOS platforms. It involves adversaries abusing Visual Basic (VB) and its derivatives like VBScript and VBA to execute malicious commands. Common implementations include using VBScript to automate execution or embedding VBA macros into spearphishing attachments. The technique is associated with numerous threat groups, including Lazarus Group, FIN7, and APT32.

12416.name: T1573.001
12416.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]T1573.001, Symmetric Cryptography, is a command-and-control technique used on Windows, Linux, macOS, ESXi, and Network Devices. It conceals C2 traffic by employing known symmetric encryption algorithms like AES, DES, 3DES, Blowfish, or RC4, which use the same key for both encryption and decryption. This method is distinct from relying on inherent protocol protections and is associated with groups including MuddyWater, Lazarus Group, and APT28.

12417.name: T1057
12417.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Process Discovery is technique T1057 within the Discovery tactic, applicable to Windows, Linux, macOS, ESXi, and Network Devices. It involves adversaries enumerating running processes to understand system software and shape follow-on actions. Technical execution includes using the `tasklist` command or `Get-Process` in PowerShell on Windows, the `ps` command or enumerating `/proc` on Linux/macOS, `esxcli system process list` on ESXi, and `show processes` CLI commands on network devices. The technique is commonly used by numerous threat groups including APT28, Lazarus Group, and MuddyWater.[/profile]

12418.name: T1016
12418.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]System Network Configuration Discovery, designated T1016, is a Discovery tactic technique applicable to Windows, Linux, macOS, Network Devices, and ESXi platforms. It involves adversaries using native OS utilities like arp, ipconfig/ifconfig, nbtstat, and route to discover network details such as IP and MAC addresses. On network devices, commands like `show ip route` via a CLI are used, while on ESXi, adversaries may execute `esxcli network nic list` to retrieve MAC addresses. This gathered information is used to map the network and plan subsequent actions.

12419.name: T1074.001
12419.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]T1074.001, known as Local Data Staging, is a Collection tactic technique used on Windows, Linux, macOS, and ESXi platforms. It involves adversaries staging collected data in a central location or directory on the local system, such as separate files or a single archive, prior to exfiltration. Common command shells like cmd or bash are often used to copy data into this staging area, and data may also be placed in local databases or the Windows Registry. This technique is employed by numerous threat groups including APT28, Lazarus Group, and MuddyWater.

12420.name: T1112
12420.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]T1112, named Modify Registry, is a defense evasion and persistence technique for Windows. Adversaries interact with the Windows Registry using tools like the built-in Reg utility or remote access software to modify keys and values. This can be used to hide configuration data or payloads, impair security defenses by altering system settings, enable remote execution for lateral movement, or conceal persistence mechanisms by creating keys with names that cause errors when read. It is commonly used by groups like APT41, Wizard Spider, and Volt Typhoon.

12421.name: T1140
12421.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]T1140, Deobfuscate/Decode Files or Information, is a Defense Evasion technique for macOS, Linux, Windows, and ESXi. It involves using separate mechanisms to decode or deobfuscate hidden artifacts, such as using built-in malware functionality or system utilities like `certutil` to decode a file hidden inside a certificate, or using Windows commands like `copy /b` or `type` to reassemble binary fragments into a malicious payload. User action may sometimes be required to open or provide a password for these files.

12422.name: T1106
12422.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]T1106, known as Native API, is an execution technique within the MITRE ATT&CK framework applicable to Windows, Linux, and macOS. It involves adversaries directly or indirectly invoking low-level OS kernel services through native application programming interfaces (APIs) or system calls to perform actions like process creation (e.g., via `NtCreateProcess`, `CreateProcess()`, or `fork()`). This method can be used to execute binaries or commands and is often leveraged to subvert user-mode API hooks monitored by security tools. The technique is associated with groups including APT37, Lazarus, and Sandworm Team.[/profile]

12423.name: T1082
12423.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]T1082, System Information Discovery, is a Discovery technique targeting macOS, Linux, Windows, Network Devices, IaaS, and ESXi platforms. It involves adversaries gathering detailed OS and hardware data like version, patches, and architecture to inform follow-on actions. This is executed using tools like `systeminfo` on Windows, the `systemsetup` tool on macOS with privileges, CLI commands like `show version` on network devices, and ESXi commands such as `system version get`. In cloud environments, adversaries use provider APIs to query instance metadata. The gathered information aids in payload development and evasion, as seen when data from this discovery is used to spoof browser attributes for blending with traffic.

12424.name: T1566.001
12424.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]T1566.001 Spearphishing Attachment is an Initial Access technique in the MITRE ATT&CK framework, applicable to Windows, Linux, and macOS. It involves sending targeted emails with malicious attachments like Office documents, executables, PDFs, or archives to gain a foothold. Execution typically relies on user interaction to open the file, which may exploit vulnerabilities (e.g., CVE-2017-11882, CVE-2023-0669) or directly run a payload. Adversaries often use social engineering, manipulate file extensions, or provide archive passwords to evade defenses. This technique is widely used by numerous threat groups including APT29, Lazarus Group, and FIN7.

12425.name: T1204.002
12425.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]T1204.002, known as User Execution: Malicious File, is an Execution tactic technique for Windows, Linux, and macOS. It relies on a user opening a malicious file, such as .doc, .pdf, .exe, .lnk, or .iso, to execute adversary code, often following spearphishing. Adversaries use masquerading and obfuscation, like familiar names or password protection, to trick users. This activity is associated with numerous threat groups including APT29, Lazarus Group, and FIN7.

12426.name: T1033
12426.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]System Owner/User Discovery is the MITRE ATT&CK technique T1033 under the Discovery tactic, applicable to Windows, Linux, macOS, and Network Devices platforms. It involves adversaries identifying active or primary users on a system to inform follow-on actions. Specific technical mechanics include querying system information via commands like `whoami`, `w`, `who`, and on macOS `dscl . list /Users | grep -v '_'`, checking environment variables such as `%USERNAME%` or `$USER`, and on network devices using CLI commands like `show users` or `show ssh`. This information is often gathered through other discovery techniques that expose user details in process ownership, file permissions, and system logs.

12427.name: T1083
12427.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]The entity is MITRE ATT&CK technique T1083, File and Directory Discovery, under the Discovery tactic. It operates on platforms including Windows, Linux, macOS, ESXi, and Network Devices. The technique involves adversaries enumerating files and directories using command shell utilities like `dir`, `ls`, `find`, and `tree`, or network device commands like `show flash`. It can also be performed via hypervisor CLIs such as `esxcli` on ESXi systems. The information gathered is used to shape follow-on adversarial behaviors. Numerous threat groups, including APT28, Volt Typhoon, and MuddyWater, have been associated with this technique.[/profile]

12429.name: unkown_apt_group
12429.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]This intrusion set is likely associated with the Silence Group or TA505, also known as Backdoordiplomacy, Cloudcomputating, Backdip, and Quarian. It employs malware such as PaperCut and Truebot, leveraging tools like Impair Defenses (T1562) and Obfuscated Files or Information (T1027) for defense evasion, and uses Web Services (T1102) for command and control via domains including updateservicecenter.com and windowservicecenter.com. The group's activities show overlaps with other APTs like Lotus Panda, and it is attributed to financially motivated cybercriminal operations, targeting vulnerable software like PaperCut servers for initial access.[/profile]

12430.name: Truebot
12430.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Truebot is a malware attributed to the Silence Group and TA505. It employs defense evasion techniques including T1562 (Impair Defenses) to disable security tools, T1036.004 (Masquerade Task or Service) to disguise malicious tasks, and T1218.011 (Rundll32) to proxy execution. It performs input capture (T1056) for credential access and abuses local accounts (T1078.003) for persistence and lateral movement. The malware enumerates OS version, processor architecture, and system hostnames. Associated infrastructure includes domains like qweastradoc.com, updateservicecenter.com, and anydeskupdates.com.[/profile]

12432.name: PaperCut
12432.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]PaperCut is a malware that exploits the PaperCut software vulnerability CVE-2023-27350. It is associated with threat groups including Silence Group and TA505. Its key technical behaviors involve using the Command and Scripting Interpreter (T1059) for execution, employing Web Services (T1102) like deceptive domains for command and control, and utilizing Obfuscated Files or Information (T1027) for defense evasion. It targets PaperCut servers and uses infrastructure such as the domains windowservicecemter.com, windowservicecenter.com, windowservicecentar.com, updateservicecenter.com, and anydeskupdate.com.[/profile]

12453.name: T1102
12453.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]T1102, known as Web Service, is a Command and Control technique within the MITRE ATT&CK framework applicable to Windows, Linux, macOS, and ESXi platforms. Adversaries abuse legitimate external web services like Google, Microsoft, or Twitter to relay data, hiding C2 traffic within expected, SSL/TLS-encrypted communications to a compromised system. This method provides operational resiliency by allowing dynamic infrastructure changes and can protect backend servers from discovery through malware analysis. Associated threat groups include Gamaredon Group, FIN6, and Turla.

12454.name: T1562
12454.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]T1562, Impair Defenses, is a Defense Evasion technique applicable across Windows, Linux, macOS, and cloud platforms. It involves maliciously modifying a victim environment to hinder or disable defensive mechanisms, including preventative tools like firewalls and detection capabilities such as audit logging. Adversaries may also impair routine security hygiene operations, like blocking system shutdowns or modifying update processes, to enable persistent malicious activity. This technique can involve spoofing security alerting to present false evidence of a healthy system status even after legitimate tools are disabled. Specific sub-techniques include Disable or Modify Tools (T1562.001) and Disable or Modify Cloud Logs (T1562.008), which adversaries may employ after discovering cloud services.[/profile]

12455.name: Obfuscated Files or Information
12455.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Obfuscated Files or Information is the MITRE ATT&CK technique T1027 under the Defense Evasion tactic, applicable to Windows, Linux, macOS, ESXi, and Network Devices. It involves making files or executables difficult to detect or analyze by encrypting, encoding, compressing, or archiving their contents. Specific technical mechanics include splitting payloads into benign-separate files for later reassembly, using password-protected archives, embedding payloads in documents or certificates, and employing command obfuscation within scripts to evade signature-based defenses. This technique is commonly used by numerous threat groups, including APT41 and Lazarus Group, to hide malicious artifacts during initial access and subsequent execution.[/profile]

12456.name: T1056
12456.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]T1056, Input Capture, is a technique used for Collection and Credential Access on platforms including Windows, Linux, macOS, and Network Devices. It involves capturing user input to steal credentials or information, operating either transparently to the user through methods like Credential API Hooking or deceptively via mechanisms such as Web Portal Capture. Associated threat groups include Storm-1811, APT39, and APT42, and it is linked to vulnerabilities CVE-2022-41352 and CVE-2024-30088.

12457.name: Web Service
12457.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Web Service is identified as MITRE ATT&CK technique T1102 under the Command and Control tactic, applicable to Windows, Linux, macOS, and ESXi platforms. It involves adversaries using legitimate external web services like Google, Microsoft, or Twitter for command and control, blending traffic with common, pre-existing SSL/TLS-encrypted communications to hide operations and protect backend infrastructure. This technique is associated with groups like Gamaredon and FIN6, and can exploit vulnerabilities such as CVE-2021-44228.[/profile]

12458.name: Impair Defenses
12458.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Impair Defenses is a defense-evasion technique (MITRE ATT&CK T1562) applicable across Windows, Linux, macOS, and network platforms. It involves maliciously modifying a victim environment to hinder or disable defensive mechanisms, including preventative tools like firewalls and detection capabilities such as audit logging. Specific sub-techniques include impairing command history logging by manipulating environment variables like `HISTFILE` or `HISTCONTROL` on Unix systems and `PSReadLine` settings on Windows, as well as executing downgrade attacks to use less-secure software versions that lack security controls like logging. It is associated with threat groups including UNC3886 and APT38.[/profile]

12459.name: Input Capture
12459.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Input Capture, identified as T1056, is a Credential Access and Collection technique used across Windows, Linux, macOS, and Network Devices. It involves intercepting user input to steal credentials, employing methods like Credential API Hooking for transparent capture or deceptive Web Portal Capture on login pages. Associated threat groups include APT39 and APT42.

12460.name: Ingress Tool Transfer
12460.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Ingress Tool Transfer, identified as T1105, is a Command and Control tactic used across Windows, Linux, macOS, ESXi, and Network Devices. It involves transferring tools into a compromised environment via the C2 channel or protocols like FTP, using native utilities such as `certutil`, `PowerShell`'s `IEX(New-Object Net.WebClient).downloadString()`, `curl`, `scp`, `wget`, and package managers like `yum` or `winget`. Adversaries may also abuse cloud sync services like Dropbox or the Windows `search-ms` protocol for file delivery. This technique is foundational, enabling subsequent actions like Lateral Tool Transfer (T1570) and is associated with numerous threat groups including APT29 and Volt Typhoon.[/profile]

12461.name: Command and Scripting Interpreter
12461.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Command and Scripting Interpreter, designated as MITRE ATT&CK T1059, is an Execution tactic technique that abuses built-in or cross-platform interpreters to execute arbitrary commands. It operates across Windows, Linux, macOS, Network Devices, and cloud platforms. Adversaries use interpreters like Unix Shell, Windows Command Shell, PowerShell, Python, JavaScript, and Visual Basic, often embedding commands in initial access payloads, scripts, or macros, or executing them interactively via remote services. This technique is foundational, with numerous sub-techniques for specific interpreters, and is commonly associated with threat groups like APT37, FIN7, and Oilrig.[/profile]

12463.name: PoisonIvy
12463.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]PoisonIvy, also known as poison ivy, is a popular remote access tool (RAT) used by numerous threat groups including APT1, Tropic Trooper, Axiom, APT5, Mustang Panda, Gallium, PittyTiger, MenuPass, Dragonok, Elderwood, Molerats, IndigoZebra, TA428, and various Panda-associated clusters. Its technical behaviors involve exploitation for client execution (T1203), command and script execution via JavaScript (T1059.007) and Visual Basic (T1059.005), and virtualization/sandbox evasion (T1497). It primarily targets Windows platforms and has been associated with infrastructure such as the domains web.outlooksysm.net and outlooksysm.net.[/profile]

12464.name: PoisonIvy - S0012
12464.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]PoisonIvy, also known as S0012, is a remote access tool (RAT) used by numerous groups including APT1, Tropic Trooper, Axiom, APT5, Moafee, Mustang Panda, Gallium, PittyTiger, MenuPass, Admin@338, Dragonok, Elderwood, Molerats, and IndigoZebra. Its key behaviors include performing system checks for virtualization/sandbox evasion, exploiting client applications for execution, and using command and scripting interpreters like JavaScript. It targets Windows, Linux, and macOS platforms and has been associated with infrastructure such as the domains web.outlooksysm.net and outlooksysm.net.[/profile]

12465.name: unkown_apt_group
12465.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]This intrusion set is most likely the APT group MirrorFace, also known as backdoordiplomacy, cloudcomputating, backdip, and quarian. Its key malware includes LODEINFO, which abuses Office Application Startup for persistence, and it has also used tools like PoisonIvy and NOOPDOOR/NOOPLDR loaders. Its techniques involve Virtualization/Sandbox Evasion, System Checks, and Impair Defenses to disable security tools. The group is attributed to Chinese state-sponsored actors and primarily targets entities in Japan, as evidenced by its infrastructure and malware distribution. Its motivation is believed to be espionage, focusing on diplomatic and political organizations.[/profile]

12471.name: T1059.001
12471.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]T1059.001, named PowerShell, is a MITRE ATT&CK technique under the Execution tactic for Windows platforms. It involves adversaries abusing the PowerShell scripting environment to execute commands and scripts, often for discovery or code execution. This can be done directly via powershell.exe or indirectly through its underlying .NET assembly, enabling actions like downloading and running executables from the Internet, potentially in-memory to avoid disk. The technique is associated with numerous threat groups, including APT29, Lazarus Group, and MuddyWater.[/profile]

12472.name: T1203
12472.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Exploitation for Client Execution, designated T1203 under the Execution tactic, targets platforms including Windows, Linux, and macOS. This technique involves adversaries exploiting vulnerabilities in client applications like web browsers, Microsoft Office, or common third-party software (e.g., Adobe Reader) to achieve arbitrary code execution. Exploitation often occurs via user interaction with malicious links or documents from spearphishing or drive-by compromises, leveraging specific CVEs such as CVE-2017-0199. It is commonly used by numerous threat groups including APT28, Lazarus Group, and OilRig.

12473.name: T1497
12473.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]T1497, Virtualization/Sandbox Evasion, is a Defense Evasion and Discovery technique for Windows, Linux, and macOS. It involves detecting artifacts of virtual machine environments (VMEs) or sandboxes, such as security monitoring tools or lack of user activity, and then altering malware behavior to disengage, conceal core functions, or delay execution via sleep timers to evade analysis. Groups like Contagious Interview, Saint Bear, and DarkHotel have used this technique.[/profile]

12474.name: Visual Basic
12474.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Visual Basic, identified as T1059.005, is an Execution technique within the MITRE ATT&CK framework targeting Windows, Linux, and macOS platforms. Adversaries abuse this Microsoft programming language and its derivatives, VBA and VBScript, to execute malicious commands. Common mechanics include using VBScript to automate behaviors or embedding VBA macros into spearphishing attachments to run payloads. It is also leveraged in techniques like PubPrn for proxy execution and VBA Stomping to hide malicious code within documents. Numerous threat groups, including FIN7, Lazarus, and APT32, have employed this technique.

12475.name: T1497.001
12475.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]T1497.001, also known as System Checks, is a Defense Evasion and Discovery technique within the MITRE ATT&CK framework applicable to Windows, Linux, and macOS. It involves adversaries performing automated checks for artifacts indicative of a virtual machine or sandbox environment, such as specific hardware, processes, file system entries, or registry keys. If a virtual environment is detected, malware may alter its behavior, disengage, or exit to avoid analysis. This technique is associated with groups like Gamaredon Group, Evilnum, Darkhotel, OilRig, and Volt Typhoon.

12476.name: T1059.003
12476.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]T1059.003, known as Windows Command Shell, is an execution technique within the MITRE ATT&CK framework targeting Windows platforms. It involves adversaries abusing the native cmd.exe prompt to run commands and payloads, either interactively or via batch files (.bat, .cmd). The shell can be invoked remotely through services like SSH, and it is commonly leveraged by numerous threat groups, including APT28, Lazarus Group, and FIN7, for direct command execution and to run scripts as part of broader attack sequences.

12477.name: T1059.007
12477.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]T1059.007, also known as JavaScript, is an Execution technique within the MITRE ATTACK framework applicable to Windows, Linux, and macOS platforms. It involves abusing platform-specific JavaScript implementations like JScript on Windows or JavaScript for Automation (JXA) on macOS to execute adversary-controlled code. This can occur through malicious web scripts in drive-by compromises, by running compiled JXA scripts via command-line utilities like `osascript`, or by leveraging scripting engines integrated with system components. The technique is commonly associated with groups like FIN7, Turla, and MuddyWater and is frequently paired with obfuscation to hide malicious payloads.

12478.name: Virtualization/Sandbox Evasion
12478.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Virtualization/Sandbox Evasion is MITRE technique T1497, used for Defense Evasion and Discovery on Windows, Linux, and macOS. It involves detecting analysis environments by checking for artifacts like security monitoring tools, virtual machine hardware/processes, or registry keys. Malware may alter its behavior, use sleep timers, or check for user activity to avoid sandboxes, and adversaries may search for these artifacts before deploying additional payloads.[/profile]

12479.name: Exploitation for Client Execution
12479.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Exploitation for Client Execution, identified as T1203, is an execution tactic targeting macOS, Linux, and Windows platforms. It involves exploiting vulnerabilities in client applications like web browsers, Microsoft Office, or Adobe Reader to achieve arbitrary code execution. This technique is often delivered via spearphishing links or drive-by compromises, requiring user interaction for document-based exploits but sometimes executing automatically in browsers. It is associated with numerous threat groups and specific CVEs including CVE-2022-24934 and CVE-2024-7262.[/profile]

12480.name: PowerShell
12480.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]PowerShell is a Windows command-line and scripting environment used for execution, categorized as MITRE ATT&CK T1059.001 under the Execution tactic. Adversaries abuse it to run commands locally or remotely via cmdlets like Start-Process and Invoke-Command, download and execute payloads from the internet, and run scripts directly in memory without disk interaction. Execution can also occur without powershell.exe by leveraging the underlying System.Management.Automation assembly through .NET interfaces.[/profile]

12481.name: System Checks
12481.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]System Checks is a Defense Evasion and Discovery technique used on Windows, Linux, and macOS. Adversaries perform various checks to detect and avoid virtualization and analysis environments (VMEs or sandboxes). This involves using tools like WMI, PowerShell, and registry queries to examine system properties, hardware, processes, and installed software for VME artifacts. If a virtual environment is detected, the malware may alter its behavior, disengage, or exit to evade analysis. The technique is associated with groups like Gamaredon Group, OilRig, and Volt Typhoon.[/profile]

12482.name: JavaScript
12482.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]JavaScript is identified as MITRE ATT&CK technique T1059.007 (Command and Scripting Interpreter), primarily used for the Execution tactic on Windows, Linux, and macOS platforms. It is a platform-independent scripting language abused to run malicious code, often executed via web browsers in drive-by compromises or through runtime environments like Node.js. Adversaries commonly host or download these text-based scripts, frequently obfuscating them to evade detection. Specific implementations include JScript on Windows and JavaScript for Automation (JXA) on macOS, which can be run via utilities like osascript or compiled in memory using the OSAKit Framework.[/profile]

12483.name: Windows Command Shell
12483.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Windows Command Shell, identified as T1059.003, is an Execution tactic technique within the MITRE ATT&CK framework targeting Windows platforms. Adversaries abuse the native cmd.exe shell to execute commands and payloads, either as single commands or interactively with input/output forwarded over a command and control channel. It can be invoked remotely via services like SSH and is commonly used to run batch files (.bat, .cmd) for scripting repetitive tasks or deploying commands across multiple systems. Numerous threat groups, including FIN7, Lazarus Group, and APT28, have employed this technique.[/profile]

12485.name: LODEINFO
12485.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]LODEINFO, also known as lodeinfo, is a malware attributed to the MirrorFace group. It is deployed via phishing emails containing malicious links to ZIP archives with LNK files that download and execute an HTA script. For persistence, it abuses Microsoft Office application startup mechanisms (T1137). It performs process injection by launching svchost.exe and injecting a payload (T1055), and communicates with command-and-control servers over encrypted channels (T1573). Its primary target is Japan, and it has been distributed via links such as https://45.76.222.130/template.dotm.[/profile]

12490.name: T1055
12490.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]T1055, Process Injection, is a Defense Evasion and Privilege Escalation technique for Windows, Linux, and macOS. It involves executing arbitrary code within the address space of a separate, legitimate live process to evade detection and potentially gain elevated privileges. Specific methods include Dynamic-link Library Injection, which can be performed by abusing tools like `mavinject.exe` with commands such as `mavinject.exe PID /INJECTRUNNING PATH_DLL`, and Thread Local Storage (TLS) Callback Injection, which manipulates pointers in a portable executable to redirect execution before the legitimate entry point.

12494.name: T1573
12494.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]T1573, Encrypted Channel, is a Command and Control tactic used across Windows, Linux, macOS, ESXi, and Network Devices. It involves using encryption algorithms to hide C2 traffic, with implementations potentially vulnerable if secret keys are embedded within malware. A specific sub-technique, T1573.002 Asymmetric Cryptography, uses public-key algorithms like RSA for initial key establishment, often within protocols like SSL/TLS. This method is employed by groups including APT29, OilRig, and FIN6, and can be supported by adversaries creating self-signed digital certificates.

12495.name: T1137
12495.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]T1137, Office Application Startup, is a persistence technique within the MITRE ATT&CK framework targeting Windows and Office Suite platforms. It involves abusing Microsoft Office application startup mechanisms, such as Outlook rules, forms, Home Page settings, Office Template Macros, and add-ins, to maintain access when an Office-based application is launched. This technique has been used by groups including Gamaredon Group and APT32.

12496.name: T1566
12496.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]T1566, known as Phishing, is an Initial Access technique applicable to Windows, Linux, macOS, and SaaS platforms. It involves adversaries sending fraudulent electronic messages, such as emails with malicious attachments or links, to trick victims into executing code or revealing credentials. This can be targeted (spearphishing) or broad, and may utilize third-party services, social engineering, email spoofing, or thread hijacking to appear legitimate and evade detection.[/profile]

12497.name: Office Application Startup
12497.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Office Application Startup is the MITRE ATT&CK technique T1137 under the Persistence tactic, targeting Windows and the Office Suite. It involves abusing Microsoft Office's startup mechanisms to execute malicious code each time an application like Word or Excel launches. Specific sub-techniques include using Office Template Macros (T1137.001) by modifying files like Normal.dotm, abusing the "Office Test" Registry key (T1137.002) to load a DLL, and leveraging malicious add-ins (T1137.006). It has been associated with threat groups including APT28, APT32, Gamaredon Group, MuddyWater, and Naikon.[/profile]

12498.name: Encrypted Channel
12498.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Encrypted Channel is MITRE ATT&CK technique T1573 under the Command and Control tactic, applicable to Windows, Linux, macOS, ESXi, and Network Devices. It involves adversaries using encryption algorithms to conceal C2 traffic, separate from any inherent protocol encryption. This technique can be vulnerable to reverse engineering if secret keys are embedded within malware or its configuration files, and it is associated with groups like APT29, BITTER, Tropic Trooper, and Magic Hound.[/profile]

12500.name: Phishing
12500.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Phishing, identified as MITRE ATT&CK technique T1566, is an Initial Access tactic that targets platforms including Windows, Linux, macOS, Office Suite, Identity Provider, and SaaS. It involves sending fraudulent electronic messages, such as emails with malicious attachments or links, to trick victims into executing code, often leveraging social engineering by posing as a trusted source. Evasive methods include email spoofing, thread hijacking, and manipulating email headers or metadata from compromised accounts. It is distinct from T1598 (Phishing for Information), which focuses on credential harvesting rather than code execution.[/profile]

12501.name: Process Injection
12501.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Process Injection is formally identified as MITRE ATT&CK technique T1055, used for Defense Evasion and Privilege Escalation across Windows, Linux, and macOS. The core technique involves executing arbitrary code within the address space of a separate, legitimate live process to evade detection and potentially gain elevated privileges. This is achieved through various sub-techniques like DLL injection, which uses Windows API calls such as VirtualAllocEx and CreateRemoteThread, and PE injection, which writes and executes code directly in process memory. Adversaries, including groups like APT41 and Wizard Spider, also leverage methods like proc memory injection on Linux by manipulating the /proc filesystem to overwrite a process's memory map. The technique is associated with several CVEs, including CVE-2020-1380 and CVE-2022-41328.[/profile]

12503.name: NOOPDOOR
12503.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]NOOPDOOR is a malware targeting Japan, using domains like foeake.org, mangoaiml.com, paunsonaz.com, temmans.com, and torefrog.com. Its techniques include abusing software deployment tools (T1072) for execution and lateral movement, manipulating access tokens (T1134) for privilege escalation and defense evasion, compiling source code after delivery (T1027.004) to evade detection, impairing defenses (T1562) by disabling security tools, and bypassing User Account Control (T1548.002) to elevate privileges on Windows systems.[/profile]

12504.name: NOOPLDR
12504.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]NOOPLDR is a malware loader associated with the GuLoader family, which is used to deploy secondary payloads like NetWire RAT. Its key TTPs include impairing defenses (T1562), establishing C2 via dynamic resolution (T1568), lateral tool transfer (T1570), and using encrypted channels (T1573). It is delivered via phishing (T1566) and has been linked to infrastructure domains such as mangoaiml.com, torefrog.com, inbullar.com, temmans.com, and saraosting.com. The malware targets Windows platforms and has been associated with APT33 in some campaigns.[/profile]

12521.name: T1127
12521.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Trusted Developer Utilities Proxy Execution, designated T1127, is a Defense Evasion technique for Windows. It involves adversaries abusing signed developer utilities (e.g., msxsl.exe, WinDbg) to proxy the execution of malicious code, leveraging the trusted status of these tools to bypass application control solutions like Smart App Control. The technique is also referenced in other methods, such as XSL Script Processing, where msxsl.exe is used to execute scripts embedded in stylesheet files.

12522.name: T1047
12522.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]T1047, known as Windows Management Instrumentation (WMI), is an execution technique for Windows. It involves abusing the WMI infrastructure to execute malicious commands and payloads locally or remotely, often via tools like `wmic.exe` or PowerShell. A specific variation, "Squiblytwo," uses WMI with the `/FORMAT` switch to invoke scripts embedded in XSL files for evasion. It is commonly leveraged by groups like Lazarus and MuddyWater and can interact with remote services like WinRM.

12523.name: T1190
12523.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]T1190, Exploit Public-Facing Application, is an initial-access technique targeting platforms including Windows, Linux, macOS, Network Devices, Containers, IaaS, and ESXi. It involves exploiting weaknesses like software bugs or misconfigurations in internet-facing systems such as web servers, databases (e.g., SQL), standard services (e.g., SMB, SSH), and device management protocols (e.g., SNMP). This can provide initial network access and, in cloud or containerized environments, may lead to compromise of underlying instances or APIs. The technique is commonly associated with numerous threat groups, including APT28, APT29, and Volt Typhoon.

12524.name: T1053
12524.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]T1053, Scheduled Task/Job, is an execution, persistence, and privilege-escalation technique applicable to Windows, Linux, macOS, ESXi, and Containers. It involves abusing built-in OS utilities like cron or Task Scheduler to execute malicious code at specified times or upon system events, enabling recurring execution, persistence, and privilege context manipulation. This method can be used remotely with proper authentication and is often leveraged in conjunction with other techniques, such as Group Policy modification for deployment or as part of time-based evasion strategies.

12525.name: T1543
12525.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]T1543, Create or Modify System Process, is a MITRE ATT&CK technique for Persistence and Privilege Escalation on Windows, Linux, macOS, and Container platforms. Adversaries install or alter system-level processes like Windows services, Linux daemons, or macOS launch agents/daemons to execute malicious payloads at system startup or on a schedule, often to gain persistence. This can involve commands such as `launchctl load -w` on macOS. The technique is related to vulnerabilities like CVE-2023-46604 and the abuse of system services for execution.[/profile]

12526.name: T1568
12526.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]T1568 (Dynamic Resolution) is a command and control technique used on Windows, Linux, macOS, and ESXi platforms. It involves malware dynamically establishing connections to C2 infrastructure by using a shared algorithm to adjust parameters like domain names, IP addresses, or port numbers, often to evade detection or as a fallback mechanism. A specific sub-technique, T1568.003 (DNS Calculation), uses calculations on DNS response data to determine the IP and port for C2 traffic. It has been associated with groups including APT29, Gamaredon Group, and Transparent Tribe.

12527.name: Exploit Public-Facing Application
12527.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Exploit Public-Facing Application, identified as T1190, is an Initial Access tactic targeting platforms including Windows, Linux, macOS, Network Devices, Containers, IaaS, and ESXi. It involves exploiting software bugs, glitches, or misconfigurations in internet-facing systems like web servers, databases (e.g., SQL), standard services (e.g., SMB, SSH), and device management protocols (e.g., SNMP, Smart Install) to gain initial network access. This can provide a path to compromise underlying cloud instances or containers and exploit weak identity management. Specific vulnerabilities like CVE-2020-1380 and CVE-2024-1709 are linked to this technique.[/profile]

12528.name: T1546
12528.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]T1546, Event Triggered Execution, is a persistence and privilege-escalation technique for Windows, Linux, macOS, IaaS, SaaS, and Office Suite platforms. Adversaries abuse system mechanisms that monitor and subscribe to specific events—like logons or application runs—to trigger execution of malicious code. By creating or modifying these event triggers to point to their payload, they can maintain persistent access, and by proxying execution through high-permission accounts like SYSTEM, they can escalate privileges.

12529.name: T1574
12529.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]T1574, Hijack Execution Flow, is a Defense Evasion, Persistence, and Privilege Escalation technique applicable to Windows, Linux, and macOS. It involves adversaries manipulating how an operating system locates and loads programs or libraries to execute malicious payloads. A specific sub-technique, Path Interception by Search Order Hijacking (T1574.008), exploits when programs call executables without a full path, allowing an adversary to place a malicious file with the same name in the calling program's directory to be executed instead. This method can also be used to target system components like LSASS drivers for persistent execution.

12530.name: T1570
12530.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]T1570 (Lateral Tool Transfer) is a Lateral Movement technique applicable to Windows, Linux, macOS, and ESXi platforms. It involves transferring tools or files between compromised systems within a victim network to stage operations. Adversaries achieve this using inherent file sharing protocols like SMB/Windows Admin Shares or authenticated RDP connections, as well as native tools such as scp, rsync, curl, sftp, or FTP. In some cases, they may leverage web services like Dropbox or OneDrive via automatically synced folders. This technique is often used in conjunction with automated data collection to identify and move files.

12531.name: T1569
12531.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]T1569, known as System Services, is an execution technique within the MITRE ATT&CK framework applicable to Windows, Linux, and macOS. It involves adversaries abusing system services or daemons to execute commands or programs, either locally or remotely, by interacting with or creating these services. This method can facilitate persistence when services are set to run at boot, but is also used for one-time execution. The technique is associated with vulnerabilities like CVE-2023-46604 and CVE-2023-42793, and related sub-techniques include Launchctl for agent execution.[/profile]

12532.name: Trusted Developer Utilities Proxy Execution
12532.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Trusted Developer Utilities Proxy Execution is MITRE ATT&CK technique T1127 under the Defense Evasion tactic for Windows platforms. It involves adversaries abusing legitimate, often digitally signed, software development utilities—such as debuggers or compilers—to proxy and execute malicious payloads. This method exploits the trusted status of these tools to bypass application control solutions, including Windows Smart App Control, by hijacking their reputation to run arbitrary code.

12533.name: Dynamic Resolution
12533.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Dynamic Resolution, also known as T1568, is a Command and Control technique used on Windows, Linux, macOS, and ESXi platforms. It involves malware using a shared algorithm with adversary infrastructure to dynamically adjust C2 parameters like domain names, IP addresses, or port numbers, enabling evasion and facilitating reconnection as a fallback channel. It is associated with groups including APT29, Gamaredon Group, and Bitter.

12534.name: Create or Modify System Process
12534.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]The entity is the MITRE ATT&CK technique "Create or Modify System Process" (T1543), used for Persistence and Privilege Escalation on Windows, Linux, macOS, and container platforms. It involves adversaries installing or altering system-level processes like Windows services, Linux daemons, or macOS launch agents to execute malicious payloads at system startup or on a scheduled basis, thereby maintaining access and potentially escalating to root or SYSTEM privileges.

12535.name: Scheduled Task/Job
12535.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Scheduled Task/Job is MITRE ATT&CK technique T1053 under the Execution, Persistence, and Privilege Escalation tactics, applicable to Windows, Linux, macOS, ESXi, and Containers. It involves abusing OS utilities like Windows Task Scheduler (via schtasks, WMI, or PowerShell's Invoke-CimMethod), cron, at, or launchd to schedule malicious code execution at specific times or system startup for persistence, lateral movement, or privilege escalation. Tasks can be scheduled remotely on Windows with proper authentication, and adversaries may hide tasks by deleting Security Descriptor registry values. This technique is linked to vulnerabilities like CVE-2020-14883.[/profile]

12536.name: Windows Management Instrumentation
12536.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Windows Management Instrumentation, identified as T1047 within the MITRE ATT&CK framework, is an Execution technique for Windows platforms. It abuses the built-in WMI infrastructure to execute commands and payloads locally or remotely, with remote access facilitated by protocols like DCOM (port 135) or WinRM (ports 5985/5986). Adversaries use tools like the deprecated `wmic.exe` (e.g., for commands like `wmic.exe Shadowcopy Delete`) or interact programmatically via PowerShell, COM APIs, or `wbemtool.exe` to perform actions ranging from discovery to system manipulation. It is commonly used by numerous threat groups for execution and lateral movement.[/profile]

12537.name: Event Triggered Execution
12537.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Event Triggered Execution is MITRE ATT&CK technique T1546, used for Persistence and Privilege Escalation across Windows, Linux, macOS, IaaS, SaaS, and Office Suite platforms. It involves adversaries abusing system or cloud event monitoring mechanisms to trigger malicious code execution upon specific events like logons or application activity. This execution is often proxied through higher-permission accounts (e.g., SYSTEM) for privilege escalation, with a common sub-technique being Windows Management Instrumentation (WMI) event subscription, where filters and consumers are installed to run code.

12538.name: Hijack Execution Flow
12538.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Hijack Execution Flow (T1574) is a defense evasion, persistence, and privilege escalation technique used on Windows, Linux, and macOS. It involves adversaries executing malicious payloads by manipulating how the operating system locates and runs programs or libraries. Specific methods include poisoning file directories or the Windows Registry, hijacking the KernelCallbackTable in a process's PEB to redirect function calls, and using VDSO hijacking to redirect library calls in Linux processes. This technique is associated with vulnerabilities like CVE-2019-0859 and CVE-2019-0797.[/profile]

12539.name: Lateral Tool Transfer
12539.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Lateral Tool Transfer (T1570) is a Lateral Movement technique used on Windows, Linux, macOS, and ESXi platforms. It involves copying adversary tools or files between compromised internal systems to stage for further operations. This transfer is executed using inherent file sharing protocols like SMB/Windows Admin Shares or authenticated RDP sessions, as well as native system tools including scp, rsync, curl, sftp, and ftp. Adversaries may also abuse syncing web services like Dropbox or OneDrive for this internal file movement.[/profile]

12540.name: System Services
12540.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]System Services is a technique for execution, identified as T1569 in the MITRE ATT&CK framework, applicable to Windows, Linux, and macOS platforms. It involves adversaries abusing system services or daemons to execute commands or programs, which can be done by interacting with or creating services either locally or remotely. This method can be used for one-time execution or leveraged for persistence by configuring services to run at system boot, as seen in related techniques like Create or Modify System Process (T1543).

12541.name: Modify Registry
12541.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Modify Registry, identified as MITRE ATT&CK technique T1112, is a defense evasion and persistence technique used on Windows platforms. Adversaries interact with the Windows Registry using tools like Reg.exe or remote APIs to hide configuration data, impair defenses, store malicious payloads, or maintain persistence. Specific modifications include prepending keys with null characters to hide them, altering service `binPath` or `ImagePath` to execute adversary-controlled code, and changing file association commands in `HKEY_CLASSES_ROOT` to run arbitrary programs. It is associated with vulnerabilities like CVE-2020-1380 and groups including APT41 and Wizard Spider.[profile]

12544.name: Amadey - S1025
12544.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Amadey, also known as Amadey - S1025, is a Trojan bot used since at least 2018 and has been associated with threat groups TA505 and KIMSUKY. Its key behaviors include establishing persistence, injecting a proxy bot into memory, and accepting command-line options for installation and execution. It is delivered via phishing and user execution, and it performs OS credential dumping and queries the Windows Registry. The malware targets Windows platforms and has used infrastructure including compromised WordPress sites for command and control, such as okesense.oketheme.com and coworkingdeamicis.com.[/profile]

12545.name: KazuarV2
12545.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]KazuarV2 is a malware variant, also known as Kazuar v2. It is attributed to the Turla group and is maintained in parallel with Kazuar v3, sharing updated backdoor commands. Its technical behaviors include user execution (T1204), code signing for defense evasion (T1553.002), OS credential dumping (T1003), and phishing for initial access (T1566). It targets Windows systems and has been deployed via PteroPaste, with observed infrastructure including domains like vitantgroup.com and brauche-it.de.[/profile]

12547.name: Epic
12547.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Epic, also known as epic, is a backdoor malware family attributed to the Turla threat group. Its key technical behaviors include leveraging User Execution via phishing to gain initial access, performing OS Credential Dumping, and using Process Injection and Windows Management Instrumentation (WMI) for execution and defense evasion. It primarily targets Windows platforms and utilizes a large network of compromised servers for command and control, with observed infrastructure including domains like plagnol-charpentier.fr and brauche-it.de, and it has been used in attacks against Ukraine.[/profile]

12548.name: unkown_apt_group
12548.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]This intrusion set is most likely the APT group Turla, also known as Snake and Uroburos. Its key malware includes the sophisticated Uroburos rootkit, the TinyTurla-NG backdoor, and tools like Chisel. Its technical profile involves disabling Windows Event Logging (T1562.002), using asymmetric cryptography for C2, and establishing persistence via Windows services. The group is attributed to Russian origins. It has historically targeted entities in the Philippines and uses infrastructure such as files.philbendeck.com, buy-new-car.com, and carleasingguru.com. Its operations are believed to be espionage-motivated.[/profile]

12579.name: T1018
12579.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]T1018, also known as Remote System Discovery, is a Discovery tactic technique applicable to Windows, Linux, macOS, ESXi, and Network Devices. It involves adversaries enumerating other systems on a network to enable lateral movement, using utilities like ping, `net view`, or `esxcli network diag ping` on ESXi. They may also analyze local host files, ARP cache, or execute network device CLI commands such as `show cdp neighbors` and `show arp`. The technique is associated with numerous threat groups including Volt Typhoon and APT41, and can be facilitated by vulnerabilities like CVE-2020-14883.[/profile]

12580.name: T1003
12580.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]T1003, OS Credential Dumping, is a Credential Access technique for macOS, Linux, and Windows. It involves dumping credentials from OS caches, memory, or structures to obtain hashes or clear-text passwords, which are then used for lateral movement. Associated groups include APT28 and APT29, and it is related to the abuse of local and domain accounts.

12581.name: T1078
12581.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]T1078, Valid Accounts, is a technique used across Initial Access, Persistence, Privilege Escalation, and Defense Evasion on platforms including Windows, Linux, macOS, and cloud services. It involves adversaries obtaining and abusing credentials of existing accounts, including inactive ones, to bypass access controls, gain persistent access to remote systems like VPNs and network devices, and pivot across the network without deploying malware, making detection difficult. This technique is foundational and can enable other actions, such as accessing SMB admin shares for lateral movement.[profile]

12582.name: T1204
12582.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]User Execution is a technique under the MITRE ATT&CK ID T1204, categorized under the Execution tactic and applicable across Windows, Linux, macOS, Containers, and IaaS platforms. It involves adversaries deceiving users into performing specific actions to execute malicious code, such as opening malicious documents or links delivered via phishing, clicking on files placed in shared directories, enabling remote access tools, running malicious browser JavaScript, or manually copying and pasting malicious commands. This technique is frequently associated with threat groups like Scattered Spider and LAPSUS$.

12583.name: T1553.002
12583.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]T1553.002, known as Code Signing, is a Defense Evasion technique applicable to macOS and Windows platforms. It involves adversaries creating, acquiring, or stealing digital certificates to sign their malware, resulting in a valid signature that can bypass security policies requiring signed code for execution. This differs from techniques that use invalid signatures and is not typically used on Linux systems.

12584.name: T1133
12584.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]External Remote Services (T1133) is an initial-access and persistence technique used across Windows, Linux, macOS, and container platforms. Adversaries leverage externally accessible services like VPNs, Citrix, Windows Remote Management, VNC, or exposed container APIs (e.g., Docker, Kubernetes) to gain and maintain network access, often requiring valid accounts. It serves as a redundant access mechanism, and in container environments, persistence can be achieved through unauthenticated exposed services. The technique is associated with groups including APT29, Volt Typhoon, and Scattered Spider.[/profile]

12585.name: Valid Accounts
12585.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Valid Accounts is technique T1078 within the MITRE ATT&CK framework, used for Initial Access, Persistence, Privilege Escalation, and Defense Evasion across platforms including Windows, Linux, macOS, and cloud services. It involves adversaries obtaining and abusing credentials of existing legitimate accounts, such as domain, local, or cloud accounts, to bypass access controls, move laterally, and maintain persistent access without deploying malware. This technique is foundational, often enabling follow-on actions like Account Discovery or Account Manipulation, and is extensively used by numerous threat groups including APT29, FIN7, and Scattered Spider.

12586.name: User Execution
12586.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]User Execution, identified as T1204, is an Execution tactic technique targeting macOS, Linux, Windows, Containers, and IaaS platforms. It relies on a user performing specific actions to execute malicious code, such as opening a malicious document or link delivered via phishing, clicking on a file placed in a shared directory, or being deceived into enabling remote access tools, running malicious browser JavaScript, or manually copying and pasting malicious code. This technique is commonly associated with threat groups like Scattered Spider and LAPSUS$.[/profile]

12587.name: OS Credential Dumping
12587.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]OS Credential Dumping is technique T1003 under the Credential Access tactic, targeting Windows, Linux, and macOS platforms. It involves adversaries dumping credential material like password hashes or clear-text passwords from operating system components such as memory, caches, or security structures. This stolen data is often used for lateral movement, and the technique is associated with tools like Mimikatz and numerous threat groups including APT28 and APT32. Credentials can also be extracted from system backups or saved virtual machine files.[/profile]

12588.name: Masquerading
12588.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Masquerading is the MITRE ATT&CK technique T1036 under Defense Evasion, applicable to Windows, Linux, macOS, ESXi, and Containers. It involves manipulating the name, location, or metadata of malicious files or processes to appear legitimate, such as by renaming system utilities, using deceptive file extensions, or assigning legitimate-looking service names to evade detection. The technique is commonly used by threat groups like APT28, Sandworm Team, and OilRig.

12589.name: Deobfuscate/Decode Files or Information
12589.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Deobfuscate/Decode Files or Information is MITRE ATT&CK technique T1140 under the Defense Evasion tactic, applicable to Windows, Linux, macOS, and ESXi platforms. It involves adversaries using separate mechanisms to decode or deobfuscate hidden artifacts, such as employing built-in malware functionality or system utilities like certutil to decode a remote access tool from a certificate file, or using Windows commands like copy /b to reassemble binary fragments into a malicious payload. This technique is often a prerequisite for User Execution and is associated with numerous threat groups including APT28, Lazarus Group, and FIN7.[/profile]

12590.name: External Remote Services
12590.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]External Remote Services (T1133) is an Initial Access and Persistence technique used on Windows, Linux, macOS, and Containers. Adversaries leverage externally-facing services like VPNs, Citrix, RDP, VNC, and SSH to gain network access, often using Valid Accounts obtained through credential theft. Persistence can be achieved by using these services as a redundant access channel or by exploiting exposed, unauthenticated services in containerized environments, such as Docker or Kubernetes APIs. The technique is associated with numerous threat groups, including APT28, APT29, and Scattered Spider.[/profile]

12591.name: Remote System Discovery
12591.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Remote System Discovery is the MITRE ATT&CK technique T1018 under the Discovery tactic, applicable to Windows, Linux, macOS, ESXi, and Network Devices. It involves adversaries discovering other systems on a network for lateral movement using utilities like Ping, `net view`, or `esxcli network diag ping`, analyzing local host files or ARP cache, and employing network device commands such as `show cdp neighbors`. It is commonly used by groups like Volt Typhoon, Turla, and APT41.

12592.name: System Network Configuration Discovery
12592.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]System Network Configuration Discovery, identified as T1016, is a Discovery tactic technique used across Windows, Linux, macOS, ESXi, and Network Devices. Adversaries gather network details like IP and MAC addresses using built-in OS utilities such as arp, ipconfig/ifconfig, nbtstat, and route. On network devices, they may use CLI commands like `show ip route`, and on ESXi, commands like `esxcli network nic list` and `esxcli network ip interface ipv4 get`. This information is used to map the network and plan subsequent actions.

12593.name: Code Signing
12593.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Code Signing, identified as T1553.002 within the MITRE ATT&CK framework, is a Defense Evasion technique applicable to Windows and macOS platforms. It involves adversaries creating, acquiring, or stealing digital certificates to apply valid signatures to their malicious binaries. This process provides a false level of authenticity, making the software appear legitimate and untampered with to users and security tools, thereby bypassing policies that require signed code to execute. The technique is distinct from using invalid signatures and is commonly used by threat actors like Lazarus Group, FIN7, and APT41.

12595.name: File and Directory Discovery
12595.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]File and Directory Discovery is technique T1083 under the Discovery tactic. It operates on Windows, Linux, macOS, ESXi, and Network Devices. Adversaries enumerate files and directories to gather information, using command shell utilities like `dir`, `tree`, `ls`, `find`, and `locate`. They may also use custom tools or network device CLI commands such as `show flash` or `nvram`. This reconnaissance helps shape subsequent attack behaviors.[/profile]

12596.name: Query Registry
12596.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Query Registry is the MITRE ATT&CK technique T1012 under the Discovery tactic, targeting Windows platforms. It involves adversaries gathering system intelligence by querying the Windows Registry for configuration, software, and security data, often using the built-in Reg utility (reg.exe) to inform follow-on attack decisions. This technique is associated with groups like APT41, Lazarus, and Volt Typhoon, and it can be used to find insecurely stored credentials, as illustrated by commands such as `reg query HKLM /f password /t REG_SZ /s`.

12597.name: System Information Discovery
12597.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]System Information Discovery is the MITRE ATT&CK technique T1082 under the Discovery tactic, targeting platforms including Windows, Linux, macOS, ESXi, Network Devices, and IaaS. It involves adversaries gathering detailed OS and hardware data like version, patches, and architecture to inform follow-on actions. Technical execution includes using tools like `systeminfo` on Windows, the `systemsetup` command on macOS with privileges, network device CLI commands such as `show version`, ESXi `esxcli` utilities like `system version get`, and querying cloud provider APIs (AWS, GCP, Azure) for instance metadata. This information aids in payload development and target selection.

12599.name: Wainscot
12599.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Wainscot is a malware entity. It employs techniques including Trusted Relationship for initial access, Keylogging for credential theft, Web Shell for persistence, Screen Capture for data collection, and System Owner/User Discovery for reconnaissance. Its infrastructure is associated with domains like hostelhotels.net and connectotels.net. It has been observed targeting locations including Afghanistan, British Indian Ocean Territory, and India, and may exploit vulnerabilities such as CVE-2022-38028.[/profile]

12600.name: CrimsonRAT
12600.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]CrimsonRAT, also known as Oblique RAT, is a remote access trojan attributed to Operation C-Major. It employs techniques such as User Execution via malicious documents and Account Discovery to enumerate valid accounts. The malware targets Windows systems and uses C2 infrastructure including domains like connectotels.net and hostelhotels.net, along with IP addresses such as 151.106.14.125 and 23.254.119.118, to exfiltrate data from victims primarily in South Asia, including Pakistan, Afghanistan, and India.[/profile]

12601.name: Statuezy
12601.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Statuezy is a malware that exploits vulnerability CVE-2022-38028 for initial access and uses infrastructure like hostelhotels.net and connectotels.net. Its behaviors include data collection from information repositories, account and software discovery, abuse of trusted relationships, and credential theft from password stores. It has been deployed against targets in Pakistan, Afghanistan, the British Indian Ocean Territory, and India.[/profile]

12603.name: MiniPocket
12603.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]MiniPocket is a malware that uses the CVE-2022-38028 vulnerability for initial access, establishes persistence via a Web Shell, and performs Keylogging and Screen Capture for credential and data collection. It communicates with infrastructure such as connectotels.net and hostelhotels.net. Its operations have been observed targeting systems in Afghanistan, British Indian Ocean Territory, and India.[/profile]

12604.name: TwoDash
12604.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]TwoDash is a malware entity. It is associated with the attack patterns Data from Information Repositories (T1213), Account Discovery (T1087), Trusted Relationship (T1199), Software Discovery (T1518), and Credentials from Password Stores (T1555), indicating behaviors for initial access, credential theft, and data collection. Its infrastructure includes domains like hostelhotels.net and connectotels.net. It has been observed targeting locations including Pakistan, Afghanistan, British Indian Ocean Territory, and India, and may exploit vulnerability CVE-2022-38028.[/profile]

12605.name: TinyTurla - S0668
12605.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]TinyTurla - S0668, also known as TinyTurla, is a backdoor attributed to the Russian-based Turla group. It is installed via a Windows Service and stores its C2 server list and authentication password in the Windows registry. Its key TTPs include exploiting Trusted Relationships for initial access, deploying a Web Shell for persistence, and using Keylogging and Screen Capture for credential and information collection. It primarily targets Windows platforms, with infrastructure involving domains like connectotels.net and hostelhotels.net, and it has exploited vulnerabilities such as CVE-2022-38028.[/profile]

12615.name: T1199
12615.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]This entity is the MITRE ATT&CK technique T1199, known as Trusted Relationship, which falls under the Initial Access tactic and targets platforms including Windows, Linux, macOS, and cloud services like IaaS and SaaS. It involves an adversary compromising or leveraging an organization that has existing, trusted access to an intended victim, such as IT service providers, managed security providers, or cloud infrastructure contractors, to gain network entry. This access often involves abusing the valid accounts of these third parties. In specific cloud scenarios, like Office 365, compromising a Microsoft partner account can allow an adversary to abuse delegated administrator permissions to gain control over a client tenant. The technique is associated with threat groups including APT28, APT29, and Hafnium.

12617.name: DLL Side-Loading
12617.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]DLL Side-Loading is a technique identified as T1574.002 under the MITRE ATT&CK framework, falling under the Persistence tactic and primarily targeting the Windows platform. It involves an adversary planting a malicious DLL alongside a legitimate, vulnerable application and then invoking that application, which causes the system's loader to execute the malicious DLL from the local directory due to the DLL search order. This method masks malicious actions under a trusted process, and payloads may be encrypted or obfuscated until loaded into memory. The technique is associated with vulnerabilities like CVE-2022-38028 and is distinct from general DLL search order hijacking as it requires the active planting and invocation of the host application.[/profile]

12618.name: T1547.001
12618.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]The attack pattern T1547.001, known as Registry Run Keys / Startup Folder, is a persistence and privilege-escalation technique within the MITRE ATT&CK framework for Windows. It works by adding malicious program references to specific Windows Registry run keys—such as HKEY_CURRENT_USER\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run—or by placing executables in system startup folders like C:\Users\[Username]\AppData\Roaming\Microsoft\Windows\Start Menu\Programs\Startup. This causes the referenced program to execute automatically upon user login, running under the user's context and permissions. The technique is commonly exploited by numerous threat groups, including APT28, Lazarus Group, and FIN7, to maintain persistent access.

12619.name: T1505.003
12619.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]T1505.003, also known as Web Shell, is a persistence technique within the MITRE ATT&CK framework applicable to Windows, Linux, macOS, and Network Devices. It involves placing a malicious web script on an accessible server to provide adversaries with a persistent gateway into a network, often offering functions for command execution or a command-line interface. This technique is frequently associated with groups like APT28, APT29, and Volt Typhoon and is commonly deployed by exploiting vulnerabilities such as CVE-2021-26857 and CVE-2023-32315.

12620.name: T1056.001
12620.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]T1056.001, known as Keylogging, is a technique within the Credential Access and Collection tactics targeting macOS, Linux, Windows, and Network Devices. It works by intercepting user keystrokes to capture credentials, often employing methods like hooking API callbacks for keystroke data, reading from the hardware buffer, making Windows Registry modifications, installing custom drivers, or modifying system images on network devices. It is commonly used by groups like APT28 and Lazarus when credential dumping is ineffective.[/profile]

12621.name: T1113
12621.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]T1113, Screen Capture, is a collection technique used on Windows, Linux, and macOS. Adversaries capture desktop screenshots to gather information, often using native utilities or API calls like `CopyFromScreen`, `xwd`, or `screencapture`, or as a feature within a remote access tool. It is distinct from video capture via peripheral devices. Groups like APT28, MuddyWater, and Fin7 have employed this technique.[/profile]

12622.name: Trusted Relationship
12622.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Trusted Relationship is MITRE ATT&CK technique T1199 under the Initial Access tactic, applicable across Windows, Linux, macOS, IaaS, SaaS, and other platforms. It involves adversaries compromising or abusing the access granted to external third parties, such as IT service providers, managed security firms, or Microsoft partners with delegated administrator permissions in Office 365, to gain initial entry into a victim's network. This method exploits existing, often less-scrutinized connections, potentially using the compromised valid accounts of these trusted entities.

12623.name: T1574.002
12623.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]The entity is the MITRE ATT&CK technique DLL Side-Loading, identified as T1574.002 under the Privilege Escalation and Persistence tactics for Windows. This technique involves adversaries placing a malicious DLL in a location where a legitimate, trusted application will load it during its standard execution, thereby hijacking the DLL search order to run their own payload. Specific vulnerabilities like CVE-2025-5777, CVE-2025-20337, and CVE-2019-0797 can be exploited to facilitate this process. The retrieved information on junk data, custom C2 protocols, and multilayer encryption is irrelevant to the core DLL side-loading execution mechanism and is therefore excluded from this profile.

12624.name: Registry Run Keys / Startup Folder
