12624.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Registry Run Keys / Startup Folder is MITRE ATT&CK technique T1547.001 under the Persistence and Privilege Escalation tactics for Windows. It works by adding entries to specific Registry keys like HKEY_CURRENT_USER\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run or by placing executables in user or system-wide startup folders (e.g., C:\Users\[Username]\AppData\Roaming\Microsoft\Windows\Start Menu\Programs\Startup), causing the referenced program to execute automatically at user logon or system boot. A specific technical example is using the RunOnceEx key with a "Depend" subkey to load a DLL, such as via the command `reg add HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\RunOnceEx\0001\Depend /v 1 /d "C:\temp\evil.dll"`. This technique is widely used by numerous threat groups, including APT28, Lazarus Group, and FIN7.[/profile]

12625.name: Process Discovery
12625.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Process Discovery, identified as T1057, is a Discovery tactic technique used on Windows, Linux, macOS, ESXi, and Network Devices. It involves adversaries enumerating running processes to understand system software and guide follow-on actions. Specific technical mechanics include using the `tasklist` command or `Get-Process` in PowerShell on Windows, the `ps` command or enumerating `/proc` on Linux/macOS/ESXi, the `esxcli system process list` command on ESXi, and `show processes` CLI commands on network devices.[/profile]

12626.name: Web Shell
12626.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Web Shell, identified as MITRE ATT&CK T1505.003, is a persistence technique within the Defense Evasion tactic, applicable to web servers across Windows, Linux, and macOS. It involves placing a malicious server-side script on a compromised web server, providing adversaries with a backdoor for command execution and remote access. This script often functions as a command-line interface, enabling file manipulation, system reconnaissance, and data exfiltration, and can be paired with a client-side controller like China Chopper. It serves as a redundant access point to maintain persistence if primary channels are lost.

12627.name: Keylogging
12627.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Keylogging, identified as T1056.001, is a technique within the Credential Access and Collection tactics, applicable to Windows, Linux, macOS, and Network Devices. It works by intercepting user keystrokes to capture credentials, often employed when OS credential dumping fails. Technical methods include hooking API callbacks for keystroke processing, reading raw data from the hardware buffer, modifying the Windows Registry, deploying custom drivers, or altering system images on network devices to gain access. Adversaries may clear browser cookies to force reauthentication and increase capture speed.

12628.name: Malicious File
12628.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Malicious File is the MITRE ATT&CK technique T1204.002 under the Execution tactic for Windows, Linux, and macOS platforms. It involves an adversary relying on a user to open a malicious file to gain execution, often following spearphishing. Common file types used include .doc, .pdf, .xls, .rtf, .scr, .exe, .lnk, .pif, .cpl, .reg, and .iso. To increase success, adversaries employ masquerading with familiar names, obfuscation, or password protection with instructions. This activity is frequently associated with numerous threat groups, including APT29, FIN7, and Lazarus Group, and can leverage vulnerabilities like CVE-2017-0199 and CVE-2017-11882.[/profile]

12629.name: System Owner/User Discovery
12629.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]System Owner/User Discovery, designated as T1033, is a Discovery tactic technique used on Windows, Linux, macOS, and Network Devices. It involves identifying active, primary, or common system users to inform follow-on actions. Specific technical mechanics include using commands like `whoami` on Windows, `w` or `who` on Linux/macOS, `dscl . list /Users | grep -v '_'` on macOS, and environment variables like `%USERNAME%` or `$USER`. On network devices, CLI commands such as `show users` and `show ssh` are employed. Information is also gathered from system artifacts like process ownership, file ownership, and logs.[profile]

12630.name: Screen Capture
12630.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Screen Capture is MITRE ATT&CK technique T1113 under the Collection tactic, applicable to Windows, Linux, and macOS platforms. Adversaries capture desktop screenshots to gather information, often using features in remote access tools or native utilities and API calls like `CopyFromScreen`, `xwd`, or `screencapture`. The technique has been used by groups including APT28, FIN7, and MuddyWater.[/profile]

12646.name: Chisel
12646.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Chisel is a malware tool that establishes command and control (C2) channels using the T1573.002 technique for Asymmetric Cryptography to encrypt C2 traffic. It employs T1543.003 to achieve persistence via Windows Service creation, uses T1562.001 to disable security tools, and performs T1041 to exfiltrate data over its C2 channel. Its infrastructure includes domains like buy-new-car.com, caduff-sa.chjeepcarlease.com, carleasingguru.com, and hanagram.jpthefinetreats.com. The tool is also utilized by other malware, such as MagicSocks, which incorporates Chisel's code to tunnel traffic to an actor-controlled server.[/profile]

12647.name: TinyTurla-NG
12647.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]TinyTurla-NG is a backdoor malware, also known as TinyTurla. It is attributed to the Russian-based Turla group and is deployed via a Windows Service for persistence and privilege escalation. Its key technical behaviors include using Asymmetric Cryptography (e.g., RSA) to conceal command and control traffic, exfiltrating stolen data over this same C2 channel, and employing techniques to disable or modify security tools for evasion. It targets Windows platforms and has used infrastructure including domains like carleasingguru.com, buy-new-car.com, hanagram.jpthefinetreats.com, and caduff-sa.chjeepcarlease.com for C2 communications.[/profile]

12656.name: T1562.001
12656.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]T1562.001, also known as Disable or Modify Tools, is a Defense Evasion technique applicable to Windows, Linux, macOS, Network Devices, Containers, and IaaS platforms. Its technical mechanics involve killing security software processes, modifying/deleting registry keys or configuration files to impair tool operation, and tampering with artifacts like Sysmon logging by altering registry values. Adversaries may also abuse legitimate drivers or tools like GMER to shut down hidden processes, exploit Windows process mitigation policies to block non-Microsoft binaries, and disable cloud monitoring agents. This technique is associated with groups including FIN6, Lazarus Group, and Wizard Spider.

12657.name: T1573.002
12657.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]T1573.002 (Asymmetric Cryptography) is a command-and-control technique used on Windows, Linux, macOS, ESXi, and network devices. It conceals C2 traffic by using public key encryption algorithms like RSA or ElGamal, where data is encrypted with a recipient's public key and decrypted with their private key, ensuring only the intended recipient can read it. This method is often used to establish a secure channel before switching to symmetric encryption for efficiency. Groups like FIN6, OilRig, and APT42 have employed this technique, and it has been associated with vulnerabilities such as CVE-2022-3236.[/profile]

12658.name: T1041
12658.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]T1041, Exfiltration Over C2 Channel, is an Exfiltration technique for Windows, Linux, macOS, and ESXi platforms. It involves adversaries stealing data by encoding and transmitting it over an existing command and control channel, using the same communication protocol established for C2. This method is often associated with groups like Lazarus, Gamaredon, and Wizard Spider, and can be used in conjunction with automated or scheduled data transfer processes.[/profile]

12659.name: Exfiltration Over C2 Channel
12659.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Exfiltration Over C2 Channel is technique T1041 under the Exfiltration tactic, targeting platforms including Windows, Linux, macOS, and ESXi. It involves adversaries stealing data by encoding and transmitting it over the same, existing command and control channel protocol used for communications, avoiding the need to establish a separate connection. This technique is commonly used by groups such as Lazarus Group, Wizard Spider, and APT32. Related procedures include automated or scheduled data transfers that utilize this channel for the actual exfiltration.

12660.name: T1543.003
12660.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]T1543.003: Windows Service is a MITRE ATT&CK technique for persistence and privilege escalation on Windows platforms. Adversaries create or modify Windows services to execute malicious payloads at system startup, often using utilities like sc.exe, direct Registry modification, or Windows API calls. Services run with SYSTEM privileges, enabling privilege escalation. Techniques include installing malicious drivers, using BYOVD for exploitation, and hiding services via SDDL permissions with commands like `sc sdset`. Related groups include Lazarus Group, APT41, and FIN7.

12661.name: Asymmetric Cryptography
12661.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Asymmetric Cryptography, also known as T1573.002, is a Command and Control technique used across Windows, Linux, macOS, ESXi, and Network Device platforms. It involves adversaries using public-key cryptography, where data is encrypted with a recipient's public key and decrypted with their corresponding private key, to conceal C2 traffic. Common algorithms include RSA and ElGamal. This method is distinct from symmetric encryption and is also referenced in the context of data exfiltration over non-C2 protocols. It has been associated with threat groups including FIN6, OilRig, and APT42.[/profile]

12662.name: Disable or Modify Tools
12662.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Disable or Modify Tools is MITRE ATT&CK technique T1562.001 under the Defense Evasion tactic, targeting platforms including Windows, Linux, macOS, Network Devices, Containers, and IaaS. Its technical mechanics involve killing security software processes or services, modifying or deleting Registry keys or configuration files to impair operation, and disabling updates to security tools. Specific methods include using the Windows Time Travel Debugging driver to hook into and crash EDR processes, abusing the PROCESS_CREATION_MITIGATION_POLICY_BLOCK_NON_MICROSOFT_BINARIES_ALWAYS_ON attribute to block non-Microsoft DLLs, tampering with Sysmon logging via registry keys, altering network device startup configurations to bypass firmware verification, and disabling cloud monitoring agents. It is associated with numerous threat groups, including FIN6, Lazarus Group, and Wizard Spider.

12663.name: Windows Service
12663.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Windows Service is a persistence and privilege escalation technique identified as MITRE ATT&CK T1543.003, operating on Windows platforms. It involves creating or modifying Windows services to execute malicious payloads at system startup. Adversaries configure services using utilities like sc.exe, direct Registry modification, or Windows API calls such as CreateServiceW(). Services run with SYSTEM privileges, enabling privilege escalation, and can be hidden using commands like sc sdset to evade detection via standard enumeration tools.

12671.name: TinyTurla
12671.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]TinyTurla, also known as TinyTurla backdoor, is a malware family attributed to the Turla group, a Russian-based APT active since 2004. It operates as a backdoor installed via a Windows Service, storing its C2 server list and authentication password in the Windows registry. Its infrastructure includes domains like connectotels.net and hostelhotels.net, and it uses files such as ArsenalV2%.exe, ConnectionInfo.db, and DownloadPriority.db. The primary target platform is Windows.

12765.name: Uroburos
12765.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Uroburos, also known as Snake, is a malware family attributed to the Turla group. It uses techniques including T1562.002 (Disable Windows Event Logging) and T1562.001 (Disable or Modify Tools) for defense evasion, Masquerading (T1036) to appear legitimate, and T1059.001 (PowerShell) for execution. It also employs Deobfuscate/Decode Files or Information (T1140). The malware targets Windows platforms and has used infrastructure such as the domain files.philbendeck.com for its operations.[/profile]

12767.name: Uroburos - S0022
12767.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Uroburos - S0022, also known as Snake, is a sophisticated malware attributed to the Turla threat group. It employs defense evasion techniques including disabling Windows Event Logging (T1562.002) and masquerading (T1036). For command and control, it uses web protocols (T1071.001), with observed infrastructure such as files.philbendeck.com. The malware utilizes obfuscation keys shared with the older Agent.BTZ malware and targets Windows platforms, with historical targeting noted in the Philippines.

12782.name: T1127.001
12782.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]The entity is MSBuild (T1127.001), a Defense Evasion technique for Windows. It involves abusing the trusted, signed Microsoft Build Engine (MSBuild.exe) to proxy malicious code execution and bypass application controls. Adversaries insert C# or Visual Basic code into XML project files, which MSBuild compiles and executes, leveraging its trusted status to run arbitrary commands.

12785.name: T1562.002
12785.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]The entity is the MITRE ATT&CK technique T1562.002, named Impair Defenses: Disable Windows Event Logging, under the Defense Evasion tactic for Windows platforms. This technique involves adversaries stopping the Windows EventLog service to erase evidence, using commands like `sc config eventlog start=disabled` and `Set-Service -Name EventLog -Status Stopped`, or by modifying registry keys such as `HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services\EventLog`. They may also use `auditpol.exe` to disable specific audit categories or clear the entire audit policy with commands like `auditpol /clear /y`.

12786.name: T1071.001
12786.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]T1071.001 (Web Protocols) is a Command and Control technique where adversaries use common application layer protocols like HTTP/S and WebSocket to blend malicious communications with normal web traffic. It operates on platforms including Windows, Linux, macOS, ESXi, and Network Devices. Commands and exfiltrated data are embedded within standard protocol fields and headers to avoid detection and network filtering, mimicking legitimate traffic. This technique is associated with numerous threat groups, including APT28, Lazarus Group, and MuddyWater.

12787.name: MSBuild
12787.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]MSBuild, identified as MITRE ATT&CK technique T1127.001, is a Defense Evasion technique targeting Windows platforms. It involves abusing the trusted Microsoft Build Engine (MSBuild.exe) to proxy execution of malicious code, bypassing application controls. Adversaries insert C# or Visual Basic code into XML project files, leveraging the inline task capability introduced in .NET version 4, which MSBuild will then compile and execute, exploiting its status as a signed binary.

12788.name: Disable Windows Event Logging
12788.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Disable Windows Event Logging is MITRE ATT&CK technique T1562.002 under the Defense Evasion tactic for Windows platforms. Adversaries disable logging to erase evidence by stopping the EventLog service via commands like `Set-Service -Name EventLog -Status Stopped` or `sc config eventlog start=disabled`, or by modifying registry keys such as `HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services\EventLog`. They may also use `auditpol.exe` to disable specific audit categories with commands like `auditpol /set /category:"Account Logon" /success:disable /failure:disable` or clear the entire policy with `auditpol /clear /y`. This technique has been associated with threat groups like Threat Group-3390 and Magic Hound.

12794.name: T1070.001
12794.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]The attack pattern T1070.001, known as Clear Windows Event Logs, is a Defense Evasion technique for Windows. It involves clearing or deleting Windows Event Logs to hide intrusion activity. Administrators can use utility commands like `wevtutil cl system`, `wevtutil cl application`, and `wevtutil cl security`, or PowerShell commands such as `Remove-EventLog -LogName Security`. Log files may also be directly deleted from the `C:\Windows\System32\winevt\logs\` directory. This technique has been associated with groups including APT28, APT38, and Volt Typhoon.

12795.name: T1132.002
12795.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]T1132.002, Non-Standard Encoding, is a command-and-control technique for macOS, Linux, Windows, and ESXi. It operates by encoding C2 traffic with a non-standard or modified data encoding system, such as a custom variant of Base64 within an HTTP message body, to evade detection. This method diverges from standard protocol specifications and can be combined with other obfuscation layers like custom protocols or junk data insertion to further complicate analysis.

12796.name: T1095
12796.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]T1095, named "Non-Application Layer Protocol", is a command-and-control technique within the MITRE ATT&CK framework applicable to Windows, Linux, macOS, ESXi, and Network Devices. It involves adversaries using OSI network, transport, or session layer protocols like ICMP, UDP, or SOCKS for C2 communications, which are less commonly monitored than application-layer traffic. In ESXi environments, this includes leveraging the Virtual Machine Communication Interface (VMCI) for host-guest VM communications that are invisible to external network monitoring tools.

12797.name: T1036.004
12797.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]T1036.004 - Masquerade Task or Service is a Defense Evasion technique for Windows, Linux, and macOS. Adversaries manipulate the name or description of a scheduled task (e.g., via Task Scheduler or systemd) or a Windows service to appear legitimate by mimicking benign system tasks. This technique is used by groups like FIN7, Lazarus Group, and APT41. The vulnerability CVE-2025-22457 is related to this behavior.[/profile]

12798.name: T1572
12798.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]The entity is T1572 Protocol Tunneling, a Command and Control tactic applicable to Windows, Linux, macOS, and ESXi platforms. It works by explicitly encapsulating one network protocol within another to evade detection and filtering, with common implementations including SSH port forwarding for encrypted tunnels and the abuse of DNS over HTTPS (DoH) during dynamic resolution. It is often used in conjunction with proxy techniques and is associated with threat groups like FIN7 and OilRig.

12799.name: T1132.001
12799.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]T1132.001, known as Data Encoding: Standard Encoding, is a command and control technique within the MITRE ATT&CK framework. It operates on Windows, Linux, macOS, and ESXi platforms. 12831.name: T1553.004

A specific implementation for macOS uses the command `/usr/bin/security add-trusted-cert -d -r trustRoot -k /Library/Keychains/System.keychain` to add a certificate to the system keychain. Cloned legitimate certificates can also be reinstalled to sign malicious code and evade signature-based defenses.

This can be achieved through various methods like command-line interfaces (e.g., `esxcli network firewall set` on ESXi), editing Windows Registry keys, or using system control panels, which facilitates unauthorized command and control, lateral movement, or data exfiltration. 12863.name: T1078.001

12867.name: SilentCrystal

12868.name: unkown_apt_group

12900.name: T1218

This technique has been associated with groups including Lazarus Group, Volt Typhoon, and Cobalt Group.[profile]

12901.name: T1020

This technique can be facilitated by compromising network boundary devices to bypass traffic policies, enabling data transfer, and may leverage mechanisms like webhooks for repeated, automated data pushes to blend with normal traffic. 12902.name: System Binary Proxy Execution
12902.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]System Binary Proxy Execution, identified as T1218, is a Defense Evasion technique applicable to Windows, Linux, and macOS platforms. Specific examples include abusing Microsoft-signed utilities like odbcconf.exe with the REGSVR flag to run DLLs or using InstallUtil.exe to execute .NET installer components, as well as leveraging trusted Linux binaries such as split. This method exploits the inherent trust in these native operating system files to evade signature-based detection and application whitelisting.

12903.name: T1132

It involves encoding C2 traffic using standard systems like Base64, MIME, or Unicode to obfuscate content and evade detection. This can include binary-to-text conversions and may incorporate data compression methods such as gzip. 12904.name: Automated Exfiltration

It typically operates in conjunction with other exfiltration methods like Exfiltration Over C2 Channel (T1041) or Exfiltration Over Alternative Protocol (T1048) to execute the actual data transfer.

12905.name: Data Encoding
12905.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Data Encoding is a command and control technique (T1132) used to evade detection by obfuscating C2 traffic. It operates on Windows, Linux, macOS, and ESXi platforms. Adversaries apply standard encoding systems like ASCII, Unicode, Base64, MIME, or hexadecimal that adhere to protocol specifications to transform data, with some schemes like gzip also providing compression. The technique is distinct from non-standard encoding (T1132.001) and broader data obfuscation methods.

12906.name: Application Layer Protocol

This contrasts with non-application layer or custom protocols, and is frequently employed by groups like APT29, Magic Hound, and Rocke.[/profile]

13391.name: T1104

This separation of infrastructure makes detection more difficult, and adversaries may employ backup channels if the primary path is blocked. Groups like APT3, APT41, MuddyWater, and Lazarus Group have been associated with this technique.

13393.name: T1564
