Its technical behavior includes the use of proactive blocklists or blacklists, a technique shared with other malware like TrickBot and Cobalt Strike, to evade detection by targeting specific user accounts and analysis-tool processes. The malware is not currently classified as a family.[/profile]

13499.name: JackalWorm
13499.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]JackalWorm, also known as JSWorm, is a .NET malware implant attributed to groups including UNC2452 and Lazarus Group. It is part of a toolset with JackalControl, JackalSteal, JackalPerInfo, and JackalScreenWatcher. Its key behaviors include spreading via removable drives, exfiltrating data, stealing credentials, collecting local system and web activity information, and taking screen captures to control target computers. It targets Windows systems and has been associated with infrastructure like xgraphic.ro and spy.agent.ca, with operations linked to Belarus.[/profile]

13500.name: GoldenUsbGo
13500.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]GoldenUsbGo is a malware entity with no known aliases or attributed groups. Its key technical behaviors include using command and control infrastructure at domains like spy.agent.ca and xgraphic.ro. It is associated with Belarus as a location. The retrieved information about other malware like 9002 rat, Duqu, and Stuxnet does not provide specific, verifiable context for GoldenUsbGo, so no additional TTPs or target platforms can be reliably inferred.[/profile]

13502.name: GoldenUsbCopy
13502.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]GoldenUsbCopy is a malware that targets Windows systems and spreads via infected USB drives, searching for and stealing sensitive documents and credentials based on specific file extensions and keywords. It uses domains like xgraphic.ro and spy.agent.ca for command and control. Related malware families or tools include pyxie, 9002 RAT, and Agent.BTZ, which are associated with groups such as Aurora Panda, APT31, Group 27, and Turla, though GoldenUsbCopy's direct attribution is not specified. Its primary function is data exfiltration from air-gapped or isolated networks through removable media.[/profile]

13503.name: GoldenHowl
13503.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]GoldenHowl, also known as buterat, cmoon, and latentbot, is a malware that targets systems in Belarus and communicates with command and control infrastructure at domains including spy.agent.ca and xgraphic.ro. Its technical behaviors include creating a registry key for persistence to automatically launch on system startup, monitoring specific applications on the infected host, and engaging in characteristic network interactions for command and control.

13504.name: GoldenDealer
13504.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]GoldenDealer is a malware entity associated with the APT28 group, as indicated by its relation to other APT28-linked malware like X-Agent, Zebrocy, and Seduploader. It operates from infrastructure in Belarus and uses domains such as xgraphic.ro and spy.agent.ca for command and control. Its specific technical behaviors and target platforms are not detailed in the provided information.[/profile]

13505.name: unkown_apt_group
13505.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]This intrusion set is most likely the APT group known as Scully Spider. It is also known to operate under the aliases BackdoorDiplomacy, CloudComputating, BackDip, and Quarian. Its key malware includes Satacom (also known as LegionLoader), a downloader and cryptocurrency stealer distributed via Nullmixer, as well as tools like GoldenUsbCopy, GoldenHowl, and GoldenPyBlacklist. Its primary TTPs involve Browser Session Hijacking (T1185) to steal session cookies, searching for Unsecured Credentials (T1552), establishing persistence via Boot or Logon Autostart Execution (T1547), and Impairing Defenses (T1562). The group is attributed to or shows overlaps with the threat actor Scully Spider and has targeted locations including Vietnam, Algeria, Türkiye, Egypt, and Mexico, utilizing infrastructure domains such as new-loads.com, softs-labs.com, and air-are.xyz. Its motivation appears to be financial gain, primarily through cryptocurrency theft.[/profile]

13510.name: LegionLoader
13510.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]LegionLoader, also known as Satacom, is a downloader and cryptocurrency stealer primarily distributed via the Nullmixer pay-per-install service. Its key technical behaviors include browser session hijacking (T1185) to steal web session cookies (T1539), searching for unsecured credentials (T1552), establishing persistence via boot or logon autostart execution (T1547), and impairing defenses (T1562). It targets Windows platforms and has been associated with infrastructure domains such as io-strength.cfd, air-are.xyz, die-dns.com, icl-surprise.xyz, and fbs-university.xyz.[/profile]

13512.name: Satacom
13512.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Satacom, also known as LegionLoader, is a malware discovered in 2019. It employs anti-analysis techniques potentially borrowed from the al-khazer stress tool and uses a variable embedded user agent, such as "deus vult". Its behaviors align with techniques like Browser Session Hijacking, Unsecured Credentials, Boot or Logon Autostart Execution, Clipboard Data collection, and Impair Defenses. It has been associated with the threat group Scully Spider and targets locations including Viet Nam, Algeria, Türkiye, Egypt, and Mexico, utilizing infrastructure like new-loads.com, softs-labs.com, moment-are.xyz, thousand-h.click, and oo-strategy.xyz.[/profile]

13647.name: T1185
13647.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]T1185, Browser Session Hijacking, is a collection technique within the MITRE ATT&CK framework targeting Windows platforms. It involves exploiting browser vulnerabilities or functionality to hijack sessions, such as by injecting software to inherit a user's cookies and authenticated sessions, allowing the adversary to pivot into an intranet. This can be achieved by setting up a proxy to redirect browser traffic, assuming the security context of the hijacked browser process, and may bypass 2-factor authentication.

13648.name: T1552
13648.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Unsecured Credentials (T1552) is a Credential Access technique targeting platforms like Windows, Linux, and macOS. It involves adversaries searching compromised systems to find insecurely stored credentials in locations such as plaintext files, OS/application repositories like the Windows Registry, and specialized artifacts including private keys. The technique is associated with groups like Volt Typhoon.

13649.name: T1539
13649.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]T1539, Steal Web Session Cookie, is a Credential Access technique applicable to Windows, Linux, macOS, Office Suite, and SaaS platforms. Adversaries steal session cookies from disk, browser process memory, or network traffic to gain authenticated access to web applications, often bypassing multi-factor authentication. Theft methods include malware, malicious JavaScript injection, and adversary-in-the-middle proxies like Evilginx2. Groups such as APT42, Kimsuky, and Scattered Spider have employed this technique, which is related to the subsequent use of stolen cookies via T1550.004 (Web Session Cookie).[/profile]

13650.name: T1176
13650.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]T1176, known as Browser Extensions, is a Persistence technique for macOS, Linux, and Windows. Adversaries abuse software extensions, which are modular components that enhance applications like web browsers and IDEs, to establish persistent access. They are typically installed via official marketplaces, app stores, or manually, inheriting the host application's permissions. Malicious extensions can be introduced through social engineering, compromised marketplaces, or direct installation, often masquerading as benign ones to bypass security scanners. This technique can be linked to persistence methods like shortcut modification (T1547.009).[/profile]

13651.name: T1119
13651.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]The entity is the MITRE ATT&CK technique Automated Collection (T1119), a Collection tactic technique applicable to Windows, Linux, macOS, IaaS, SaaS, and Office Suite platforms. It involves using automated methods like command scripts, cloud APIs, or CLI tools to gather internal data based on set criteria such as file type or location, often incorporating techniques like File and Directory Discovery. It is distinct from manual data gathering from sources like removable media (T1025).[profile]

13652.name: Unsecured Credentials
13652.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]This entity is the MITRE ATT&CK technique Unsecured Credentials (T1552) under the Credential Access tactic, applicable across Windows, Linux, macOS, Network Devices, Containers, IaaS, Office Suite, Identity Provider, and SaaS platforms. It involves adversaries searching compromised systems for credentials stored insecurely in various locations. Specific mechanics include finding plaintext credentials in files like shell history or configuration files, querying OS-specific repositories such as the Windows Registry with commands like `reg query`, accessing cached domain credential databases, and extracting secrets from user communication services or container API logs.

13653.name: T1115
13653.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]T1115, known as Clipboard Data, is a collection technique within the MITRE ATT&CK framework applicable to Windows, macOS, and Linux platforms. It involves adversaries collecting data users have copied to the clipboard. On Windows, this can be achieved using utilities like `clip.exe` or PowerShell's `Get-Clipboard`, while macOS and Linux systems can be targeted with commands such as `pbpaste`. This technique is commonly associated with threat groups like APT38, APT39, and OILRIG.

13654.name: Steal Web Session Cookie
13654.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Steal Web Session Cookie (T1539) is a Credential Access technique applicable to Windows, Linux, macOS, SaaS, and Office Suite platforms. It involves stealing authentication session cookies from disk, browser process memory, or network traffic to impersonate an authenticated user, bypassing multi-factor authentication. Cookies are often harvested by malware, through malicious JavaScript injection, or via adversary-in-the-middle frameworks like Evilginx2. The stolen cookie is then used in a follow-on Web Session Cookie (T1550.004) technique for unauthorized access. Associated threat groups include Kimsuky and Scattered Spider.

13655.name: Browser Session Hijacking
13655.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Browser Session Hijacking is a collection technique (MITRE ATT&CK T1185) targeting Windows platforms. It involves injecting software into a browser to inherit the user's cookies, HTTP sessions, and SSL client certificates, allowing the adversary to pivot into an authenticated intranet. Alternatively, adversaries can set up a proxy to redirect their own browser traffic through the hijacked user's browser session, assuming its security context to access internal resources and potentially bypass two-factor authentication.

13656.name: Automated Collection
13656.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Automated Collection, identified as T1119, is a Collection tactic technique used across Windows, Linux, macOS, and cloud platforms (IaaS, SaaS, Office Suite). It involves using automated scripts or command-line interpreters to search for and copy data based on specific criteria like file type or name at scheduled intervals. In cloud environments, it leverages APIs, CLIs, or ETL services, and often incorporates techniques like File and Directory Discovery to identify target resources.

13657.name: Software Extensions
13657.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Software Extensions, identified as T1176, is a Persistence technique applicable to Windows, Linux, and macOS. It involves abusing modular components of applications like browsers and IDEs to maintain access. Malicious extensions are installed via official marketplaces, social engineering, or by silently manipulating browser configuration files (e.g., Preferences files in Chromium-based browsers) to load without user consent. Once installed, they inherit the host application's permissions to execute arbitrary code, establish backdoors, steal credentials, and exfiltrate data, blending into normal workflows to evade detection.

13659.name: Clipboard Data
13659.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Clipboard Data is identified as MITRE ATT&CK technique T1115 under the Collection tactic, targeting Windows, macOS, and Linux platforms. Adversaries collect data users copy within or between applications. On Windows, this is achieved using utilities like clip.exe or the Get-Clipboard cmdlet, while macOS and Linux adversaries use commands such as pbpaste. This technique can also involve monitoring and replacing clipboard content, linking it to data manipulation activities. Associated threat groups include APT38, APT39, and OilRig.

13667.name: ComeBacker
13667.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]ComeBacker is a malware family attributed to the Lazarus Group. It uses a loader that decrypts and decompresses a final payload, then executes it by calling the payload's GetWindowSizedW export with the argument "1282". Associated techniques include Timestomp (T1070.006) for defense evasion and T1497 for Virtualization/Sandbox Evasion. Its infrastructure includes domains like angeldonationblog.com, jdkgradle.com, and pypi.online, and IPs like 91.206.178.125.[/profile]

13668.name: unkown_apt_group
13668.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]This intrusion set is most likely the North Korea-affiliated threat actor known as Contagious Interview, also referenced as Wagemole and DeceptiveDevelopment. Its key malware includes the cross-platform infostealer BeaverTail and the modular Python-based data exfiltration tool InvisibleFerret, which is often deployed by BeaverTail. The group's distinctive techniques for macOS targets include persistence via Launch Agents (T1543.001) and credential access via the macOS Keychain (T1555.001). It is attributed to North Korea and has targeted sectors including cryptocurrency, with observed infrastructure in India and the United States. Its primary motivation is financial gain and espionage, leveraging custom malware families like FrostyFerret and GolangGhost for credential theft and data collection.[/profile]

13704.name: T1070
13704.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]T1070, also known as Indicator Removal, is a Defense Evasion technique applicable to Windows, Linux, macOS, and other platforms. It involves adversaries deleting or modifying system artifacts like logs, command histories, or downloaded files to erase evidence of their presence, hinder event collection, and impede forensic analysis. This activity can compromise security solution integrity by causing events to go unreported. It is often associated with groups like Lazarus Group and APT42, and sub-techniques include actions like File Deletion (T1070.004) to clean up artifacts.

13705.name: T1195
13705.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]T1195, known as Supply Chain Compromise, is an Initial Access technique applicable to Windows, Linux, macOS, and SaaS platforms. It involves adversaries manipulating products or delivery mechanisms before consumer receipt to compromise systems. This can occur through tampering with development tools, source code repositories (including open-source dependencies), software update channels, or system images at the factory. Attackers may broadly distribute tainted software but only activate it for specific targets, and they can conduct "second-order" compromises by leveraging initial access to further infect software components, as seen in incidents like the 3CX compromise.[/profile]

13706.name: Timestomp
13706.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Timestomp, also known as T1070.006, is a Defense Evasion technique. It operates across Windows and Linux platforms by modifying file timestamps to hide malicious activity. Adversaries alter the modify, access, create, and change times of files, often to match legitimate files in the same directory, thereby evading forensic analysis. On Windows, this involves manipulating the `$STANDARD_INFORMATION` attribute via user-level APIs, with advanced "double timestomping" targeting both `$SI` and `$FILE_NAME` attributes. In Linux, commands like `touch -a -m -t` are used to set specific timestamps. The technique is frequently paired with Masquerading (T1036) and is associated with threat groups including APT28, APT29, and Lazarus Group.[/profile]

13707.name: Indicator Removal
13707.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Indicator Removal is a defense evasion technique (T1070) applicable across Windows, Linux, macOS, and other platforms. It involves adversaries deleting or modifying system artifacts like logs, command histories, or downloaded files to erase evidence of their presence and hinder forensic analysis and security monitoring. This action can compromise security solutions by causing critical events to go unreported.

13708.name: T1064
13708.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]This entity, T1064 (Scripting), is a deprecated technique within the MITRE ATT&CK framework, now superseded by T1059 (Command and Scripting Interpreter). It was associated with the Defense Evasion and Execution tactics on Windows, Linux, and macOS platforms. The technique involved using scripts like VBScript, PowerShell, or batch files to automate malicious operations, speed up tasks, and potentially bypass monitoring by interacting directly with OS APIs. Scripts could be embedded as macros in documents for execution via spearphishing.

13709.name: T1099
13709.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]The entity is the MITRE ATT&CK technique Timestomp, identified as T1099, which falls under the Defense Evasion tactic. It operates across multiple platforms. This technique involves adversaries modifying file timestamps—such as modify, access, create, and change times—to hide the deployment or alteration of files, often making them blend with other files in a directory to evade forensic detection. It is frequently used in conjunction with file name Masquerading (T1036) to conceal malware and tools.

13711.name: Supply Chain Compromise
13711.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Supply Chain Compromise is identified as MITRE ATT&CK technique T1195 under the Initial Access tactic, targeting macOS, Linux, Windows, and SaaS platforms. This technique involves adversaries manipulating products or their delivery mechanisms before they reach the end consumer to compromise systems or data. Specific methods include tampering with development tools, source code repositories, open-source dependencies, software update channels, or physical hardware and firmware to insert backdoors. It can be broadly targeted or initially widespread with follow-on actions against specific victims, and notable threat groups like Sandworm Team and OilRig have employed it.[/profile]

13726.name: Scripting
13726.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]This entity is the deprecated MITRE ATT&CK technique Scripting, ID T1064, which has been consolidated under Command and Scripting Interpreter (T1059). It is associated with the Defense Evasion and Execution tactics and targets Windows, Linux, and macOS platforms. The technique involves using scripts like VBScript, PowerShell, or batch files to automate malicious operations, interact directly with OS APIs to bypass monitoring, and embed macros within documents for execution, often delivered via spearphishing.

13728.name: LazarLoader
13728.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]LazarLoader is a malware loader attributed to the Lazarus group. It employs techniques such as Access Token Manipulation (T1134) and Bypass User Account Control (T1548.002) for defense evasion and privilege escalation, and uses Web Shell (T1505.003) for persistence. Its command and control (C2) communications leverage Application Layer Protocols (T1071) like HTTP, and it can gain initial access by Exploiting Public-Facing Applications (T1190). The malware primarily targets Windows systems and has been observed exploiting vulnerabilities in specific South Korean financial security software like INISAFE CrossWeb EX and MagicLine4NX.[profile]

13729.name: T1134
13729.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]T1134, Access Token Manipulation, is a Windows technique used for Defense Evasion and Privilege Escalation. It involves modifying Windows access tokens to change a process's security context, enabling actions like token stealing to impersonate other users or escalate to SYSTEM level. Adversaries use API functions such as DuplicateToken or DuplicateTokenEx to duplicate tokens and then apply them via ImpersonateLoggedOnUser or SetThreadToken to existing processes, or use CreateProcessWithTokenW to spawn new ones. This allows bypassing access controls and operating under stolen privileges, often from an administrator to SYSTEM context.

13730.name: T1548.002
13730.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]T1548.002, known as Bypass User Account Control, is a Windows-specific technique under the Defense Evasion and Privilege Escalation tactics. It involves circumventing the Windows User Account Control (UAC) mechanism to elevate process privileges without proper user consent. Methods include exploiting auto-elevated programs like eventvwr.exe to execute payloads, using crafted DLLs with tools like Rundll32 to load elevated COM objects, or injecting into trusted processes. The UACME project documents numerous specific bypass methods, and this technique is commonly associated with threat groups like APT37, APT38, and MuddyWater.

13731.name: Bypass User Account Control
13731.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Bypass User Account Control, identified as T1548.002 in the MITRE ATT&CK framework, is a Defense Evasion and Privilege Escalation technique for Windows. It involves circumventing the User Account Control (UAC) prompt to elevate process privileges. Specific methods include abusing auto-elevating Windows programs like `eventvwr.exe` to execute payloads, using tools like Rundll32 to load crafted DLLs that leverage elevated COM objects, or injecting code into trusted processes. The UACME project documents numerous such bypasses, which are commonly used by threat groups including APT37, MuddyWater, and APT29.

13732.name: Access Token Manipulation
13732.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Access Token Manipulation, identified as T1134, is a Defense Evasion and Privilege Escalation technique for Windows. It involves using built-in Windows API functions to copy access tokens from processes, a method known as token stealing. These stolen tokens can be applied to an existing process (Token Impersonation/Theft) or used to spawn a new one (Create Process with Token), allowing an adversary to operate under a different security context, such as elevating from administrator to SYSTEM level. The standard `runas` command can also create impersonation tokens.

13733.name: T1074
13733.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]The entity is MITRE ATT&CK technique T1074, known as Data Staged, which falls under the Collection tactic and operates on platforms including Windows, Linux, and macOS. This technique involves adversaries staging collected data in a central location or directory, such as a specific instance in cloud environments, prior to exfiltration to minimize connections and evade detection. Data may be kept in separate files or combined using utilities like tar or zip, and common command shell functionality in cmd or bash is often used to copy data into the staging location.

13735.name: SplitLoader
13735.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]SplitLoader is a malware loader. Its key technical behaviors include supply chain compromise for initial access, using encrypted channels for command and control, and exfiltration over web services. It has been associated with infrastructure domains such as bestonlinefilmstudio.org, matrixane.com, pointdnt.com, defitankzone.com, and starglowventures.com. It is related to other driver loader malware like Robinhood, Slingshot, and Lojax, the latter of which is attributed to APT28.[/profile]

13736.name: DeTankWar
13736.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]DeTankWar is a malware with aliases including bibi-linux and dark. It is attributed to the groups Void Manticore and Wizard Spider. Its key technical behaviors include using the supply chain compromise technique T1195 for initial access, leveraging the vulnerability CVE-2023-42793, and establishing command and control via application layer protocols (T1071) and encrypted channels (T1573). It exfiltrates data over web services (T1567) and utilizes acquired infrastructure (T1583). Associated infrastructure includes domains such as detankwar.com, ccwaterfall.com, mingeloem.com, freenet-zhilly.org, and bestonlinefilmstudio.org.[/profile]

13737.name: YouieLoad
13737.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]YouieLoad is a malware loader. It is associated with the Buer loader family and has been linked to the threat group UNC1878. Its tactics include Supply Chain Compromise for initial access and the use of Encrypted Channels for command and control. It has been observed using domains such as bestonlinefilmstudio.org, mingeloem.com, and defitankzone.com for its infrastructure.[/profile]

13739.name: FakePenny
13739.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]FakePenny is a malware associated with the TA578 threat group. It employs Supply Chain Compromise for initial access, uses Phishing to deliver malicious payloads, and establishes an Encrypted Channel for command and control. Its primary function is data exfiltration, achieved via the Exfiltration Over Web Service technique. The malware's infrastructure includes domains such as bestonlinefilmstudio.org, starglowventures.com, mingeloem.com, detankwar.com, and defitankzone.com, which are likely acquired through the Acquire Infrastructure tactic. It is known to exploit the vulnerability CVE-2023-42793.[/profile]

13773.name: T1588
13773.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]T1588 (Obtain Capabilities) is a Resource Development tactic on the PRE platform. Adversaries acquire capabilities like malware, exploits, software licenses, and vulnerability information to support operations, rather than developing them internally. This can involve purchasing from third-party entities or criminal marketplaces, freely downloading, or stealing these resources from other adversaries. The technique is related to vulnerabilities such as CVE-2018-0824 and CVE-2023-0669.

13774.name: T1122
13774.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]T1122, also known as Component Object Model Hijacking, is a persistence technique within the MITRE ATT&CK framework, primarily targeting the Windows platform. It operates by adversaries hijacking COM references through malicious Windows Registry modifications, replacing legitimate system component references to execute their own code when the hijacked component is invoked. This method can be facilitated by tools like Regsvr32.exe to register a malicious COM object. The technique is associated with the exploitation of vulnerabilities such as CVE-2023-42793.

13775.name: T1583
13775.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]T1583 (Acquire Infrastructure) is a resource development technique in the MITRE ATT&CK framework for the PRE platform. Adversaries obtain infrastructure like physical/cloud servers, domains, third-party web services, or botnets by purchasing, leasing, renting, or exploiting free trials to stage and launch operations, often to blend in with normal traffic or support proxy chains. Associated vulnerabilities include CVE-2024-3400 and CVE-2023-42793, and groups like SEA TURTLE and Sandworm Team have used this technique.[/profile]

13776.name: Obtain Capabilities
13776.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Obtain Capabilities is a pre-attack technique with MITRE ATT&CK ID T1588 under the Resource Development tactic, applicable to the PRE platform. It involves adversaries acquiring, rather than building, tools for operations by purchasing, freely downloading, or stealing malware, software, exploits, certificates, and vulnerability information from third-party entities, criminal marketplaces, or other adversaries. This is distinct from in-house development (T1587) and subsequent staging (T1608) of these capabilities.

13777.name: Acquire Infrastructure
13777.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Acquire Infrastructure (T1583) is a Resource Development tactic within the MITRE ATT&CK framework, applicable to pre-attack platforms (PRE). This technique involves adversaries buying, leasing, renting, or otherwise obtaining infrastructure—such as physical servers, cloud servers (VPS), domains, third-party web services, or botnets—to stage and execute operations. Acquired infrastructure helps blend malicious traffic with normal activity, supports proxy services, and can be rapidly provisioned or shut down. It is distinct from compromising existing infrastructure and is often used by groups like Sea Turtle and Kimsuky.[/profile]

13778.name: Exfiltration Over Web Service
13778.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Exfiltration Over Web Service (T1567) is an Exfiltration tactic used on Windows, Linux, macOS, ESXi, Office Suite, and SaaS platforms. It involves adversaries using legitimate external web services like cloud storage or social media to covertly transfer stolen data, leveraging existing SSL/TLS encrypted connections and common firewall rules for cover. Groups like APT28 and BlackByte have employed this technique, and it is conceptually related to exfiltration over webhooks or to code repositories.

13815.name: T1059.002
13815.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]This entity is the MITRE ATT&CK technique T1059.002, named "AppleScript", categorized under the Execution tactic and specific to the macOS platform. It involves abusing the AppleScript language to control applications and the OS via AppleEvents. Execution methods include the command-line `osascript` utility, embedding scripts in Mail rules or Automator workflows, or using native APIs like `NSAppleScript` within binaries. It can be used to interact with remote applications, present fake dialog boxes, and launch further payloads like Python reverse shells.

13817.name: Kaolin
13817.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Kaolin, also known as Kaolin RAT, is a Remote Access Trojan attributed to the Lazarus Group. It is deployed in memory after decryption and decompression of a data blob, with the decryption key and IV embedded within the initial 32 bytes of that blob. Its associated techniques include Data Obfuscation (T1001) for C2 communication, Subvert Trust Controls (T1553), Permission Groups Discovery (T1069), Supply Chain Compromise (T1195), and Input Capture (T1056). It targets Windows, Linux, and macOS platforms.[/profile]

13830.name: T1553
13830.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]T1553, Subvert Trust Controls, is a Defense Evasion technique for macOS, Linux, and Windows. It involves undermining OS and security product trust mechanisms, such as code signing certificates or file attribute warnings, to allow untrusted programs to execute. This can be achieved by modifying file permissions or registry settings, or by creating or stealing code signing certificates. The vulnerability CVE-2023-46805 is a related weakness that could be exploited in this process.

13831.name: T1001
13831.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]T1001, Data Obfuscation, is a command-and-control technique used on Windows, Linux, macOS, and ESXi platforms. It involves hiding C2 communications to make detection and analysis difficult, not necessarily through encryption. Specific methods include adding junk data to protocol traffic, using steganography, or impersonating legitimate protocols to blend in. This technique is distinct from custom protocols (T1094) or protocol tunneling (T1572), focusing on obfuscating the content or appearance of the communication channel itself.[/profile]

13832.name: T1051
13832.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]T1051, also known as Shared Webroot, is a deprecated lateral movement technique for Windows. It involves adversaries placing malicious files into a web server's accessible webroot directory via an open network share. When a user or process browses to the compromised content, the web server executes it, potentially granting the adversary the privileges of the web server process. This method could be used to deploy remote access tools for further system compromise.

13833.name: T1024
13833.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]T1024, also known as Custom Cryptographic Protocol, is a Command and Control technique. Adversaries use custom or self-implemented cryptographic algorithms to obfuscate C2 traffic, which can range from simple XOR operations with a fixed key to more sophisticated schemes. This differs from using junk data (T1001.001) or a custom C2 protocol (T1094), as it specifically focuses on the encryption layer to hide the traffic's content, making analysis and detection more difficult.

13834.name: T1069
13834.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]T1069, Permission Groups Discovery, is a Discovery tactic technique applicable to Windows, Linux, macOS, and cloud platforms. Adversaries use it to enumerate user groups and their permissions, such as by querying local groups with commands like `net localgroup` or leveraging tools like BloodHound for Active Directory, to identify accounts with elevated privileges for follow-on targeting. It is associated with groups including FIN13, APT41, and Scattered Spider.

13835.name: Permission Groups Discovery
13835.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Permission Groups Discovery is the MITRE ATT&CK technique T1069 under the Discovery tactic. It operates across Windows, Linux, macOS, Containers, IaaS, Office Suite, Identity Provider, and SaaS platforms. Adversaries execute this technique to discover group memberships and permission settings, identifying accounts with elevated privileges for follow-on targeting. Specific technical mechanics include using commands like `net localgroup` and `net group /domain` on Windows, `dscl . -list /Groups` on macOS, `groups` on Linux, and cloud-specific APIs such as Azure's `az ad user get-member-groups` or AWS's `GetBucketAcl`.

13836.name: Shared Webroot
13836.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Shared Webroot, also known as T1051, is a deprecated lateral movement technique for Windows. It involves adversaries placing malicious content, such as a PHP script and a remote access tool, into an open network file share that serves as a web server's content directory. When a user later visits the compromised webpage via a browser, the web server executes the malicious payload, potentially granting the adversary the privileges of the web server process.

13838.name: Subvert Trust Controls
13838.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Subvert Trust Controls is a Defense Evasion technique (MITRE ATT&CK T1553) targeting Windows, Linux, and macOS platforms. It involves undermining security mechanisms that warn about or block untrusted activity, such as code signing or internet download warnings. Specific technical methods include modifying file/directory permissions or registry keys to bypass controls, and creating or stealing code signing certificates to gain system trust. The technique is associated with the threat group Axiom and is linked to several CVEs.

13839.name: Data Obfuscation
13839.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Data Obfuscation, corresponding to MITRE ATT&CK technique T1001 under the Command and Control tactic, is applicable across Windows, Linux, macOS, and ESXi platforms. It involves hiding C2 communications to evade detection, not necessarily through encryption, but by methods such as adding junk data to protocol traffic, using steganography, or impersonating legitimate protocols. This technique has been associated with groups like Gamaredon Group.[/profile]

13841.name: RustBucket
13841.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]RustBucket is a macOS-targeting malware attributed to the BlueNoroff APT group, a sub-group of Lazarus. It employs obfuscation and masquerading for defense evasion, uses native API calls for execution, and establishes persistence via boot or logon autostart execution. Its command and control infrastructure includes domains like buy2x.com, www.thecloudnet.org, and azure.protection-service.cloud.[/profile]

13843.name: KANDYKORN
13843.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]KANDYKORN is a remote access trojan (RAT) attributed to the Lazarus Group. Its key technical behaviors include using the Native API for execution, employing a command and scripting interpreter, and utilizing obfuscation for defense evasion. It establishes persistence via boot or logon autostart execution (T1547) and uses masquerading (T1036). The malware targets macOS systems, as indicated by its infrastructure overlap with RustBucket, and has been used in intrusions against blockchain engineers. Associated infrastructure includes the domain buy2x.com.[/profile]

13845.name: TodoSwift
13845.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]TodoSwift is a malware that employs the Boot or Logon Autostart Execution (T1547) technique for persistence on macOS, Linux, and Windows. It utilizes Native API (T1106) for execution, leverages Command and Scripting Interpreters (T1059), and employs Masquerading (T1036) and Obfuscated Files or Information (T1027) for defense evasion. Its associated infrastructure includes the domain buy2x.com.[/profile]

13859.name: T1195.002
13859.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]T1195.002, Compromise Software Supply Chain, is an Initial Access technique applicable to Windows, Linux, and macOS. It involves adversaries manipulating software prior to consumer receipt to enable compromise, typically by tampering with the application source code, its update mechanism, or compiled releases. This activity is associated with groups including APT41, FIN7, and Sandworm Team, and has been exploited in incidents leveraging vulnerabilities such as CVE-2023-0669.

13860.name: T1552.001
13860.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]T1552.001, known as Credentials In Files, is a credential-access technique applicable to Windows, Linux, macOS, Containers, and IaaS platforms. Adversaries search local file systems and remote shares for insecurely stored credentials, which can include user-created files, shared credential stores, configuration files containing passwords, or source code with embedded secrets. In cloud environments, credentials are often found in local configuration files or as parameters within container logs, and can be read or copied for reuse. This technique is associated with groups including APT33, MuddyWater, and Scattered Spider.

13903.name: T1585
13903.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]The entity is MITRE ATT&CK technique T1585: Establish Accounts, a Resource Development tactic on the PRE platform. Adversaries create and cultivate accounts on services like social media, email providers, or cloud platforms to build operational personas, support social engineering, or acquire infrastructure. This activity is associated with groups like APT17 and Kimsuky.

13904.name: T1059.004
13904.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]The entity T1059.004, known as Unix Shell, is a MITRE ATT&CK technique under the Execution tactic for Linux, macOS, ESXi, and Network Device platforms. It involves adversaries abusing Unix shell commands and scripts (e.g., sh, bash, zsh) for execution, which can control all system aspects and support scripts for sequential commands, conditionals, and loops. This technique is used interactively via C2 channels or lateral movement like SSH, or through scripts for payload delivery and persistence, with stripped-down shells like Busybox common on embedded systems. It is associated with groups including UNC3886, Volt Typhoon, and APT41, and has been linked to vulnerabilities such as CVE-2025-4428 and CVE-2025-22457.[/profile]

13905.name: T1110
13905.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]T1110 (Brute Force) is a Credential Access technique applicable to multiple platforms including Windows, Linux, and macOS. It involves systematically guessing passwords through repetitive attempts, which can be performed interactively against a live service or offline against previously acquired password hashes. This technique is often used to gain initial access or leverage other compromised data, and it is associated with vulnerabilities like CVE-2017-10271 and numerous threat groups including APT28 and APT41.

13906.name: T1586
13906.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]T1586 "Compromise Accounts" is a Resource Development technique in the MITRE ATTACK framework for the PRE platform. Adversaries compromise existing online accounts to create trusted personas for operations, using methods like credential phishing, purchasing credentials, brute forcing with breached password dumps, or bribing insiders. Compromised accounts, such as email, can be further developed and directly leveraged for subsequent phishing attacks.

13908.name: FrostyFerret
13908.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]FrostyFerret is a macOS malware family also known as FROSTYFERRET_UI, FRIENDLYFERRET_SECD, and MULTI_FROSTYFERRET_CMDCODES, attributed to the Wagemole group. It achieves persistence via Boot or Logon Autostart Execution (T1547) by creating a system registry key. It uses Data Encoding (T1132) for command-and-control obfuscation and is associated with infrastructure domains like vidintermaster.com, api.camdriverhub.cloud, and videorecruitpro.com. Its technical behaviors include Account Discovery (T1087), Clipboard Data collection (T1115), and Input Capture (T1056). It is distributed in files such as VCam_ARM64.zip, CameraAccess.zip, and VCam_x86_64.zip.[/profile]

13909.name: GolangGhost
13909.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]GolangGhost, also known as golangghost, is a malware attributed to the Wagemole group. It employs techniques including Boot or Logon Autostart Execution (T1547) for persistence, Clipboard Data (T1115) and Input Capture (T1056) for credential collection, Data Encoding (T1132) for command and control obfuscation, and relies on User Execution (T1204). It targets cryptocurrency sectors in India and uses infrastructure such as videorecruitpro.com, api.videodriverzone.cloud, jobinterview360.com, api.drivercamhub.cloud, and vidassess360.com.[profile]

14062.name: CookieTime
14062.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]CookieTime is a malware associated with the Lazarus Group. It employs Data Obfuscation and Encrypted Channel techniques for command and control to evade detection. Its infection procedure is referenced in the context of other Lazarus-associated malware families like AppleJeus and DTRATZARUS.[/profile]

14063.name: LPEClient
14063.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]The malware LPEClient, also known as lpeclient, is a profiling tool attributed to the Lazarus Group. It is associated with the ThreatNeedle and Bookcode clusters and has been used in attacks targeting South Korea and the defense industry. Its technical behaviors involve exploiting vulnerabilities like CVE-2019-0859 and CVE-2019-0797 for initial access, and it employs command and control techniques including Data Obfuscation, Data Encoding, and Encrypted Channel to evade detection. The malware's delivery mechanisms include Phishing and reliance on User Execution. Its primary target platform is Windows.[/profile]

14064.name: ServiceChanger
14064.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]ServiceChanger, also known as SAVService, is a malware that employs Data Obfuscation and Data Encoding techniques to hide its command and control communications, and uses an Encrypted Channel to conceal its traffic. Its initial access is facilitated through User Execution, often triggered by Phishing campaigns. The malware has been associated with exploiting vulnerabilities CVE-2019-0797 and CVE-2019-0859, and has been mentioned in the context of threat groups like Lazarus Group.[/profile]

14065.name: Charamel Loader
14065.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Charamel Loader is a malware loader. It employs Data Obfuscation and Data Encoding to hide its command and control traffic, uses an Encrypted Channel for C2 communications, and relies on User Execution and Phishing for initial deployment. Its operations leverage vulnerabilities CVE-2019-0797 and CVE-2019-0859. The loader has been associated with the USBCulprit Loader cluster and shares infrastructure or code patterns with other loaders like Nitrogen and Vetta. It is linked to threat groups including APT22, APT26, APT31, APT41, Aurora Panda, Calypso Group, Dragonok, Emissary Panda, Hellsing, Hurricane Panda, Leviathan, Mirage, Mustang Panda, Nettraveler, Nightshade Panda, Slime29, Samurai Panda, Stone Panda, UPS, and Violin Panda.[/profile]

14066.name: CookiePlus
14066.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]CookiePlus is a malware that targets browser cookies from Chrome, msedge, brave, opera, 360se, 360browser, yandex, UCBrowser, and QQBrowser, storing stolen data in ZIP files within the %TEMP%\cookies_data folder. It leverages vulnerabilities like CVE-2019-0797 and CVE-2019-0859 for initial access and employs TTPs including User Execution (T1204) and Phishing (T1566) for deployment, with Data Obfuscation (T1001), Data Encoding (T1132), and Encrypted Channel (T1573) to hide its command and control communications.[/profile]

14067.name: RollMid
14067.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]RollMid, also known as Kaolin RAT, is a malware attributed to the Lazarus Group. It employs a loader that retrieves key components and configuration data from a binary blob, establishes command and control (C2) communication, and utilizes techniques including Data Obfuscation, Data Encoding, and Encrypted Channel for its C2 traffic. It targets Windows systems and has been associated with exploiting vulnerabilities CVE-2019-0797 and CVE-2019-0859.[/profile]

14068.name: MISTPEN
14068.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]MISTPEN, also known as mistpen, is a malware variant associated with the threat group UNC2970. It employs techniques for command and control, including Data Obfuscation to hide communications, Data Encoding to transform C2 traffic, and uses an Encrypted Channel to conceal its traffic. Initial access is facilitated through User Execution, often via Phishing. The malware leverages vulnerabilities CVE-2019-0797 and CVE-2019-0859. A specific variant is identified as TSVIPsrv.dll.[/profile]

14070.name: Ranid Downloader
14070.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Ranid Downloader, also known as a Downloader, is a malware downloader associated with groups like APT29, APT32, APT41, and FIN7. Its key technical behaviors include using Data Obfuscation and Data Encoding to hide command and control traffic, employing an Encrypted Channel for C2 communication, and relying on User Execution and Phishing for initial deployment. It targets Windows platforms and has been linked to exploitation of vulnerabilities such as CVE-2019-0797 and CVE-2019-0859.[/profile]

14074.name: Filebroser
14074.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Filebroser is a malware with no known aliases, attributed to the threat actor group Comment Crew. Its key technical behaviors include data collection from information repositories (T1213), data encoding for command and control (T1132), deploying web shells for persistence (T1505.003), using remote access tools for C2 (T1219), and leveraging external remote services for initial access (T1133). Its target platforms are Windows, Linux, and macOS, and it has been associated with infrastructure domains like dgtmeta.com and learning.gensci-china.com.[/profile]

14075.name: JSPSpy
14075.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]JSPSpy, also known as JSPSpy, is a remote access tool (RAT) that establishes command and control via web shells, uses data encoding for obfuscation, and leverages techniques like Remote Desktop Protocol for lateral movement and Data from Information Repositories for collection. It targets web servers on platforms including Windows and Linux, with associated infrastructure domains such as dgtmeta.com and learning.gensci-china.com, and has been observed in activities linked to China.[/profile]

14079.name: Remote Access Tools
14079.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Remote Access Tools is the MITRE ATT&CK technique T1219 under the Command and Control tactic, targeting Windows, Linux, and macOS platforms. It involves the abuse of legitimate software like desktop support or remote management tools to establish interactive C2 channels via graphical interfaces, command lines, or protocol tunnels, often installing persistence mechanisms like Windows Services. Adversaries use these tools post-compromise for redundant access, remote desktop sessions, or as malware components for reverse connections, and groups like CARBANAK and FIN7 have employed this technique.[/profile]

14082.name: Manuscrypt
14082.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Manuscrypt is a Remote Access Trojan (RAT) attributed to the Lazarus group, primarily targeting Windows with a Linux variant also identified. It employs techniques including Exploitation for Defense Evasion (T1211) and Exploitation for Privilege Escalation (T1068), and utilizes adversary-controlled domains (T1583.001) and digital certificates (T1588.004) for resource development and command and control. The malware is associated with vulnerability CVE-2024-4947 and shares configuration structural similarities with the DACLS malware.[/profile]

14084.name: T1608.004
14084.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]T1608.004 Drive-by Target is a Resource Development technique (PRE platform) where adversaries stage malicious content on controlled or compromised websites to exploit visiting systems, often through browser vulnerabilities like CVE-2024-4947 or CVE-2019-0859. This involves uploading malicious scripts (e.g., JavaScript) into web pages, using malvertising, or compromising sites to profile and target specific user communities in watering hole attacks, as employed by groups like APT32 and FIN7.

14088.name: T1211
14088.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]T1211, Exploitation for Defense Evasion, is a Defense Evasion technique for macOS, Linux, Windows, IaaS, and SaaS platforms. It involves exploiting vulnerabilities, particularly in defensive security software, to bypass or disable security features. Adversaries may target these defenses directly after discovery, as seen with groups like Velvet Ant and APT28, using exploits to execute adversary-controlled code and evade detection. A related vulnerability is CVE-2024-4947.[/profile]

14089.name: T1588.002
14089.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]T1588.002, also known as Tool, is a Resource Development technique in the MITRE ATT&CK framework for the PRE platform. Adversaries acquire software tools, such as by purchasing, stealing, or downloading them, to support their operations, including post-compromise execution and testing against security software. This includes obtaining commercial red teaming tools like Cobalt Strike, cracking trial versions, or stealing licenses from other entities. The technique is widely used by numerous threat groups including APT29, FIN7, and Lazarus Group.

14090.name: T1588.001
14090.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]T1588.001 (Malware) is a Resource Development technique in the MITRE ATTACK framework, operating on the PRE platform. Adversaries acquire malware—including payloads, droppers, backdoors, and C2 tools—by purchasing, stealing, or downloading it from criminal marketplaces or third-party developers to support their operations. This technique is associated with groups like UNC3886, APT1, and Scattered Spider, and is linked to vulnerabilities such as CVE-2024-4947 and CVE-2023-0669.[/profile]

14091.name: T1588.004
14091.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]T1588.004, also known as Digital Certificates, is a Resource Development technique within the MITRE ATT&CK framework for the PRE platform. Adversaries may purchase or steal SSL/TLS certificates to enable trusted, encrypted command and control communications, such as using Asymmetric Cryptography with Web Protocols, or to facilitate Adversary-in-the-Middle attacks if the certificate is installed as a trusted root. Certificates can be acquired through front organizations, stolen validation data from compromised entities, or directly from compromised certificate authorities, including free domain validation services.

14092.name: Exploitation for Defense Evasion
14092.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Exploitation for Defense Evasion is MITRE ATT&CK technique T1211 under the Defense Evasion tactic, targeting platforms including Windows, Linux, macOS, IaaS, and SaaS. It involves exploiting vulnerabilities, particularly in defensive security software or cloud infrastructure, to bypass or disable security features, evade logs, or deploy hidden resources. Threat groups like APT28 and Velvet Ant have employed this technique.

14093.name: T1068
14093.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]This technique is MITRE ATT&CK T1068: Exploitation for Privilege Escalation, a Privilege Escalation tactic. It targets macOS, Linux, Windows, and Containers. Adversaries exploit software vulnerabilities, often in OS components or high-privilege software, to execute code and elevate permissions from user to SYSTEM/root or escape containerized environments. A specific method is Bring Your Own Vulnerable Driver (BYOVD), where a signed, vulnerable driver is delivered to the host and exploited for kernel-mode execution. It is associated with vulnerabilities like CVE-2021-26858 and used by groups including APT28, APT29, and Volt Typhoon.

14094.name: Tool
14094.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Tool is a Resource Development technique (T1588.002) in the MITRE ATTACK framework, primarily on the PRE platform. It involves adversaries acquiring software tools—through purchase, theft, or download—that are not inherently malicious, such as PsExec or Cobalt Strike, to support their operations. These tools are obtained to enable post-compromise behaviors, for testing against security software, and may involve stealing licenses or cracking trial versions.

14095.name: Drive-by Target
14095.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Drive-by Target is MITRE ATT&CK technique T1608.004 under the Resource Development tactic, applicable to PRE platforms. It involves staging malicious resources on adversary-controlled or compromised websites to facilitate Drive-by Compromise (T1189). Specific mechanics include injecting malicious scripts like JavaScript into web pages or forum posts, modifying script files from writeable cloud storage, and crafting malicious advertisements (Malvertising). Adversaries may also use these sites to profile a victim's browser for vulnerabilities prior to exploitation, often in targeted watering hole attacks.[/profile]

14096.name: Digital Certificates
14096.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Digital Certificates is a Resource Development technique (T1588.004) for the PRE platform. Adversaries obtain valid certificates, such as SSL/TLS or code signing certificates, from third-party providers to enable encrypted command and control, add legitimacy to malicious infrastructure, or sign malicious payloads. This acquisition supports subsequent activities like establishing secure channels or bypassing security checks.

14097.name: Exploitation for Privilege Escalation
14097.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Exploitation for Privilege Escalation (T1068) is a Privilege Escalation technique applicable to Windows, Linux, macOS, and Container platforms. It involves exploiting software vulnerabilities, often in OS components or high-privilege software, to execute adversary-controlled code and elevate permissions from user to SYSTEM/root or escape a container to the host. A specific method is Bring Your Own Vulnerable Driver (BYOVD), where a signed vulnerable driver is delivered to a machine to exploit it for kernel-mode execution. This technique is used by numerous threat groups, including APT28, APT29, and FIN6, and is associated with vulnerabilities like CVE-2021-26855.[/profile]

14106.name: T1608
14106.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]The entity is Stage Capabilities, MITRE ATT&CK technique T1608 under the Resource Development tactic for PRE platforms. This technique involves adversaries uploading, installing, or setting up capabilities—developed or obtained—on infrastructure they control, such as purchased, rented, or compromised servers, or on web services like GitHub, Pastebin, or PaaS offerings. These staged capabilities support various operations, including hosting web resources for drive-by compromises or spearphishing links, enabling ingress tool transfer, or installing SSL/TLS certificates for encrypted command and control.

14119.name: T1040
14119.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]T1040, Network Sniffing, is a credential-access and discovery technique applicable to Windows, Linux, macOS, Network Devices, and IaaS platforms. It involves passively capturing network traffic by placing a network interface into promiscuous mode or using span/mirroring services (like AWS Traffic Mirroring) to monitor data in transit. This can capture unencrypted user credentials and reveal system configuration details, often supporting subsequent lateral movement or adversary-in-the-middle attacks. The technique is associated with groups like APT28 and Sandworm Team, and a related vulnerability is CVE-2023-20198.[/profile]

14120.name: T1048
14120.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]T1048, Exfiltration Over Alternative Protocol, is an Exfiltration tactic technique applicable across Windows, Linux, macOS, and cloud platforms. It involves stealing data by sending it over a network protocol different from the primary command and control channel, such as FTP, SMTP, HTTP/S, DNS, or SMB, potentially to an alternate destination. Execution commonly leverages native OS utilities like Net/SMB, FTP, or curl, and can target IaaS/SaaS platforms via web consoles or Cloud APIs. The technique is associated with groups like TEAMTNT and PLAY, and it can be used in conjunction with automated exfiltration processes.[/profile]

14121.name: T1070.006
14121.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]T1070.006, also known as Timestomp, is a Defense Evasion technique for Windows, Linux, macOS, and ESXi platforms. It modifies file timestamps (like modify, access, create, and change times) to hide malicious files among legitimate ones. On Windows, adversaries typically alter the user-accessible `$STANDARD_INFORMATION` attribute via API calls, and may also modify the kernel-level `$FILE_NAME` attribute in a "double timestomping" process to evade forensic detection. On Linux and ESXi, commands like `touch -a -m -t` are used to set specific timestamps. This technique is often paired with file Masquerading and has been used by groups like APT28, APT29, and Lazarus.[/profile]

14123.name: InvisibleFerret
14123.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]InvisibleFerret is a modular Python malware family used for data exfiltration and remote access, attributed to the North Korea-affiliated threat actor Contagious Interview (also referenced as DeceptiveDevelopment or Wagemole). It consists of four modules: main, payload, browser, and AnyDesk, and is historically deployed via the BeaverTail malware. Its key techniques include credential access via macOS Keychain (T1555.001), persistence via Launch Agents (T1543.001), subverting trust controls (T1553), and browser information discovery. It targets macOS platforms and has used infrastructure like block-digital.online and 45.159.248.110.[/profile]

14124.name: LightlessCan
14124.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]LightlessCan, also known as lightlesscan, is a Remote Access Trojan (RAT) attributed to the Lazarus group. It is a significant evolution from its predecessor, BlindingCan, with a notable focus on mimicking legitimate red-teaming Windows commands such as wmic, whoami, systeminfo, netstat, and netsh. Its technical behaviors include Subverting Trust Controls for defense evasion, using Data Encoding (like Base64) for C2 obfuscation, staging data prior to exfiltration, capturing user input for credential access, and relying on user execution via phishing. It primarily targets Windows platforms and has been observed using C2 infrastructure at IP addresses like 86.104.72.247 and 103.35.190.170 with proxy scripts such as Proxy.php.[/profile]

14125.name: Tropidoor
14125.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Tropidoor is a malware distributed via recruitment emails, often alongside BeaverTail, and is associated with the threat group Wagemole. Its technical behaviors include subverting trust controls to bypass security warnings, encoding C2 traffic to evade detection, staging collected data before exfiltration, capturing user input for credential theft, and removing indicators to hinder forensic analysis. Its known infrastructure involves C2 servers using HTTP/HTTPS endpoints like http://103.35.190.170/Proxy.php and https://45.8.146.93/proxy/Proxy.php.

14126.name: BeaverTail
14126.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]BeaverTail is a cross-platform infostealer malware family attributed to the North Korea-affiliated threat group Contagious Interview (also known as Wagemole). It employs techniques like Launch Agent for persistence on macOS, Keychain for credential access, and Browser Information Discovery to harvest data from browsers. The malware targets Windows, Linux, and macOS systems, and is used to deploy follow-on payloads like InvisibleFerret. Associated infrastructure includes domains like driverservices.store and block-digital.online, and IPs such as 45.159.248.110.[/profile]

14134.name: Data Staged
14134.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Data Staged, known as T1074 within the MITRE ATT&CK framework, is a Collection tactic technique applicable across Windows, Linux, macOS, IaaS, and ESXi platforms. It involves adversaries centralizing collected data into a specific location or directory before exfiltration, often using common command shell utilities like cmd or bash to copy files. Data may be kept in separate files or archived into one, and in cloud environments, staging can occur within a specific instance or virtual machine. This process minimizes connections to the command and control server to evade detection, with groups like Scattered Spider and Volt Typhoon employing it.

14136.name: RollSling
14136.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]RollSling is a malware loader, an in-memory stage deployed by the Kaolin Rat malware and attributed to the Lazarus Group. Its key technical behavior is to locate and load a subsequent binary payload from the same directory or a Package Cache folder. It connects to command and control infrastructure using the HTTP protocol, as indicated by associated indicators like 'http://162.19.71.175:7443/bottom.gif'. It is associated with the exploitation of vulnerability CVE-2023-42793 and utilizes tactics including Automated Collection, Automated Exfiltration, and System Service Discovery.

14137.name: FeedLoad
14137.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]FeedLoad is a malware that uses HTTP POST requests for command and control, as seen in its communication to '/rssnews.php'. It employs Application Layer Protocol (HTTP) for C2 and is associated with Automated Exfiltration to transfer data. Its infrastructure includes domains like 3dkit.org and IPs such as 147.78.149.201, and it exploits vulnerability CVE-2023-42793. It performs System Service Discovery and Automated Collection, and indicators include URLs like http://www.mge.sn/themes/classic/modules/ps_rssfeed/feedmd.zip. It is linked to or shares behaviors with malware families like infy, tonnerre, and stabuniq.[/profile]

14138.name: HazyLoad
14138.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]HazyLoad, also known as hazyload, is a malware attributed to the Silent Chollima group. Its key technical behaviors include vulnerability scanning for initial access, automated collection and exfiltration of data, system service discovery for reconnaissance, and command and control using application layer protocols like HTTP. It has targeted materials research sectors and leveraged infrastructure such as the domains dersmarketim.com and bandarpowder.com, along with specific IP addresses and URLs for C2 communications.[/profile]

14140.name: ForestTiger
14140.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]ForestTiger is a malware, also known as scoringmathtea, and is adopted by the QUILTED TIGER group, which is associated with the Lazarus group. Its key technical behaviors include using Application Layer Protocol for command and control, conducting System Service Discovery, and performing Automated Collection and Automated Exfiltration of data. It targets Windows, Linux, and macOS platforms and has been linked to infrastructure indicators such as the domains galerielamy.com and dersmarketim.com.

14180.name: T1595.002
14180.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]T1595.002, also known as Vulnerability Scanning, is a reconnaissance technique within the MITRE ATT&CK framework, applicable to the PRE platform. This technique involves scanning victim systems to identify exploitable vulnerabilities by checking software configurations, versions, and network artifacts like server banners and listening ports. Information gathered can enable further reconnaissance, capability development, or initial access via exploits. The technique is associated with groups like APT41 and Sandworm Team, and a specific example includes scanning for vulnerabilities such as CVE-2023-42793.

14181.name: Vulnerability Scanning

14227.name: T1564.004

14228.name: NTFS File Attributes
14228.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]NTFS File Attributes is a Defense Evasion technique under MITRE ATT&CK ID T1564.004, targeting Windows platforms. 14229.name: T1569.002

14230.name: Service Execution

This method is commonly used for remote execution and in conjunction with persistence techniques like New Service (T1050) or Windows Service (T1543.003). 14231.name: T1189

This method is distinct from server exploitation and is frequently used in targeted campaigns like strategic web compromises or watering hole attacks by various threat groups.

14232.name: Web Protocols

14233.name: Drive-by Compromise
14233.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Drive-by Compromise, identified as T1189, is an Initial Access technique targeting macOS, Linux, and Windows platforms. It involves compromising a user's system when they visit a website, typically by exploiting vulnerabilities in their web browser or plugins. The process often includes injecting malicious scripts into legitimate or compromised websites, using malicious advertisements (malvertising), or abusing browser push notifications to deliver exploit code. Upon visiting the site, scripts automatically execute to scan for and exploit vulnerable software versions, potentially leading to code execution without requiring further user interaction beyond the initial page load. This method is distinct from server-focused exploits and is commonly associated with strategic web compromises or watering hole attacks. A related vulnerability is CVE-2019-0797.[/profile]

14234.name: T1049

On ESXi, the specific command `esxi network ip connection list` is used. This activity helps adversaries map connected systems and services, including within cloud VPCs. 14235.name: System Network Connections Discovery
14235.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]System Network Connections Discovery, identified as MITRE ATT&CK technique T1049 under the Discovery tactic, operates across Windows, Linux, macOS, Network Devices, IaaS, and ESXi platforms. Specific mechanics include using netstat, "net use," and "net session" on Windows; netstat, lsof, who -a, and w on Linux and macOS; commands like `show ip sockets` on network devices; and `esxi network ip connection list` on ESXi servers. 14236.name: T1583.003

14237.name: T1135

14238.name: Network Share Discovery

14289.name: Browser Information Discovery

14293.name: Keychain

14303.name: Non-Application Layer Protocol
