Its key technical behaviors include using Binary Padding (T1027.001) for defense evasion, DNS (T1071.004) and Asymmetric Cryptography (T1573.002) for command and control, and Service Execution (T1035) for execution on Windows. It also leverages SSH (T1021.004) for lateral movement on Linux, macOS, and ESXi. Associated infrastructure includes domains such as systemupdate.info, servicechecker[.]top, servicesupdate[.]info, mail-update[.]info, freeheadlines[.]top, and servicepackupdate[.]info.[/profile]

16549.name: BellaCPP
16549.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]BellaCPP is a malware attributed to the Wagemole group. It employs Asymmetric Cryptography (T1573.002) to conceal C2 traffic, uses DNS (T1071.004) for command-and-control communication, and leverages SSH (T1021.004) for lateral movement on Linux, macOS, and ESXi platforms. It also uses Service Execution (T1569.002) on Windows and Binary Padding for defense evasion. Its infrastructure includes the domain systemupdate.info.[/profile]

16551.name: unkown_apt_group
16551.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]This intrusion set is most likely the APT group known as Charming Kitten, also known as APT35, Phosphorus, and TA453. Its key malware includes BellaCiao and BellaCPP, which utilize DNS and asymmetric cryptography for command and control, SSH for lateral movement, and binary padding for evasion. Key TTPs involve spear phishing with malicious links (T1566.002) for initial access and credential API hooking (T1056.004). The group is attributed to Iran and primarily targets entities in the United States, Germany, and other Western nations, with motivations centered on espionage and information gathering.[/profile]

16554.name: Binary Padding
16554.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Binary Padding is a Defense Evasion technique (MITRE ATT&CK T1027.001) applicable to Windows, Linux, and macOS. It works by appending junk data to a malicious binary, increasing its file size to bypass security tool scanning limits and altering its checksum to evade hash-based blocklists and static signatures. This padding, often generated by a function, does not affect the binary's core functionality but can hinder analysis by services with file size restrictions.

16555.name: T1071.004
16555.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]T1071.004, also known as DNS, is a command-and-control technique within the MITRE ATT&CK framework applicable to Windows, Linux, macOS, ESXi, and network devices. It involves adversaries using the Domain Name System (DNS) protocol to covertly communicate with compromised systems, often by tunneling commands and data within DNS queries and responses, such as embedding them in TXT or A records, to blend with legitimate administrative traffic and bypass network defenses.

16556.name: T1027.001
16556.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]T1027.001, known as Binary Padding, is a Defense Evasion technique applicable to Windows, Linux, and macOS. It works by appending junk data to a malicious binary's end or sections, altering its on-disk checksum and file size to evade hash-based blocklists, static antivirus signatures, and bypass security tools with file size limitations. It is associated with groups like APT29 and Patchwork, and a related vulnerability is CVE-2025-22457.[/profile]

16557.name: DNS
16557.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]DNS is the standardized MITRE ATT&CK technique T1071.004 under the Command and Control tactic, applicable across Windows, Linux, macOS, ESXi, and Network Devices. It involves adversaries using the Domain Name System protocol for C2 communication to blend with normal traffic, often by tunneling data within DNS queries and responses, embedding commands in fields like TXT or A records, and using low-frequency beaconing to evade detection.

16558.name: AnvilEcho
16558.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]AnvilEcho is a malware that employs T1497 Virtualization/Sandbox Evasion to detect analysis environments and alter its behavior, uses T1204 User Execution to trick users into running malicious code, utilizes T1056 Input Capture to intercept and steal credentials, and establishes command-and-control via T1095 Non-Application Layer Protocol using protocols like ICMP or UDP. It leverages T1021 Remote Services, such as SSH or RDP, for lateral movement. Associated infrastructure includes domains like deepspaceocean.info and understandingthewar.org.[/profile]

16560.name: BlackSmith
16560.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]BlackSmith is a malware used by the Lazarus Group in Operation Blacksmith to target manufacturing, agriculture, and physical security sectors. Its technical behaviors include Input Capture (T1056) to steal credentials, Credentials from Password Stores (T1555), and the use of Remote Services (T1021) for lateral movement. It employs Virtualization/Sandbox Evasion (T1497) to avoid detection and relies on User Execution (T1204). Associated infrastructure includes domains like deepspaceocean.info and understandingthewar.org.[/profile]

16578.name: T1009
16578.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]T1009, known as Binary Padding, is a Defense Evasion technique. It involves appending junk data to malware binaries to alter their on-disk checksum and file size, thereby evading hash-based blocklists and bypassing security tools with file size limitations. This padding does not affect the malware's core functionality.

16606.name: T1056.004
16606.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Credential API Hooking (T1056.004) is a Collection and Credential Access technique for Windows, Linux, and macOS. It works by intercepting API or system function calls that contain credential parameters. On Windows, adversaries implement hooks via hook procedures, Import Address Table (IAT) hooking, or inline hooking to redirect function execution. On Linux and macOS, they can use environment variables like `LD_PRELOAD` or `DYLD_INSERT_LIBRARIES` to load malicious libraries that hook functions such as `libc read` used by SSH. This method specifically targets credential parameters within function calls, distinguishing it from general keylogging.

16607.name: T1585.001
16607.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]T1585.001 (Social Media Accounts) is a Resource Development technique on the PRE platform. Adversaries create and cultivate social media accounts to build fictitious or impersonated personas, which involves developing profiles, networks, and photos to appear legitimate. These personas are then used to establish connections with targets, facilitating operations like social engineering and spearphishing for initial access. Groups including APT32, Lazarus Group, and Scattered Spider have employed this technique.

16608.name: T1593.002
16608.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]T1593.002, also known as Search Engines, is a reconnaissance technique within the MITRE ATT&CK framework, applicable to the PRE platform. It involves adversaries using search engines to gather victim information by crafting specialized queries with specific syntax to index and locate sensitive data such as network details or credentials, which can facilitate subsequent operations like phishing or establishing initial access.

16609.name: T1592
16609.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]T1592, known as Gather Victim Host Information, is a reconnaissance technique within the MITRE ATT&CK framework operating on the PRE platform. It involves collecting details about a victim's hosts, such as administrative data, operating system, and language, to inform targeting. This information can be gathered through methods like active scanning, phishing, or by exploiting compromised websites to collect data from visitors, including via User-Agent HTTP headers to identify software and system versions. The technique may reveal vulnerabilities, as indicated by its association with CVE-2022-2294, and is used by groups like Volt Typhoon to enable follow-on actions such as developing capabilities or gaining initial access.

16633.name: unkown_apt_group
16633.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]This intrusion set, likely a South Asia-focused APT group, uses malware families including AndroRAT and CrimsonRAT (also known as Oblique RAT), which has been used to target victims in Pakistan, Afghanistan, and India. Its technical profile includes TTPs such as Unix Shell Configuration Modification (T1546.004) for persistence on Linux/macOS, Junk Data (T1001.001) for C2 obfuscation, and Token Impersonation/Theft (T1134.001) for privilege escalation on Windows. The group's infrastructure has used domains like kp85.cyou and sorlastore.com. Analysis indicates potential overlaps with other clusters, including Lotus Panda (also known as Lotus Blossom and Spring Dragon), and possible links to the group known as BackdoorDiplomacy (also known as CloudComputating and Quarian). Its operations are primarily motivated by espionage targeting the South Asia region.[/profile]

16668.name: T1529
16668.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]T1529, System Shutdown/Reboot, is an Impact technique used on Windows, Linux, macOS, ESXi, and Network Devices. Adversaries execute shutdowns or reboots to disrupt system availability and impede recovery, often following other destructive actions. This can be performed via OS commands, remote CLI tools like 'reload', hypervisor consoles, or Windows API functions such as InitializeSystemShutdownExW and NtRaiseHardError, the latter potentially causing a BSOD. Groups like Lazarus Group, APT37, APT38, and Medusa Group have employed this technique.

16672.name: T1564.003
16672.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]The attack pattern T1564.003, known as Hidden Window, is a Defense Evasion technique for Windows, Linux, and macOS. It conceals malicious activity by hiding application windows from users. Specific technical mechanics include using the `-WindowStyle Hidden` flag in PowerShell, editing the Windows Registry's `WindowPosition` key to move windows off-screen, setting the `apple.awt.UIElement` tag in macOS plist files to hide Dock icons, and leveraging the Windows `CreateDesktop()` API to run processes like hidden VNC sessions on an invisible desktop. This technique is associated with threat actors including APT3, APT28, and FIN7.

16673.name: T1485
16673.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]T1485, Data Destruction, is an Impact technique targeting Windows, Linux, macOS, Containers, IaaS, and ESXi platforms. It aims to render data irrecoverable, often by overwriting files with random or specific data (like political imagery) instead of using simple OS deletion commands like `del` or `rm`. Malware may propagate via worm-like features using techniques such as Valid Accounts and SMB shares. In cloud environments, adversaries destroy crucial infrastructure like storage objects and VMs. Associated threat groups include APT38, Sandworm Team, and Lazarus Group.

16674.name: T1614
16674.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]System Location Discovery, designated T1614, is a Discovery technique used on Windows, Linux, macOS, and IaaS platforms to infer a victim's geographical location. Technical mechanics include checking system settings like time zone, keyboard layout, and language, using Windows API functions such as GetLocaleInfoW, querying cloud instance metadata services for availability zone, and performing IP address geolocation lookups. This information is used to shape follow-on adversarial actions.

16675.name: T1497.002
16675.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]T1497.002, Virtualization/Sandbox Evasion: User Activity Based Checks, is a Defense Evasion and Discovery technique for macOS, Linux, and Windows. It involves detecting analysis environments by checking for artifacts of virtual machines or sandboxes and monitoring user activity indicators like mouse movement speed, click frequency, browser history, or file counts in common directories. Upon detection, malware may alter its behavior, delay payload activation until specific user interactions occur (e.g., closing a document or double-clicking an image), or cease execution to evade analysis.

16676.name: T1134.001
16676.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]T1134.001, known as Token Impersonation/Theft, is a Defense Evasion and Privilege Escalation technique for Windows. It involves duplicating an existing user's token using functions like `DuplicateToken` or `DuplicateTokenEx` and then impersonating that security context via `ImpersonateLoggedOnUser` or `SetThreadToken` to attach to an existing thread, which is useful for targeting a user's non-network logon session. This is distinct from creating a new token or process.

16677.name: T1542
16677.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]T1542, also known as Pre-OS Boot, is a defense evasion and persistence technique applicable to Windows, Linux, macOS, and Network Devices. It involves adversaries establishing persistence by overwriting data in boot drivers or firmware components like BIOS or UEFI during the system boot process, before the operating system loads. This low-level execution makes detection by host-based security software difficult. Related rootkit functionality, specifically bootkits, can target the boot process to hide malware.

16678.name: T1222
16678.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]T1222, File and Directory Permissions Modification, is a Defense Evasion technique for macOS, Linux, Windows, and ESXi. It works by modifying file or directory permissions or attributes to bypass access control lists (ACLs), which may require taking ownership or using elevated privileges. This enables actions like modifying, replacing, or deleting protected files and is often a prerequisite for establishing persistence or hijacking execution flow, as seen in techniques like Unix Shell Configuration Modification.

16679.name: T1547.009
16679.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]T1547.009, known as Shortcut Modification, is a persistence and privilege-escalation technique for Windows. It involves creating or modifying shortcuts, such as those in the startup folder, to execute malicious programs during system boot or user login. Adversaries may edit the target path of a legitimate shortcut or replace it entirely to run their malware, often using masquerading to appear benign. This method has been used by groups like Lazarus Group, Gorgon Group, APT39, and Leviathan.

16680.name: T1542.003
16680.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]T1542.003, known as Bootkit, is a Defense Evasion and Persistence technique targeting Linux and Windows platforms. It operates by modifying a system's boot sectors, such as the Master Boot Record (MBR) or Volume Boot Record (VBR) on BIOS systems, or files within the EFI System Partition (ESP) on UEFI systems. This allows malicious code to execute before the operating system loads, residing below the OS layer to evade detection and complicate remediation. The technique has been associated with groups like Lazarus Group, APT41, and APT28.

16704.name: T1543.002
16704.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]T1543.002 - Systemd Service is a MITRE ATT&CK technique within the Persistence and Privilege Escalation tactics for Linux platforms. It involves creating or modifying systemd service unit files (`.service`) to execute malicious payloads repeatedly. Adversaries manipulate directives like `ExecStart` within these files, which are stored in directories such as `/systemd/system`, to establish persistence and potentially escalate privileges by altering the `User` directive or using systemd generators for dynamic unit file creation.

16708.name: T1001.001
16708.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]T1001.001, known as Junk Data, is a command and control technique within the MITRE ATT&CK framework applicable to Windows, Linux, macOS, and ESXi platforms. It operates by adding random or meaningless data to C2 protocols, such as appending, prepending, or inserting junk characters between significant ones, to obfuscate traffic and hinder trivial decoding or analysis methods. This technique has been associated with groups like APT28.

16709.name: T1546.004
16709.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]T1546.004, known as Unix Shell Configuration Modification, is a persistence and privilege-escalation technique for Linux and macOS platforms. It works by adversaries inserting malicious commands into shell configuration scripts—such as /etc/profile, ~/.bash_profile, or ~/.zshrc—that are automatically executed during user login, shell initialization, or session termination, thereby establishing persistence at the user or root level depending on the file modified.

16710.name: T1011.001
16710.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]T1011.001, Exfiltration Over Bluetooth, is an Exfiltration technique applicable to Windows, Linux, and macOS. It involves adversaries bypassing monitored primary networks by using a Bluetooth communication channel for data theft. This method is chosen when the adversary has physical proximity and sufficient access, exploiting that Bluetooth connections are often less secured and not routed through the defended enterprise network.

16711.name: T1037
16711.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]T1037, Boot or Logon Initialization Scripts, is a MITRE ATT&CK technique used for Persistence and Privilege Escalation on platforms including Windows, Linux, and macOS. It involves adversaries placing scripts that are automatically executed during system boot or user logon to establish and maintain access. This can require local or administrator credentials, and these scripts often run with higher privileges, enabling privilege escalation. The technique is associated with threat groups such as APT29 and APT41.

16721.name: Poseidon
16721.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Poseidon is a malware entity, also known as Poseidon Stealer or Odyssey Stealer. It is a Golang-based agent that compiles into executables for Linux and macOS x64 platforms. Its key behaviors include credential theft, aligning with the T1552 (Unsecured Credentials) technique, and establishing command-and-control using dynamic resolution (T1568) and data encoding (T1132) for evasion. It has been delivered via malspam campaigns, such as one using AGOV-themed lures targeting users in Switzerland. Associated infrastructure includes domains like mod.gov.in.indiandefence.directory and mea.gov.in.indiandefence.services.[/profile]

16803.name: Stage Capabilities
16803.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Stage Capabilities, identified as T1608, is a Resource Development technique within the MITRE ATT&CK framework applicable to pre-compromise platforms. It involves adversaries uploading, installing, or setting up previously developed or obtained tools—such as malware, exploits, or SSL/TLS certificates—onto infrastructure they control. This staging occurs on purchased, compromised, or public infrastructure like GitHub, PaaS services, or web servers to enable subsequent attack behaviors including drive-by compromises, spearphishing link targets, tool transfer, and command-and-control setup.

16805.name: AndroRAT
16805.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]AndroRAT, also known as androrat, is an Android Remote Access Trojan (RAT) family. It is associated with the attack techniques Stored Application Data for collecting local app data and User Execution for initial compromise. Its technical behaviors include command and control communication, as indicated by network traffic analysis and commands like 'rat_connect' and 'rat_cmd', and it functions by building malicious APKs to target the Android platform.[/profile]

16806.name: CapraRAT
16806.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]CapraRAT, an Android Remote Access Trojan (RAT), is attributed to the APT group APT36, also known as Earth Karkaddan or Transparent Tribe. It is deployed via trojanized applications, requiring user execution to install. Its key technical behaviors include extensive data collection from compromised devices, such as SMS messages, call recordings, audio, screenshots, photos, device files, location data, running apps, and notifications. It accesses this data through the Stored Application Data technique. The malware is part of the group's broader attack chain, showing design similarities to their Windows-based Crimson RAT.

16812.name: Stored Application Data
16812.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Stored Application Data is a mobile attack technique within the Collection tactic, targeting Android and iOS platforms. It involves adversaries accessing and collecting sensitive data stored locally by applications, such as databases, configuration files, or cached information, to gather credentials, personal data, or other valuable information from a compromised device.

16813.name: T1409
16813.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]T1409 is an attack pattern within the MITRE Mobile-ATT&CK framework, categorized under the Collection tactic. It operates on Android and iOS platforms and is also known as "Stored Application Data". This technique involves adversaries accessing and collecting sensitive data from application-specific storage locations on mobile devices.

16816.name: T1590
16816.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]T1590, known as Gather Victim Network Information, is a reconnaissance technique within the MITRE ATT&CK framework applicable to the PRE platform. It involves collecting details about a victim's networks, such as IP ranges, domain names, and topology, through methods like active scanning (e.g., scanning IP blocks), phishing for information, or querying open technical databases like WHOIS and DNS Dumpster. This intelligence gathering can enable subsequent activities like establishing operational resources or gaining initial access, as observed in campaigns by groups including Hafnium, Indrik Spider, and Volt Typhoon.[/profile]

16817.name: Akira
16817.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Akira is a ransomware family attributed to the threat group Storm-1567. It targets organizations by exploiting SSL VPN services, often found on default port 4433, and uses valid domain accounts for initial access and persistence. Its techniques include loading shared modules for execution and stopping services to inhibit response. The malware primarily impacts Windows, Linux, and ESXi platforms.

16818.name: unkown_apt_group
16818.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]This intrusion set is likely associated with the Akira ransomware operation, which has been attributed to the threat group Storm-1567 and shows connections to the Conti ransomware operation. Its key malware is Akira ransomware, which exploits remote services like SSL VPNs for initial access and uses enterprise software deployment tools for lateral movement. Its TTPs include Shared Modules (T1129), Subverting Trust Controls (T1553), and abusing Valid Accounts (T1078.001/.002) and Default Accounts for persistence and privilege escalation. The group is believed to operate with a financial motivation, primarily targeting Windows, Linux, and ESXi platforms across various sectors.

16819.name: T1129
16819.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]T1129, known as Shared Modules, is an execution technique within the MITRE ATT&CK framework applicable to Windows, Linux, and macOS. It involves adversaries executing malicious payloads by loading shared modules like DLLs or shared objects into processes. On Linux/macOS, this is achieved using functions like `dlopen` from `dlfcn.h` to load `.so` or `.dylib` files from arbitrary paths. On Windows, the module loader (e.g., via `LoadLibrary` or the Native API in `NTDLL.dll`) can load DLLs from local or UNC network paths, allowing adversaries to modularize malware functionality for tasks like command and control.

16820.name: Shared Modules
16820.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Shared Modules, identified as MITRE ATT&CK technique T1129 under the Execution tactic, operates on Windows, Linux, and macOS platforms. It involves executing malicious payloads by loading shared modules like DLLs or shared objects. Adversaries modularize malware functionality into these files, which are loaded via system APIs such as `LoadLibrary` on Windows or `dlopen`/`dlsym` from `dlfcn.h` on Linux/macOS, allowing execution from arbitrary local or UNC network paths.

16826.name: Cloud Accounts
16826.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Cloud Accounts is a sub-technique of Valid Accounts (T1078.004) within the MITRE ATT&CK framework, primarily used for Defense Evasion, Initial Access, Persistence, and Privilege Escalation on IaaS, SaaS, Office Suite, and Identity Provider platforms. It involves adversaries abusing legitimate user, service, or administrative accounts within cloud environments to gain access, often by compromising credentials via phishing or brute force. These accounts, which can be cloud-only or federated with on-premises directories, allow attackers to perform actions like pivoting to on-premises systems, creating additional credentials for persistence, and assuming elevated privileges through misconfigured roles or managed identities to move laterally and access sensitive data.

16827.name: T1547.006
16827.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]T1547.006, known as Kernel Modules and Extensions, is a technique for Persistence and Privilege Escalation on macOS and Linux platforms. It involves adversaries using Loadable Kernel Modules (LKMs) on Linux or kernel extensions (kexts) on macOS to run malicious code with the highest operating system privileges (Ring 0). On Linux, LKMs can be loaded to extend kernel functionality without a reboot, while on macOS, kexts are loaded via `kextload` commands and bypass security policies unless System Integrity Protection (SIP) is enabled, with kexts being deprecated in favor of System Extensions since macOS Catalina.

16828.name: T1078.004
16828.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]T1078.004, known as Valid Accounts: Cloud Accounts, is a technique used across Initial Access, Persistence, Privilege Escalation, and Defense Evasion tactics. It targets platforms including IaaS, SaaS, Office Suite, and Identity Providers. The technique involves adversaries compromising valid user or service accounts in cloud environments, which may be cloud-only or hybrid-joined via federation with on-premises directories like Active Directory. Attackers may gain access through methods like Brute Force or Phishing and then create additional cloud credentials for persistence, bypass multi-factor authentication, or abuse misconfigured roles to assume elevated privileges, such as leveraging Azure Managed Identities to steal access tokens for lateral movement. Groups like APT29, APT28, and Scattered Spider have used this technique.

16829.name: T1078.002
16829.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]T1078.002, also known as Domain Accounts, is a Valid Accounts sub-technique used for Initial Access, Persistence, Privilege Escalation, and Defense Evasion on Windows, Linux, macOS, and ESXi platforms. It involves adversaries obtaining and abusing credentials of Active Directory-managed domain accounts, which can cover users, administrators, and services. Compromise is often achieved via methods like OS Credential Dumping or password reuse, granting access to privileged domain resources and is associated with groups like Volt Typhoon and Wizard Spider.

16830.name: Kernel Modules and Extensions
16830.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Kernel Modules and Extensions is identified as MITRE ATT&CK technique T1547.006, serving the Persistence and Privilege Escalation tactics on Linux and macOS platforms. It involves loading malicious Loadable Kernel Modules (LKMs) or kernel extensions (kexts) to execute code with kernel-level (Ring 0) privileges. On Linux, LKMs are loaded to function as rootkits for hiding files, processes, and network activity, or to provide backdoors. On macOS, kexts are loaded via `kextload` commands; they bypass standard security policies, though loading typically requires a valid developer signature or disabling System Integrity Protection (SIP). This technique enables persistent, high-privilege access to the system.

16831.name: Default Accounts
16831.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Default Accounts (T1078.001) is a technique for defense evasion, initial access, persistence, and privilege escalation across platforms including Windows, Linux, macOS, and network devices. Adversaries abuse built-in or factory-set credentials, such as the Windows Guest/Administrator, AWS root, ESXi root, or Kubernetes default service accounts, to gain legitimate access. This includes preset accounts on appliances or accounts like 'vpxuser' created when integrating systems like ESXi with vCenter, often using known credentials or stolen keys to connect via remote services.

16833.name: Domain Accounts
16833.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Domain Accounts, identified as MITRE ATT&CK technique T1078.002, is a sub-technique under Valid Accounts used for Defense Evasion, Initial Access, Persistence, and Privilege Escalation on Windows, Linux, macOS, and ESXi platforms. It involves adversaries abusing credentials from accounts managed by Active Directory Domain Services, which provide configured access across domain systems. Compromise is achieved through methods like OS Credential Dumping or exploiting password reuse, granting access to privileged domain resources. The technique is associated with threat groups including Volt Typhoon, Wizard Spider, and Sandworm Team.

16834.name: Akira ransomware
16834.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Akira ransomware, also known as Akira, is a ransomware attributed to the threat group Storm-1567 and has demonstrated connections to the Conti ransomware operation. Its key technical behaviors include exploiting remote services like SSL VPNs on default port 4433 for initial access, using enterprise software deployment tools for lateral movement, and employing techniques to stop services, inhibit system recovery, and encrypt data for impact. It primarily targets Windows, Linux, and ESXi platforms.

16835.name: T1072
16835.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]T1072, Software Deployment Tools, is a technique within the Execution and Lateral Movement tactics, applicable to platforms including Windows, Linux, macOS, Network Devices, and SaaS. It involves adversaries abusing centralized enterprise software suites like SCCM, HBSS, Altiris, AWS Systems Manager, Microsoft Intune, Azure Arc, and GCP Deployment Manager to achieve remote code execution on connected systems, enabling lateral movement, information gathering, or widespread impact. Access may be achieved with local or domain administrative credentials, and these tools can be integrated into CI/CD pipelines or used for broad cloud administration commands.

16836.name: Exploitation of Remote Services
16836.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Exploitation of Remote Services is a MITRE ATT&CK technique with ID T1210 under the Lateral Movement tactic, targeting platforms including Windows, Linux, macOS, and ESXi. It involves exploiting software vulnerabilities in remote services like SMB, RDP, MySQL, or web servers to execute adversary-controlled code and gain unauthorized access to internal systems for lateral movement. Adversaries often use network service discovery to identify vulnerable systems, and successful exploitation can also lead to privilege escalation.

16837.name: Software Deployment Tools
16837.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Software Deployment Tools, also known as T1072, is a technique within the Execution and Lateral Movement tactics targeting Windows, Linux, macOS, Network Devices, and SaaS platforms. Adversaries abuse centralized enterprise administration suites like SCCM, Microsoft Intune, AWS Systems Manager, or Azure Arc to achieve remote code execution and move laterally across all connected systems, often by deploying malicious software or running scripts with high privileges, such as SYSTEM, via these management tools.

16838.name: T1210
16838.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Exploitation of Remote Services (T1210) is a Lateral Movement technique targeting Windows, Linux, macOS, and ESXi platforms. Adversaries exploit programming errors in remote services, such as SMB, RDP, MySQL, or web servers, to execute adversary-controlled code and gain unauthorized access to internal systems. This often follows network service discovery to identify vulnerable targets like servers or endpoints, and successful exploitation can also lead to privilege escalation.

16839.name: Inhibit System Recovery
16839.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Inhibit System Recovery is MITRE ATT&CK technique T1490 under the Impact tactic, targeting platforms including Windows, Linux, macOS, ESXi, and network devices. It works by adversaries disabling or deleting system recovery features to prevent restoration, such as using commands like `vssadmin.exe delete shadows /all /quiet` to remove Windows volume shadow copies, `wbadmin.exe delete catalog -quiet` to delete backup catalogs, or `bcdedit.exe` to disable automatic recovery. On ESXi, adversaries may delete VM snapshots, and on network devices, they may wipe backup firmware. This technique is often used to augment data destruction or encryption attacks and has been associated with groups like Sandworm Team and Wizard Spider.[/profile]

16841.name: unkown_apt_group
16841.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]The intrusion set, likely associated with the APT group known as Lotus Panda (also aliased as Lotus Blossom, Red Salamander, ST Group, ATK1, Dragonfish, G0030, Spring Dragon, Billbug, and Bronze Elgin), shows overlaps with other clusters like BackdoorDiplomacy. Its key TTPs include credential access via Forced Authentication (T1187), lateral movement through Exploitation of Remote Services (T1210) and Remote Services (T1021), defense evasion via Indicator Removal (T1070), and impact actions like Inhibit System Recovery (T1490). The group is believed to be of Chinese origin, primarily targeting diplomatic and governmental sectors in Southeast Asia, with motivations centered on espionage and intelligence gathering.

16845.name: T1505
16845.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]T1505, Server Software Component, is a persistence technique within the MITRE ATT&CK framework applicable to Windows, Linux, macOS, ESXi, and Network Devices. It involves adversaries abusing legitimate extensible development features of enterprise server applications to install malicious components, such as scripts or software modules, which extend and abuse the server's functionality to maintain persistent access. This method was notably referenced in the context of the 0-day Sophos firewall exploit by Volexity.

16846.name: T1187
16846.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]The entity is the MITRE ATT&CK technique Forced Authentication, identified as T1187 under the Credential Access tactic for Windows platforms. It works by tricking a system into automatically sending user credential hashes, like NTLM, to an adversary-controlled server. This is achieved by inducing the victim to access a malicious resource, such as via a spearphishing document with a remote template (file://[address]) or a crafted .SCF/.LNK file with an icon path pointing to a remote SMB share. The technique can also abuse the EfsRpcOpenFileRaw function to force SMB authentication through the MS-EFSRPC protocol. Retrieved data confirms its use in attacks, including by groups like Dragonfly, to capture hashes for offline cracking or relay attacks.

16848.name: XMRig
16848.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]XMRig, also known as xmrig, is a cryptomining malware. It is deployed by threat actors such as TeamTNT and DarthMiner, often by downloading the miner from repositories like GitHub or S3 buckets and executing it via shell scripts. Key techniques include abusing Cron for persistence and scheduling, using Unix Shell for execution, and employing Data Obfuscation in its command and control. It primarily targets Linux platforms, including Docker and Kubernetes environments, and has been delivered via scripts hosted at domains like b.9-9-8.com and m.9-9-8.com.[/profile]

16849.name: Platypus
16849.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Platypus is a malware targeting Linux systems, with infrastructure linked to domains like 9-9-8.com and URLs such as https://b.9-9-8.com/brysj/m/enbash.tar. It establishes persistence via Systemd Service and Cron job scheduling (T1543.002, T1053.003). For lateral movement, it uses SSH (T1021.004) and employs Virtualization/Sandbox Evasion (T1497) to avoid detection. The malware has been deployed in attacks targeting Germany.

16850.name: unkown_apt_group
16850.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]The intrusion set is likely the threat actor known as TeamTNT or a closely related cluster, also known as DarthMiner. Its key malware includes Platypus, XMRig, and Tsunami, and it notably uses the infrastructure domain b.9-9-8.com. Its primary TTPs involve establishing persistence on Linux systems via Cron (T1053.003) and Systemd Service (T1543.002), performing Container and Resource Discovery (T1613), and targeting unsecured credentials (T1552). The group is attributed to financially motivated actors targeting cloud and container environments, with specific campaigns observed against Germany. Its motivation is primarily cryptojacking and resource theft from Docker, Kubernetes, and Hadoop deployments.[/profile]

16905.name: Unix Shell
16905.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Unix Shell, identified as T1059.004, is an Execution tactic technique targeting macOS, Linux, Network Devices, and ESXi platforms. It involves adversaries abusing command-line shells like sh, bash, or zsh to execute arbitrary commands or scripts, which can control all aspects of a system. This abuse occurs through interactive sessions via C2 channels or lateral movement tools like SSH, or via deployment of shell scripts for payload delivery and persistence. Some systems, including ESXi servers, may use a stripped-down shell via BusyBox.

16906.name: Systemd Service
16906.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Systemd Service (T1543.002) is a Linux-specific technique for Persistence and Privilege Escalation. It involves creating or modifying systemd service unit files (.service) stored in directories like /etc/systemd/system or ~/.config/systemd/user/. Adversaries configure directives such as ExecStart within these files to execute malicious commands automatically at system boot or on service events, enabling recurring execution. While root privileges are typically required for system-level persistence, user-level unit files allow low-privilege users to establish persistence.

16907.name: Launchctl
16907.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Launchctl, identified as T1569.001 within the MITRE ATT&CK framework, is an execution technique for macOS. It abuses the native `launchctl` command to interface with the launchd service manager. Adversaries execute commands or programs by using subcommands like `launchctl submit -l <labelName> -- /Path/to/execute` or by loading malicious launch agents or daemons with commands such as `launchctl load -w`. This method can be used to establish persistence and potentially bypass application whitelisting if launchctl is a trusted process.

16908.name: Credentials In Files
16908.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Credentials In Files is the MITRE ATT&CK technique T1552.001 under the Credential Access tactic. It operates on Windows, Linux, macOS, Containers, and IaaS platforms. Adversaries search local and remote file systems for insecurely stored credentials, including user-created password files, shared credential stores, configuration files with embedded passwords, and cloud/container credential files. These files can be read directly to obtain credentials for authentication, lateral movement, or privilege escalation. Associated threat groups include FIN13, MuddyWater, and APT33.[/profile]

16909.name: Cron
16909.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Cron, identified as MITRE ATT&CK technique T1053.003, is a method for Execution, Persistence, and Privilege Escalation on macOS, Linux, and ESXi platforms. It involves abusing the cron utility, a time-based job scheduler, by creating or modifying crontab files (e.g., `/etc/crontab` or `/var/spool/cron/crontabs/root`) to schedule the execution of malicious commands or scripts at system startup or recurring intervals. This technique has been used by threat actors like APT38, Rocke, and APT5.

16910.name: T1569.001
16910.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]T1569.001: Launchctl is a macOS-specific execution technique where adversaries abuse the launchctl command-line tool to interface with the launchd service management framework. It is used to execute commands or programs by loading, unloading, or starting Launch Agents (T1543.001) or Launch Daemons (T1543.004). Common adversary commands include `launchctl load -w "%s/Library/LaunchAgents/%s"` or `/bin/launchctl load` to establish persistence and execute code.

16911.name: T1053.003
16911.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]The entity is MITRE ATT&CK technique T1053.003 (Cron), which falls under the Execution, Persistence, and Privilege Escalation tactics and targets macOS, Linux, and ESXi platforms. This technique involves abusing the cron utility, a time-based job scheduler on Unix-like systems, to schedule the execution of malicious code for persistence, often by creating or modifying crontab files such as `/var/spool/cron/crontabs/root` on ESXi. It is associated with groups like APT38 and Rocke.[/profile]

16920.name: Sliver
16920.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Sliver is a Command and Control (C2) framework. Its key technical behaviors include performing Container and Resource Discovery (T1613), Data Manipulation (T1565), and extracting Data from Information Repositories (T1213) and Unsecured Credentials (T1552). It has been used in campaigns targeting locations including the Republic of Korea, India, and the United States, and has been associated with infrastructure domains like ns1.cybertunnel.run, dnstunnel.run, and C2 URLs such as hxxps://panda.sect[.]kr.[/profile]

16922.name: Tsunami
16922.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Tsunami is a backdoor malware also known as ELF.WellMess and DACLS. It is associated with threat groups including APT29 and Lazarus Group. It leverages vulnerabilities such as CVE-2017-10271, CVE-2020-14883, and CVE-2023-46604 for initial access. Its key behaviors include using DNS (T1071.004) for command and control, employing rootkit techniques (T1014) for defense evasion, and targeting unsecured credentials (T1552). It has been deployed in campaigns against targets in Brazil and China, using domains like sck-dns.cc and run.on-demand.pw.[/profile]

16926.name: T1613
16926.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]T1613, known as Container and Resource Discovery, is a Discovery tactic technique targeting Containers. It involves adversaries querying the Docker and Kubernetes APIs or using CLI tools like `docker inspect` and `docker ps` to discover available resources such as containers, pods, nodes, images, and deployments within a containerized environment. This reconnaissance can inform subsequent lateral movement and execution methods, as seen in activities by groups like TeamTNT.

16927.name: Container and Resource Discovery
16927.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Container and Resource Discovery is a MITRE ATT&CK technique with ID T1613, categorized under the Discovery tactic and applicable to Container platforms. The technique involves adversaries querying container environments to discover available resources like containers, images, pods, nodes, and cluster status. This is typically achieved by using Docker and Kubernetes APIs, CLI tools such as `docker inspect` or `docker ps`, or accessing web dashboards like the Kubernetes dashboard. The gathered information, which can also be leaked through container logs revealing environment configuration and cloud provider details, informs subsequent adversary actions such as lateral movement and execution methods within the compromised environment.

16930.name: ReverseRAT
16930.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]ReverseRAT is a Remote Access Trojan (RAT) that uses HTTP for Command and Control (C2) communications, as indicated by its connection to MITRE ATT&CK technique T1071 (Application Layer Protocol). It employs Windows Management Instrumentation (T1047) for execution, modifies the Windows Registry (T1112) for persistence and defense evasion, and conducts Security Software Discovery (T1063). The malware is packed (T1045) to evade detection and has targeted infrastructure associated with India, including domains like 'reviewassignment.in' and 'dns1.indianblog.xyz', and C2 URLs such as 'http://dns1.indianblog.xyz/dailyworkout'. Its operations have been linked to APT attacks on industrial organizations.[profile]

16931.name: Action RAT - S1028
16931.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Action RAT - S1028, also known as Action RAT, is a remote access tool written in Delphi and attributed to the SideCopy threat group. It employs techniques including Security Software Discovery (T1518.001), Software Packing (T1027.002), and Command and Scripting Interpreter (T1059) for execution and evasion, and uses Application Layer Protocols (T1071) for command and control. The malware has been used in campaigns targeting government personnel in India and Afghanistan, with associated infrastructure including domains like reviewassignment.in and dns1.indianblog.xyz.[/profile]

16933.name: unkown_apt_group
16933.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]This intrusion set, likely associated with the SideCopy APT group, is also known as BackdoorDiplomacy, CloudComputating, BackDip, and Quarian. Its key malware includes Action RAT and ReverseRAT, which use Software Packing for evasion and Application Layer Protocols like HTTP for command and control. The group's TTPs involve Windows Management Instrumentation (WMI) for execution and Modify Registry (T1112) for persistence. It is attributed to or shows overlaps with actors targeting India and Afghanistan, with campaigns using infrastructure such as reviewassignment.in and dns1.indianblog.xyz. Its primary motivation appears to be espionage, focusing on government and industrial sectors in South Asia.[/profile]

16963.name: Kiron
16963.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Kiron is an information-stealing malware variant originating from Latin America (LATAM) and is available for purchase on underground forums. It is associated with eCrime actors. Its key technical behaviors include using data obfuscation, data encoding, and encrypted channels for command and control, and it employs automated exfiltration for data transfer. It has been observed targeting entities in Costa Rica, Peru, Chile, Mexico, and Argentina, and utilizes infrastructure such as massgrave.site, api.cacher.io, lovecollege.hosthampster.com, http://84.246.85.94:7890, and contpt.top.[/profile]

16964.name: Salve
16964.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Salve is an information-stealing malware variant originating from Latin America (LATAM) and is associated with eCrime actors. It is part of a group of LATAM-origin malware families that includes Culebra Variant, Caiman, and Kiron, and it is available for purchase on underground forums. Its key technical behaviors involve command-and-control techniques such as Data Obfuscation (T1001), Data Encoding (T1132), and using Encrypted Channels (T1573), alongside User Execution (T1204) for initial access and Automated Exfiltration (T1020). It primarily targets systems in Latin American countries including Peru, Costa Rica, Mexico, Chile, and Argentina, and has been linked to infrastructure domains like massgrave.site, adjunto.pdfxml.store, lovecollege.hosthampster.com, contpt.top, and the C2 server http://84.246.85.94:7890.[/profile]

16965.name: Astaroth
16965.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Astaroth is a modular information-stealing malware family. It employs complex obfuscation and anti-analysis techniques to inhibit detection. Its key Tactics, Techniques, and Procedures (TTPs) include Data Obfuscation (T1001) and Data Encoding (T1132) for command and control, Automated Exfiltration (T1020), and relies on User Execution (T1204).
