This technique involves adversaries hijacking environment variables like `LD_PRELOAD` on Linux or `DYLD_INSERT_LIBRARIES` on macOS to force a victim process to load malicious shared libraries before legitimate system libraries, enabling code execution within the context of that process. This hijacking can grant access to process memory and system resources, and has been used by groups like APT41 and Rocke to hook system functions like `execve` to hide artifacts.

17292.name: BRUSHFIRE
17292.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]BRUSHFIRE is a malware that employs defense evasion techniques including Disable Windows Event Logging (T1562.002) and Rootkit (T1014) to hide its presence on Windows systems. It also utilizes Traffic Signaling (T1205) for command and control.

17293.name: TrailBlazer - S0682
17293.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]TrailBlazer, also known as S0682, is a modular malware used by APT29 since at least 2019. It employs defense evasion techniques such as Disable Windows Event Logging (T1562.002) and Rootkit (T1014) to hide its activity, and uses Traffic Signaling (T1205) for command and control. The malware primarily targets Windows platforms and has been observed attempting to blend in by using a filename that matches the system name it resides on.

17295.name: DslogdRAT
17295.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]DslogdRAT is a Remote Access Trojan (RAT). Its key technical behaviors include using data encoding (T1132) like Base64 to obfuscate command-and-control (C2) traffic, scheduling data transfers (T1029) for exfiltration, employing internal spearphishing (T1534) for lateral movement, and utilizing virtualization/sandbox evasion (T1497) to avoid detection. It also performs system time discovery (T1124). The malware has been observed targeting systems in Japan.[/profile]

17301.name: T1029
17301.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]T1029, Scheduled Transfer, is an Exfiltration technique used on Windows, Linux, and macOS. Adversaries schedule data exfiltration at specific times or intervals to blend traffic with normal activity. This technique typically works in conjunction with other exfiltration methods like Exfiltration Over C2 Channel or Exfiltration Over Alternative Protocol to transfer the information out of the network.

17302.name: Internal Spearphishing
17302.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Internal Spearphishing, identified as T1534, is a Lateral Movement technique used on Windows, Linux, macOS, and SaaS platforms. It involves an adversary using a previously compromised internal account to launch spearphishing campaigns against other users within the same organization to gain further access. This often leverages trusted internal communication channels like email or chat applications (e.g., Microsoft Teams) to deliver malicious attachments or links, incorporating impersonation to increase success rates. Groups like Gamaredon, Hexane, Leviathan, and Kimsuky have been associated with this technique.

17303.name: Scheduled Transfer
17303.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Scheduled Transfer is identified as MITRE ATT&CK technique T1029 under the Exfiltration tactic, applicable to Windows, Linux, and macOS platforms. This technique involves adversaries scheduling data exfiltration at specific times or intervals to blend traffic with normal network activity and avoid detection. The actual data transfer is executed using other exfiltration methods, such as Exfiltration Over C2 Channel or Exfiltration Over Alternative Protocol.

17304.name: EDRSandBlast
17304.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]EDRSandBlast, also known as EDRKillShifter, is a tool attributed to APT29 (SVR) and Cicada3301. Its key technical behaviors involve exploiting signed, vulnerable drivers (CVE-2024-4947) to disable security software, specifically removing Protected Process Light (PPL) protection and Local Security Authority Subsystem Service (LSASS) protections using kernel and user-level evasion techniques (T1211, T1574). It targets Windows platforms to inject code into antivirus and endpoint detection and response (AV/EDR) processes for defense evasion.[/profile]

17305.name: TCESB
17305.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]TCESB is a malware entity. It employs the MITRE ATT&CK techniques Exploitation for Defense Evasion (T1211) to bypass security software and Hijack Execution Flow (T1574) for persistence and execution, with methods including registry key manipulation for automatic startup. Its target platforms include Windows, Linux, and macOS.[/profile]

17306.name: unkown_apt_group
17306.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]This intrusion set, likely linked to or overlapping with the group known as LOTUS PANDA (also known as Lotus Blossom, Red Salamander, ST Group, ATK1, Dragonfish, G0030, Spring Dragon, Billbug, and Bronze Elgin), employs key malware including TomBerBil, WAExp, and Cuthead. Its primary TTPs involve credential theft from web browsers (T1555.003), lateral movement via SMB/Windows Admin Shares (T1021.002), and data collection and exfiltration using the "Archive via Library" technique (T1560.002), often utilizing shared infrastructure domains such as ha.bbmouseme.com, 1.tcp.ap.ngrok.io, etracking.nso.go.th, and www.netportal.or.kr. The group is believed to be of Chinese origin and typically targets Windows systems, with motivations aligned with cyber espionage.[/profile]

17308.name: TomBerBil
17308.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]TomBerBil is a malware attributed to the cybercriminal group TWISTED SPIDER. Its key behaviors include collecting data from the local system (T1005) and archiving it for exfiltration using third-party libraries (T1560.002). For credential access, it steals credentials from web browsers (T1555.003). It moves laterally via SMB/Windows Admin Shares (T1021.002) and evades detection by matching legitimate resource names or locations (T1036.005). It targets Windows systems and has used infrastructure including domains like ha.bbmouseme.com and 1.tcp.ap.ngrok.io.[/profile]

17309.name: cuthead
17309.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Cuthead is a malware that targets Windows systems and uses the SMB/Windows Admin Shares technique for lateral movement. Its infrastructure includes domains like 1.tcp.ap.ngrok.io, ha.bbmouseme.com, etracking.nso.go.th, and www.netportal.or.kr. It employs the 'Archive via Library' technique to compress data and 'Credentials from Web Browsers' to steal login information. The malware also uses 'Match Legitimate Resource Name or Location' for defense evasion and collects 'Data from Local System'.[/profile]

17310.name: WAExp
17310.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]WAExp is a credential-stealing malware that targets web browsers, specifically extracting saved credentials from browser files such as Chrome's 'Login Data' database using SQL queries and system APIs for decryption. It employs defense evasion by placing its files in trusted directories or naming them to resemble legitimate system resources. For data exfiltration, it compresses collected data using programming libraries like Python's rarfile or zlib before sending it via its command-and-control infrastructure, which includes domains like www.netportal.or.kr, etracking.nso.go.th, ha.bbmouseme.com, and 1.tcp.ap.ngrok.io.[/profile]

17322.name: T1560.002
17322.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]T1560.002 (Archive via Library) is a Collection technique for macOS, Linux, and Windows. It involves compressing or encrypting collected data prior to exfiltration using third-party libraries like Python's rarfile, libzip, or zlib, which are often preinstalled (e.g., bzip2 on macOS/Linux, zip on Windows). This method allows direct library linking during compilation, avoiding the need to spawn a subshell as required by standalone utilities.

17324.name: Archive via Library
17324.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Archive via Library is a sub-technique under MITRE ATT&CK ID T1560.002 within the Collection tactic. It operates on Windows, Linux, and macOS platforms. This technique involves compressing or encrypting collected data prior to exfiltration by linking against third-party programming libraries rather than spawning separate utilities. Common libraries include Python's rarfile, libzip, and zlib, which provide built-in functionality for these tasks. Some systems have pre-installed libraries like bzip2 on macOS/Linux and zip on Windows. This method helps obfuscate data and minimize network footprint during exfiltration.

17327.name: unkown_apt_group
17327.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]This intrusion set, likely associated with APT28 (Fancy Bear), is also known as backdoordiplomacy, cloudcomputating, backdip, and quarian. Its key malware is Tickler (Tick), and its techniques include One-Way Communication (T1102.003) for command and control, NTDS (T1003.003) for credential access from domain controllers, SMB/Windows Admin Shares (T1021.002) for lateral movement, and Windows Command Shell (T1059.003) for execution. It has been observed targeting entities in Australia, the United Arab Emirates, and the United States. The group shows operational overlaps with other clusters like Lotus Panda. Its motivation is primarily cyber espionage, attributed to Russian state interests.[/profile]

17332.name: Tickler
17332.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Tickler, also known as Tick, is a malware associated with APT28. It employs techniques including One-Way Communication for command and control, T1003.003 (NTDS) for credential access from domain controllers, T1110.003 (Password Spraying) for credential acquisition, T1078.004 (Valid Accounts: Cloud Accounts) for initial access and persistence, and T1021.002 (SMB/Windows Admin Shares) for lateral movement. It targets Windows platforms and has been observed in operations affecting Australia, the United Arab Emirates, and the United States.

17348.name: T1110.003
17348.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]T1110.003 Password Spraying is a Credential Access technique where adversaries use a single or small list of commonly used passwords against many different accounts to acquire valid credentials, avoiding account lockouts typical of brute-force attacks. It targets services like SSH, SMB, LDAP, Kerberos, RDP, and cloud applications, often throttling attempts to evade detection. This technique is applicable across Windows, Linux, macOS, and network, cloud, and identity platforms.

17351.name: T1003.003
17351.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]T1003.003, NTDS, is a Credential Access technique for Windows platforms where adversaries copy the Active Directory domain database (NTDS.dit) from domain controllers to steal credential hashes and domain information. The file is typically located at %SystemRoot%\NTDS\Ntds.dit, and adversaries may also target backups. Common execution methods include using Volume Shadow Copy, the ntdsutil.exe tool, or scripts like secretsdump.py and Invoke-NinjaCopy. This technique is associated with groups like APT28, APT41, and Sandworm Team.

17352.name: One-Way Communication
17352.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]One-Way Communication (T1102.003) is a Command and Control technique used across Windows, Linux, macOS, and ESXi platforms. It involves adversaries using legitimate external web services, such as social media or popular websites, to send commands to a compromised system without receiving command output back over the same channel. The output may be sent via a different C2 channel or not at all, providing cover by blending with normal, encrypted traffic to services like Google or Twitter. This method has been associated with threat groups including Gamaredon Group and Leviathan.

17353.name: NTDS
17353.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]NTDS is the technique T1003.003 within the Credential Access tactic on Windows platforms. It involves stealing the Active Directory domain database, primarily the NTDS.dit file located at %SystemRoot%\NTDS\Ntds.dit on domain controllers. Adversaries access or copy this file using tools like Volume Shadow Copy, secretsdump.py, ntdsutil.exe, or Invoke-NinjaCopy, and may also target backups containing the database to extract credential hashes and domain information.

17354.name: T1102.003
17354.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]The entity T1102.003, known as One-Way Communication, is a command-and-control technique within the MITRE ATT&CK framework applicable to Windows, Linux, macOS, and ESXi platforms. It involves adversaries using legitimate external web services like Google or Twitter to send commands to a compromised system without receiving return output over that same channel, leveraging SSL/TLS encryption and the prevalence of these services for stealth. This technique has been associated with threat groups like Gamaredon Group and Leviathan.

17356.name: Lumma Trojan
17356.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Lumma Trojan, also known as Lumma stealer, is an infostealer malware attributed to the Angry Likho group. It employs techniques including Account Discovery (T1087), Credentials from Password Stores (T1555), and Keylogging (T1056.001) to harvest credentials and sensitive data from Windows systems. Its infrastructure utilizes domains like softcallousdmykw.shop and willingyhollowsk.shop, and it is distributed via lures such as fake browser updates. The malware is associated with operations originating from Belarus and the Russian Federation.[/profile]

17358.name: unkown_apt_group
17358.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]This intrusion set, likely associated with the Sandworm group (APT44), also known as BlackEnergy Group, TeleBots, and Voodoo Bear, is attributed to actors operating from or linked to the Russian Federation and Belarus. Its key malware includes Rhadamanthys Stealer, which shares significant design overlap with the Hidden Bee miner, and tools like DarkTrack, MetaStealer, Ozone RAT, and NETWIRE. Its TTPs emphasize defense evasion through Indirect Command Execution (e.g., abusing Forfiles, pcalua.exe), Virtualization/Sandbox Evasion, and Account Discovery. The group targets various sectors, leveraging phishing for initial access and focusing on credential access from files. Its motivation is primarily cyber-espionage and disruptive operations, with infrastructure using domains like document-cdn.org and various .shop domains.[/profile]

17418.name: NETWIRE - S0198
17418.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]NETWIRE - S0198, also known as NetWire or NetWire RC, is a publicly available, multiplatform remote administration tool (RAT) used by criminal and APT groups such as APT33, TA2541, The White Company, and SilverTerrier since at least 2012. Its key behaviors include Defense Evasion techniques like Indirect Command Execution (T1202) using utilities such as Forfiles and pcalua.exe, Virtualization/Sandbox Evasion (T1497), Masquerading (T1036), and File Deletion (T1070.004). It is typically delivered via Phishing (T1566) and operates across Windows, Linux, and macOS platforms, using infrastructure like the domain document-cdn.org.[/profile]

17419.name: Ozone RAT
17419.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Ozone RAT, also known as ozone rat, is a commercially available Remote Access Trojan (RAT) sold via a dedicated website with Standard and Platinum package options. It employs Defense Evasion techniques including Indirect Command Execution (T1202) to abuse legitimate Windows utilities, Virtualization/Sandbox Evasion (T1497), Masquerading (T1036), and Obfuscated Files or Information (T1027). It is typically delivered via Phishing (T1566) and has been associated with infrastructure such as the domain document-cdn.org. Its client interface includes a server builder and control center.[/profile]

17420.name: DarkTrack
17420.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]DarkTrack is a Remote Access Trojan (RAT) known as darktrack rat. It is associated with a public developer who maintains a dedicated website, support forums, and social media for distribution and tutorials, with versions including 4.0. Its key techniques include Defense Evasion via Masquerading (T1036) and Obfuscated Files or Information (T1027), as well as Virtualization/Sandbox Evasion (T1497) to detect analysis environments. It uses infrastructure such as the domain document-cdn.org.[/profile]

17422.name: MetaStealer
17422.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]MetaStealer is a stealer malware active since at least May 2022, attributed to UNC5537. Its key technical behaviors include using a Domain Generation Algorithm (DGA), employing string decryption and obfuscation, and performing indirect command execution, virtualization/sandbox evasion, and masquerading for defense evasion. It targets Windows platforms and has been associated with infrastructure like the domain document-cdn.org.[/profile]

17423.name: Rhadamanthys Stealer
17423.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Rhadamanthys Stealer is a malware stealer. It is associated with the Sandworm group and shares significant design and implementation overlap with the Hidden Bee coin miner, including the use of custom executable formats, virtual filesystems, steganography, and LUA scripts. Its key technical behaviors involve Defense Evasion techniques such as Indirect Command Execution (T1202) and abuse of Msiexec (T1218.007), as well as performing System Checks to detect virtual environments. It primarily targets Windows systems and has used infrastructure domains like fbetlixgee.eu and telephony.nexttradeitaly.com for command and control and data exfiltration.[/profile]

17438.name: Indirect Command Execution
17438.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Indirect Command Execution, identified as T1202, is a Defense Evasion technique primarily targeting Windows platforms. It involves abusing legitimate Windows utilities to execute commands while bypassing security restrictions that limit the use of standard command-line interpreters like cmd.exe. Specific utilities include Forfiles, the Program Compatibility Assistant (pcalua.exe), components of the Windows Subsystem for Linux (WSL), and Scriptrunner.exe. Adversaries may also abuse the ssh.exe binary via its ProxyCommand and LocalCommand options to run malicious commands, thereby evading detections or controls that block cmd.exe or common malicious file extensions.

17439.name: T1202
17439.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]T1202, known as Indirect Command Execution, is a Defense Evasion technique for Windows. It involves abusing legitimate Windows utilities like Forfiles, pcalua.exe, or Scriptrunner.exe to execute commands, often bypassing security controls that restrict direct use of command-line interpreters like cmd.exe. Adversaries may also misuse ssh.exe via its ProxyCommand option. This method allows arbitrary execution while evading detections targeting standard command-line activity.

17441.name: DCHSpy
17441.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]DCHSpy is an Android spyware family attributed to the Iranian APT group MuddyWater. It leverages compromised infrastructure for command and control, using domains and services like it1.comodo-vpn.com, r2.earthvpn.org, and hs3.iphide.net, with connections to locations including Iran, Israel, and the United States. Its key behaviors involve data exfiltration and backdoor access, utilizing techniques such as uploading malware to controlled servers and employing social engineering via social media and email accounts for initial access and resource development.

17443.name: SandStrike
17443.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]SandStrike, also known as Skipper, is a malware attributed to the Turla group. It exploits CVE-2025-4609 and uses command and control infrastructure including domains and IP addresses like http://192.121.113.60/dev/run.php and https://it1.comodo-vpn.com:1950. Its tactics involve resource development through domains, email accounts, and social media accounts, and it has been deployed against targets in Iran, the Central African Republic, South Africa, Israel, and the United States.

17444.name: unkown_apt_group
17444.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]This intrusion set is attributed to the Iranian APT group MuddyWater (also known as Mercury). It employs a suite of custom malware including DCHSpy, BugSleep, and PhonyC2, and has been observed abusing legitimate tools like the Atera Agent and PowerShell RAT. Key TTPs involve data encoding for C2 obfuscation, social media accounts for resource development, and one-way communication for command and control. The group is believed to be state-sponsored and primarily targets entities in the Middle East and surrounding regions, including Azerbaijan, Portugal, Türkiye, Saudi Arabia, Israel, and Jordan, with motivations centered on cyber espionage and data exfiltration.[/profile]

17490.name: T1596
17490.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Search Open Technical Databases (T1596) is a Reconnaissance technique in the MITRE ATT&CK framework applicable to pre-attack platforms. It involves adversaries querying freely available online technical databases and repositories to gather victim information such as domain registrations, SSL certificates, and passive DNS data. This gathered intelligence can enable subsequent phases like phishing, infrastructure acquisition, or initial access. The technique is associated with groups like APT28 and Kimsuky.

17491.name: Social Media Accounts
17491.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Social Media Accounts is a Resource Development technique (T1585.001) on the PRE platform. Adversaries create and cultivate fictitious or impersonating social media profiles on platforms like Facebook, LinkedIn, or Twitter. This involves developing a credible persona by filling out profile information, building social networks, and incorporating photos. These established accounts are then used to create connections with targets, often as a precursor to social engineering attacks like spearphishing.

17492.name: Search Open Technical Databases
17492.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Search Open Technical Databases is a reconnaissance technique (T1596) within the MITRE ATT&CK framework, applicable to the PRE platform. It involves adversaries querying freely available technical databases and repositories, such as WHOIS, DNS dumpsters, passive DNS services, SSL certificate registries, and public scan databases like Shodan, to gather victim intelligence like domain registrations, network artifacts, and certificate data. This information can enable follow-on activities like phishing, infrastructure acquisition, or initial access. Associated threat groups include APT28 and Kimsuky.

17494.name: PhonyC2
17494.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]PhonyC2 is a malware used by the MuddyWater (Mercury) cyber espionage group. Its key technical behaviors include using Valid Accounts (T1078.004) for cloud access, employing Data Encoding (T1132) for C2 traffic obfuscation, and leveraging System Binary Proxy Execution (T1218) for defense evasion. It also utilizes User Execution (T1204) and Remote Services (T1021) for initial execution and lateral movement. Its infrastructure involves servers with version identifiers like "apiv4" and "apiy7", and it has been observed targeting the United States.[/profile]

17495.name: POWERSTATS
17495.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]POWERSTATS is a malware family attributed to the MuddyWater group. It has evolved through multiple versions (v1, v2, v3) and its delivery methods have included malicious macros, template injection, and payloads encoded in VBS, JS, base52, Base64, VBE, and delivered as DLL, REG, EXE, INF, or BAT files. Its associated techniques include System Binary Proxy Execution (T1218), Remote Services (T1021), Data Encoding for C2, abuse of Cloud Accounts, and User Execution (T1204). It has been deployed against targets in the United States.[profile]

17496.name: DarkBeatC2
17496.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]DarkBeatC2 is a malware entity with associated infrastructure domains including mafateehgroup.com, microsoft-corp.com, mafatehgroup.com, softwaree-cloud.com, and websiteapicloud.com. It employs techniques for Data Encoding in command and control, Access Token Manipulation (T1134), and Cloud Accounts abuse (T1078.004) for defense evasion and privilege escalation. Its activities have been geolocated to Jordan, Saudi Arabia, Israel, and the United States. The malware is also linked to the Endpoint Denial of Service (T1499) and Supply Chain Compromise (T1195) attack patterns.[/profile]

17500.name: MuddyC2Go
17500.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]MuddyC2Go is a malware associated with the MuddyWater group. It employs Data Encoding for C2 traffic obfuscation, uses Cloud Accounts for access and persistence, and leverages System Binary Proxy Execution for defense evasion. Its delivery mechanisms involve User Execution, such as phishing, and it utilizes Remote Services for lateral movement. Its infrastructure includes the MSI download link 'https://freeupload.store/rALE7/wIHItUcE08.msi/download', and it has been observed targeting entities in the Central African Republic, South Africa, Israel, and the United States.[/profile]

17585.name: NetBird
17585.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]NetBird is a malware that uses the T1136.001 (Local Account) technique for persistence by creating local accounts, employs One-Way Communication (T1102.003) for command and control, and abuses Local Accounts (T1078.003) for defense evasion and privilege escalation. It relies on User Execution (T1204) for initial compromise and may leverage compromised Email Accounts (T1586.002) for resource development. Its operations have been geographically linked to Central African Republic, South Africa, and the United States of America.

17586.name: T1136.001
17586.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]T1136.001 (Local Account) is a Persistence technique within the MITRE ATT&CK framework applicable to Windows, Linux, macOS, Network Devices, Containers, and ESXi. It involves adversaries creating local accounts to maintain access, using specific commands like `net user /add` on Windows, `useradd` on Linux, `dscl -create` on macOS, `username` on network devices, `esxcli system account add` on ESXi, or `kubectl` for Kubernetes clusters. This establishes secondary credentialed access without requiring persistent remote tools.

17588.name: BugSleep
17588.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]BugSleep is a malware implant that implements a bespoke command and control (C2) protocol over plain TCP sockets, frequently using port 443. Its technical behaviors include process injection, file obfuscation to avoid detection, and establishing persistence on the target system to provide reverse shell and file I/O capabilities. It has been observed targeting entities in Azerbaijan, Portugal, Türkiye, Saudi Arabia, and Israel, using infrastructure domains such as softwarehosts.com, smartcloudcompany.com, smtpcloudapp.com, and onlinemailerservices.com.[/profile]

17663.name: PowerShell RAT
17663.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]PowerShell RAT is a remote access trojan that uses PowerShell for execution and command-and-control. It communicates with C2 servers such as pharmacynod.com, swordoke[.]com, and bestsecure2020[.]com/gate, and employs data encoding like Base64 to obfuscate traffic. Its TTPs include automated exfiltration (T1020) and user execution (T1204) for initial access. The malware has been associated with groups like APT29, APT41, and FIN6, and is linked to broader campaigns involving tools like Cobalt Strike and ZLoader, primarily targeting Windows platforms.[/profile]

17668.name: Tactical RMM
17668.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Tactical RMM is a legitimate Remote Monitoring and Management (RMM) tool repurposed as malware for command and control (C2). It is deployed by threat groups including Gold Cabin, Mummy Spider, Mealybug, and Vanilla Tempest, often as an alternative C2 channel in campaigns involving Emotet and Mount Locker. Key technical behaviors involve installation via command line with parameters specifying a C2 server API endpoint, such as 'api.floppasoftware[.]com'. Associated infrastructure includes domains like googleonlinee.com, security-onedrive.com, webftpcloud.com, and vatacloud.com. It primarily targets Windows systems, with observed activity in Jordan, Saudi Arabia, and Israel.[/profile]

17669.name: Atera Agent
17669.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Atera Agent is a legitimate remote monitoring and management (RMM) system that is abused by threat actors as a living-off-the-land binary (LOLBin). It has been utilized by groups like Wizard Spider (associated with Conti) and others to download and launch secondary payloads such as Cobalt Strike beacons for command and control. Its installer package is often delivered via malicious links in search engine optimization (SEO) poisoning campaigns, where it masquerades as legitimate software like Microsoft Visual Studio. Key associated infrastructure includes domains like websiteapicloud.com, mafatehgroup.com, and googleonlinee.com.

17715.name: Endpoint Denial of Service
17715.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Endpoint Denial of Service, designated as T1499 within the MITRE ATT&CK framework, is an Impact tactic technique targeting macOS, Linux, Windows, Containers, and IaaS platforms. It aims to degrade or block service availability by exhausting the host system's resources (like CPU, memory, or disk) or exploiting it to cause a persistent crash, rather than saturating the network. Attacks target various layers of the application stack, including the OS, server applications (e.g., web servers, DNS), and databases, leveraging specific bottlenecks unique to each component. This can be executed from a single endpoint or as a distributed attack (DDoS) using methods like IP spoofing and botnets to obscure the source.

17716.name: T1085
17716.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]T1085, also known as Rundll32, is an execution technique within the MITRE ATT&CK framework (ID: T1085) under the Execution tactic, primarily for Windows platforms. It involves using the legitimate rundll32.exe binary to proxy the execution of malicious code, leveraging its whitelisting to evade detection. Specific mechanics include executing Control Panel Item files (.cpl) via functions like Control_RunDLL and running scripts such as JavaScript. This technique is also referenced in evasion methods like Parent PID Spoofing, where adversaries may spoof the parent process of a Rundll32 call to appear as a benign process like explorer.exe.

17717.name: T1499
17717.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]T1499, Endpoint Denial of Service, is an Impact technique targeting macOS, Linux, Windows, Containers, and IaaS platforms. It aims to degrade or block service availability by exhausting host system resources or causing persistent crashes, rather than saturating the network. Attacks can target various layers of the application stack, including the OS, server applications like web or DNS servers, and the applications themselves. Methods may involve IP address spoofing to obscure the attack source and the use of botnets to generate high-volume traffic from distributed systems, making defense difficult.

17722.name: RomCom
17722.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]RomCom is a Remote Access Trojan (RAT) with the alias RomCom RAT. It is attributed to the threat actor group Gold Prelude. Its key technical behaviors include using a dropper file (setup.exe) and a helper file (hlpr.dat) for deployment, and it employs infrastructure such as the domains mctelemetryzone.com, redditanalytics.pm, and wirelessvezion.com. The malware targets entities in Poland and Ukraine.[/profile]

17723.name: PEAPOD
17723.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]PEAPOD is a malware entity that establishes persistence via Event Triggered Execution, such as creating a Windows registry key for automatic startup, and employs Defense Evasion techniques including Subvert Trust Controls and Deobfuscate/Decode Files or Information. 17761.name: DinodasRAT

It uses Application Layer Protocols like HTTP for command and control, employs Obfuscated Files or Information (T1027) and Masquerading (T1036) for defense evasion, and leverages Process Injection (T1055) for execution. 17846.name: T1209
17846.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]The entity T1209, known as Time Providers, corresponds to MITRE ATT&CK technique T1209 under the Persistence tactic for Windows platforms. It involves adversaries establishing persistence by registering and enabling a malicious DLL as a Windows Time service (W32Time) provider. This requires administrator privileges for registration, after which the malicious code executes in the context of the Local Service account. The technique exploits the service's architecture where time providers are DLLs registered under the system registry key HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\System\CurrentControlSet\Services\W32Time\TimeProviders\.

18447.name: T1192

It is distinct from other spearphishing methods due to its use of embedded links to deliver payloads.

18448.name: Compromise Accounts

Compromised accounts, such as email or social media profiles, may be further developed by modifying profile information and can be directly leveraged for subsequent phishing campaigns. This technique is distinguished from creating new accounts (Establish Accounts, T1585) and operates on a pre-attack platform.[/profile]

18524.name: DLL Search Order Hijacking
18524.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]DLL Search Order Hijacking is a technique within the MITRE ATT&CK framework, specifically identified as T1574.001. It falls under the Defense Evasion and Persistence tactics and primarily targets Windows platforms. This method exploits the standard Windows DLL search order by placing a malicious DLL with the same name as a required library in a directory that is searched before the legitimate location, such as the application's current working directory. This allows the adversary to execute their code when the vulnerable program loads the DLL, potentially achieving persistence and privilege escalation, especially if the program runs with elevated rights. The malicious DLL can be configured to also load the legitimate library to avoid detection and maintain normal program behavior.

18525.name: Debugger Evasion
18525.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Debugger Evasion is a technique under MITRE ATT&CK ID T1622, primarily used for Defense Evasion and Discovery on Windows, Linux, and macOS platforms. It involves detecting debuggers to alter malware behavior or avoid analysis. Specific technical mechanics include checking the Windows PEB's `BeingDebugged` flag via APIs like `IsDebuggerPresent()`, querying Linux `/proc/self/status` for `TracerPID`, using Structured Exception Handling (SEH) to test for process suspension, or flooding logs with `OutputDebugStringW()` calls. The technique is associated with groups like Mustang Panda.

18526.name: T1568.002
18526.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]T1568.002, Domain Generation Algorithms (DGAs), is a Command and Control technique for macOS, Linux, Windows, and ESXi. It works by dynamically generating a large number of potential command and control domains, often using time-based or seeded algorithms to create seemingly random strings (e.g., istgmxdejdnxuyla.ru) or concatenated words (e.g., cityjulydish.net). This makes it difficult for defenders to block all possible destinations, and it can be used as a fallback mechanism to re-establish lost C2 connections.

18527.name: Fileless Storage
18527.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Fileless Storage is a Defense Evasion technique (T1027.011) applicable to Linux and Windows platforms. It involves storing malicious data in non-file formats to evade detection by security tools that scan disk storage. Common implementations include using the Windows Registry, event logs, or WMI repository, and on Linux, using shared memory directories like `/dev/shm` where data is mapped to RAM. This method can conceal payloads or staged data and may bypass protections on read-only file systems. Associated threat groups include APT32 and Turla.

18528.name: T1564.006
18528.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]The entity is the MITRE ATT&CK technique Run Virtual Instance (T1564.006), a Defense Evasion tactic applicable to Windows, Linux, macOS, and ESXi platforms. It involves executing malicious operations within a virtual instance to hide artifacts from host-based security tools and obscure network traffic origins. Adversaries may use native hypervisors like Hyper-V, deploy emulators such as QEMU, or drop portable virtualization binaries. Specific implementations include using Windows Sandbox `.wsb` files to define shared folders and payloads, or on ESXi servers, directly executing `.vmx` files with `/bin/vmx` to create virtual machines hidden from standard administrative consoles.

18529.name: Double File Extension
18529.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Double File Extension, identified as MITRE ATT&CK technique T1036.007, is a Defense Evasion tactic primarily used on Windows platforms. It involves appending a secondary, often malicious, file extension (like .exe, .lnk, .hta, or .scr) after a benign-looking first extension (such as .txt, .doc, or .jpg), as in "File.txt.exe". This abuse of file naming conventions causes some system views and file browsers to display only the first extension, tricking users into opening what appears to be a harmless document or image but is actually executable code, commonly delivered via spearphishing attachments to facilitate initial access and user execution.

18530.name: Dynamic API Resolution
18530.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Dynamic API Resolution is a Defense Evasion technique (MITRE ATT&CK ID T1027.007) for Windows platforms. It conceals malware functionality by obfuscating and dynamically resolving API calls at runtime to evade static analysis. Adversaries store hashes of function names instead of literal strings, using functions like `GetProcAddress()` and `LoadLibrary()` to manually link and load required OS APIs during execution, thereby avoiding static artifacts in the payload.

18802.name: Web Portal Capture
18802.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Web Portal Capture, also known as T1056.003, is a Credential Access technique within the MITRE ATT&CK framework, applicable to Windows, Linux, and macOS platforms. It involves adversaries installing malicious code on externally facing web portals, such as VPN login pages, to intercept and exfiltrate user credentials during authentication attempts. This can be executed post-compromise using administrative access or as part of an initial web service exploitation, as observed in campaigns by groups like Winter Vivern.

18803.name: T1056.003
18803.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]T1056.003, known as Input Capture: Web Portal Capture, is a technique within the Credential Access and Collection tactics applicable to Windows, Linux, and macOS. Adversaries implement this by installing malicious code on externally facing portals, such as VPN login pages, to intercept and transmit user credentials during login attempts. This can be deployed as part of an initial web service compromise or post-compromise using administrative access to maintain persistence through remote services and valid accounts, as observed in activities linked to groups like Winter Vivern.

18925.name: Core Impact

18927.name: Powertrash

It targets Windows platforms and has been associated with infrastructure indicators like http://45.87.154.208/icsnd3b_64refl.ps1 and http://193.178.210.227/work_53.bin_m7.ps1.[/profile]

It targets Windows systems and has been linked to exploiting vulnerabilities like CVE-2021-34523 and CVE-2021-31207. 18968.name: T1055.001
18968.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]T1055.001, known as Dynamic-link Library Injection, is a Windows technique for Defense Evasion and Privilege Escalation. It involves writing a DLL's path into a target process's memory using APIs like VirtualAllocEx and WriteProcessMemory, then loading it via CreateRemoteThread to execute code within a legitimate process. Variations include reflective injection and module stomping to bypass relocation and hide malicious code. This method can evade detection and potentially access elevated privileges.

18971.name: Dynamic-link Library Injection
18971.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Dynamic-link Library Injection, identified as T1055.001, is a Defense Evasion and Privilege Escalation technique for Windows. It involves injecting a DLL into a remote process's address space to execute arbitrary code, commonly using Windows APIs like VirtualAllocEx, WriteProcessMemory, and CreateRemoteThread to write a DLL path and invoke LoadLibrary. Variations include reflective DLL injection and Module Stomping to bypass address relocation and conceal code. This grants access to the host process's resources and privileges while evading detection. It is associated with groups like Lazarus and Turla, and related to persistence mechanisms like AppInit DLLs.[/profile]

18972.name: T1053.002
18972.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]The entity is MITRE ATT&CK technique T1053.002 (At), a sub-technique of Scheduled Task/Job. It falls under the Execution, Persistence, and Privilege Escalation tactics and is applicable to Windows, Linux, and macOS platforms. This technique involves abusing the native 'at' command-line utility to schedule tasks for malicious code execution. On Windows, it requires the Task Scheduler service to be running and local administrator privileges; it can also be invoked via the Win32_ScheduledJob WMI class. On Linux and macOS, access is governed by 'at.allow' and 'at.deny' files, with superuser access as the default if these files are absent. It is used for persistence, remote execution, lateral movement, and privilege escalation, including breaking out of restricted environments.

18973.name: T1480.001
18973.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]T1480.001, known as Environmental Keying, is a Defense Evasion technique for Windows, Linux, and macOS. It cryptographically constrains malware execution to specific target environments by deriving decryption keys from unique environmental values such as network shares, system time, IP addresses, or software versions. This prevents payload decryption and execution in unintended environments like sandboxes, thereby impeding detection, analysis, and incident response. It has been associated with groups like APT41 and Equation.

18974.name: At
18974.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]At, also known as T1053.002 (Scheduled Task/Job: At), is a technique within the Execution, Persistence, and Privilege Escalation tactics. It operates on Windows, Linux, and macOS platforms. Adversaries abuse the native 'at' utility to schedule tasks for malicious code execution at specified times, requiring the Task Scheduler service and local administrator rights on Windows, with access on Linux/macOS governed by at.allow and at.deny files. It can be invoked via the command line or the Win32_ScheduledJob WMI class and is used for persistence, lateral movement, privilege escalation via sudo, or breaking out of restricted shells. It has been associated with groups like APT18 and Bronze Butler.

18975.name: Environmental Keying
18975.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Environmental Keying, designated as T1480.001, is a Defense Evasion technique used across Windows, Linux, and macOS platforms. It is a specific implementation of Execution Guardrails that uses cryptography to constrain malware execution to specific target environments. The technique works by deriving an encryption/decryption key from unique environmental values present on the intended victim host, such as specific network shares, system time, domain names, or IP addresses. The encrypted payload will only decrypt and execute if these exact conditions are met, thereby evading sandbox analysis, hindering reverse engineering, and preventing exposure in unintended environments. It has been associated with groups like APT41 and Equation.

18976.name: T1055.002
18976.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]T1055.002, known as Portable Executable (PE) Injection, is a defense-evasion and privilege-escalation technique for Windows. It involves executing arbitrary code within the address space of a separate, legitimate live process to evade process-based defenses and potentially gain elevated privileges. This is typically achieved by writing code into the target process's memory using Windows API calls like VirtualAllocEx and WriteProcessMemory, then invoking it with CreateRemoteThread, which masks execution under that legitimate process. It has been associated with groups like Gorgon Group and Rocke, and vulnerabilities such as CVE-2023-21839 and CVE-2021-34473 can potentially facilitate its use.[/profile]

18977.name: Portable Executable Injection
18977.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Portable Executable Injection is identified as MITRE ATT&CK technique T1055.002 under the Defense Evasion and Privilege Escalation tactics for Windows. It involves injecting a Portable Executable (PE) into the address space of a live process to execute arbitrary code, evading process-based defenses. The injection is commonly performed using Windows API calls such as VirtualAllocEx and WriteProcessMemory to copy code into the target process, which is then invoked via CreateRemoteThread or similar methods, requiring memory reference remapping. This technique has been associated with groups like Gorgon Group and Rocke, and is related to vulnerabilities including CVE-2021-31207 and CVE-2021-34523.[/profile]

18978.name: T1055.004
18978.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]T1055.004, Asynchronous Procedure Call (APC) Injection, is a defense evasion and privilege escalation technique for Windows. It works by queuing malicious code into a target thread's APC queue using API calls like OpenThread and QueueUserAPC to execute it within a legitimate process's address space, often to evade detection. Variations include Early Bird injection and AtomBombing. It is associated with groups like FIN8 and exploits such as CVE-2021-34473.

18979.name: Asynchronous Procedure Call
18979.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Asynchronous Procedure Call (APC) Injection is a Windows-specific technique (T1055.004) used for Defense Evasion and Privilege Escalation. It works by queuing malicious code into a target thread's APC queue using APIs like OpenThread and QueueUserAPC, which executes when the thread enters an alertable state. Variations include Early Bird injection and AtomBombing. This allows code execution within a legitimate process's memory space, evading detection and potentially gaining elevated privileges. It has been associated with groups like FIN8 and exploits such as CVE-2021-34523.[/profile]

18980.name: T1497.003
18980.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]T1497.003, Virtualization/Sandbox Evasion: Time Based Evasion, is a defense-evasion and discovery technique for Windows, Linux, and macOS. It works by adversaries using time-based checks, such as calling `GetTickCount` or `GetSystemTimeAsFileTime`, to detect virtualized or sandboxed environments by measuring discrepancies in system uptime or clock speed that indicate time acceleration.[/profile]

18981.name: Time Based Checks
18981.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Time Based Checks, also known as T1497.003, is a Defense Evasion and Discovery technique used on Windows, Linux, and macOS platforms. It involves adversaries using time-based methods to detect virtualization and analysis environments, such as by calling functions like GetTickCount and GetSystemTimeAsFileTime to sample timestamps before and after a sleep function to identify sandboxes that accelerate time. This technique is a sub-technique of Virtualization/Sandbox Evasion.[/profile]

18982.name: T1055.003
18982.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]T1055.003, Thread Execution Hijacking, is a defense-evasion and privilege-escalation technique for Windows. It executes malicious code within a live process by first obtaining a handle (e.g., via OpenThread), suspending a thread (SuspendThread), allocating memory (VirtualAllocEx), writing shellcode (WriteProcessMemory), redirecting execution (SetThreadContext), and resuming the thread (ResumeThread). This method evades detection by masking execution under a legitimate process and is distinct from Process Hollowing as it targets an existing, running process. It has been associated with CVE-2021-34473.[/profile]

18983.name: Thread Execution Hijacking
18983.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Thread Execution Hijacking, identified as T1055.003, is a Defense Evasion and Privilege Escalation technique for Windows. It works by injecting code into a live process: an adversary obtains a handle to a victim thread using APIs like OpenThread, suspends it with SuspendThread, writes malicious code or a DLL path into its memory using VirtualAllocEx and WriteProcessMemory, redirects the thread's execution context with SetThreadContext, and then resumes it with ResumeThread. This allows execution within a legitimate process's context to evade detection and potentially access system resources. It is distinct from Process Hollowing as it targets an already running process.[/profile]

18984.name: T1055.011
18984.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Extra Window Memory Injection (T1055.011) is a defense evasion and privilege escalation technique for Windows. It works by injecting malicious code into a process via the 40 bytes of Extra Window Memory (EWM) allocated for a window class, often using it to store a pointer to a malicious window procedure. This method evades detection by avoiding highly monitored APIs like WriteProcessMemory and may bypass defenses like DEP by triggering system functions to rewrite the payload into an executable memory region, allowing execution within a legitimate process's context.

18985.name: Extra Window Memory Injection
18985.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Extra Window Memory Injection (T1055.011) is a Defense Evasion and Privilege Escalation technique for Windows. It exploits the up to 40 bytes of Extra Window Memory (EWM) allocated to a window class. Malware writes code to a process's shared memory, places a pointer to that code in the EWM (using SetWindowLong/GetWindowLong APIs), and redirects execution to it, evading monitoring of APIs like WriteProcessMemory and potentially bypassing Data Execution Prevention (DEP).[/profile]

18991.name: r77 rootkit
18991.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]The malware is the r77 rootkit, an open-source ring-3 rootkit. It is associated with groups including APT33, Dropping Elephant, Stone Panda, and The Gorgon Group. It primarily targets Windows platforms, as indicated by its registry and service manipulation capabilities.[/profile]

19016.name: AntSword

It is used to manage web shells on compromised web servers, often exploiting vulnerabilities like CVE-2019-0604, CVE-2025-49704, CVE-2025-49706, CVE-2025-53771, and CVE-2025-53770. It is a tool in the same category as other frameworks like Godzilla and Behinder.[/profile]

19017.name: ValleyRAT
19017.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]ValleyRAT, also known as valleyrat, is a Remote Access Trojan (RAT) that has been used in campaigns targeting victims in China.
