The malware has been linked to exploitation of vulnerabilities including CVE-2019-0604, CVE-2025-49706, CVE-2025-49704, CVE-2025-53771, and CVE-2025-53770.[/profile]

19018.name: China Chopper - S0020
19018.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]China Chopper (S0020) is a web shell malware used by multiple threat groups including HAFNIUM, APT41, Mustang Panda, Leviathan, BackdoorDiplomacy, Gallium, Fox Kitten, Threat Group-3390, and ToddyCat. It provides backdoor access to compromised web servers without requiring callbacks to a C2 server, enabling attackers to maintain persistence and execute commands. It has been associated with exploitation of vulnerabilities like CVE-2019-0604 and is primarily used against web server platforms, with infrastructure and activity linked to China.[/profile]

19020.name: unkown_apt_group
19020.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]This intrusion set, likely a Chinese state-sponsored APT group, is known for exploiting vulnerabilities including CVE-2019-0604, CVE-2025-49704, CVE-2025-49706, CVE-2025-53771, and CVE-2025-53770. Its key malware and tools include the ValleyRAT remote access trojan, the China Chopper web shell, and the AntSword web shell management framework. Its TTPs encompass OS Credential Dumping (T1003), Obfuscated Files or Information (T1027), File and Directory Discovery (T1083), and DLL Side-Loading (T1574.002). The group is attributed to China and primarily targets victims within China. It shows overlaps with groups like BackdoorDiplomacy and Lotus Panda.[/profile]

19038.name: ScatterBrain
19038.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]ScatterBrain is a malware used for obfuscating ShadowPad samples, with observed use since 2022. It is attributed to clusters associated with the suspected Chinese APT umbrella actor APT41. Its key technical behaviors involve modifying authentication processes, such as using Password Filter DLLs to intercept plain-text credentials, and forging Kerberos tickets like Golden Tickets for unauthorized domain access. It targets Windows platforms and is linked to techniques for compromising host software binaries to establish persistence.[/profile]

19040.name: unkown_apt_group
19040.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]This intrusion set, likely a subgroup or cluster within the broader APT41 threat group, is also known as BackdoorDiplomacy, CloudComputating, BackDip, and Quarian. Its key malware includes the GodRAT remote access trojan and the MS Edge password stealer component. Core techniques focus on credential access, notably the use of Golden Tickets and Password Filter DLLs to forge Kerberos tickets and harvest plaintext passwords. It is attributed to China and has targeted entities in Lebanon, Jordan, Hong Kong, Malaysia, and the Central African Republic, with a motivation for espionage and data theft.

19041.name: T1556
19041.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]This entity is MITRE ATT&CK technique T1556, "Modify Authentication Process", primarily used for Credential Access, Defense Evasion, and Persistence across Windows, Linux, macOS, and cloud platforms. It involves altering authentication mechanisms—like the Windows LSASS process, Unix PAM modules, or cloud conditional access policies—to steal credentials or bypass authentication, such as by removing multi-factor authentication requirements. Adversaries may implement this by patching or replacing legitimate software binaries, as seen in UNC3886 campaigns, and it is associated with groups like FIN13, Scattered Spider, and Storm-0501.[/profile]

19044.name: T1552.003
19044.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]T1552.003, Unsecured Credentials: Bash History, is a Credential Access technique for Linux, macOS, and Windows. Adversaries search shell history files, like `~/.bash_history` or `~/.zsh_history` on Unix systems, for insecurely stored credentials users typed as command-line parameters. On Windows, they may target the persistent PowerShell history file at `%userprofile%\AppData\Roaming\Microsoft\Windows\PowerShell\PSReadline\ConsoleHost_history.txt` or use `Get-History`.

19045.name: T1027.005
19045.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]T1027.005, Indicator Removal from Tools, is a Defense Evasion technique for macOS, Linux, and Windows. It involves adversaries modifying their malicious tools by removing specific forensic or detection indicators, such as file signatures, after they have been detected or quarantined by security software. This allows the updated, "cleaner" version of the tool to evade the same defenses upon reuse. Groups like APT3, OilRig, and Turla have employed this method.

19046.name: Compromise Host Software Binary
19046.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Compromise Host Software Binary, identified as MITRE ATT&CK technique T1554, is a Persistence tactic used on Windows, Linux, macOS, and ESXi platforms. It involves modifying legitimate host binaries like SSH or FTP clients to establish persistent access, typically by replacing or backdooring the binary, patching malicious code via IAT or entry-point hooking, or infecting support files. To maintain persistence, adversaries may subsequently prevent updates using mechanisms like the Linux `yum-versionlock` command. Associated threat groups include UNC3886 and APT5.

19047.name: Golden Ticket
19047.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Golden Ticket, identified as T1558.001, is a Credential Access technique within the MITRE ATT&CK framework targeting Windows platforms. It involves forging Kerberos Ticket-Granting Tickets (TGTs) using the stolen password hash of the KRBTGT service account. This allows adversaries to generate authentication material for any account in an Active Directory domain, enabling them to subsequently request Ticket-Granting Service (TGS) tickets to access specific resources, a process that requires interaction with the domain's Key Distribution Center (KDC).

19048.name: Password Filter DLL
19048.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Password Filter DLL is a Windows-specific attack pattern (MITRE ATT&CK T1556.002) used for credential access, defense evasion, and persistence. It involves adversaries registering a malicious dynamic link library (DLL) as a password filter with the Local Security Authority (LSA). This malicious DLL intercepts and receives plain-text user credentials from the LSA for validation every time a password change or set request is made, enabling credential harvesting from local systems or entire domains.

19049.name: T1558
19049.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]The entity T1558, known as Steal or Forge Kerberos Tickets, is a Credential Access technique applicable to Windows, Linux, and macOS platforms. It involves subverting Kerberos authentication by stealing or forging tickets, such as Ticket Granting Tickets (TGTs) or service tickets, to enable unauthorized access and lateral movement via Pass the Ticket (PtT). Specific methods include creating Golden Tickets using the KRBTGT account hash for domain-wide access and forging Silver Tickets with a service account's password hash to access specific resources without interacting with the Key Distribution Center (KDC). Adversaries may use tools like the built-in Windows `klist` utility to interact with cached tickets.

19050.name: Modify Authentication Process
19050.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Modify Authentication Process is identified as MITRE ATT&CK technique T1556 under the Credential Access, Defense Evasion, and Persistence tactics. It targets platforms including Windows, Linux, macOS, and cloud services. This technique involves adversaries maliciously altering core authentication mechanisms—such as the LSASS process or SAM on Windows, PAM modules on Unix-based systems, or authorization plugins on macOS—to either steal credentials or create authentication backdoors. For example, on domain controllers, attackers may inject a "Skeleton Key" patch to authenticate as any user, while on Unix systems, they can modify PAM libraries like `pam_unix.so` to accept adversary-supplied credentials or harvest plaintext passwords.[/profile]

19051.name: Indicator Removal from Tools
19051.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Indicator Removal from Tools is a Defense Evasion technique (MITRE ATT&CK T1066) applicable to Windows, Linux, and macOS. It involves adversaries modifying a malicious tool after its detection to remove the specific indicator, such as a file signature, that triggered security alerts. For example, if antivirus software quarantines malware based on its signature, an adversary can repack or alter the file to change its signature, allowing the tool to evade detection upon reuse. This technique is distinct from general artifact deletion and is used by groups like APT3 and OilRig.

19052.name: Shell History
19052.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Shell History, also known as T1552.003 or Bash History, is a Credential Access technique targeting macOS, Linux, and Windows. Adversaries search shell command history files for insecurely stored credentials, such as passwords typed as command-line parameters. On Linux/macOS, they examine files like ~/.bash_history or ~/.zsh_history, which store the user's last 500-1000 commands. On Windows, they target the persistent PowerShell history file at %userprofile%\AppData\Roaming\Microsoft\Windows\PowerShell\PSReadline\ConsoleHost_history.txt or use the Get-History cmdlet.

19053.name: T1558.001
19053.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]The entity is the MITRE ATT&CK technique T1558.001, Golden Ticket, under the Credential Access tactic for Windows. It involves forging Kerberos Ticket-Granting Tickets (TGTs) using the stolen KRBTGT account password hash, which adversaries obtain via techniques like OS Credential Dumping. This golden ticket allows the generation of authentication material for any Active Directory account and is used to request Ticket-Granting Service (TGS) tickets for resource access, requiring interaction with the domain controller's Key Distribution Center (KDC).

19054.name: Steal or Forge Kerberos Tickets
19054.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Steal or Forge Kerberos Tickets is technique T1558 under the Credential Access tactic, applicable to Windows, Linux, and macOS platforms. It subverts Kerberos authentication by stealing cached tickets or forging new ones, such as Golden Tickets using the KRBTGT account hash or Silver Tickets using a service account hash, to enable Pass the Ticket attacks. The built-in Windows `klist` utility can be used to list cached tickets. This technique is associated with threat groups like Akira and Ke3chang.

19055.name: T1556.002
19055.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]T1556.002, known as Password Filter DLL, is a credential access, defense evasion, and persistence technique for Windows. It involves adversaries registering a malicious dynamic link library (DLL) as a password filter with the Local Security Authority (LSA). This malicious filter intercepts and receives plain-text user credentials during password change or validation requests on local systems or domain controllers, enabling credential harvesting. Groups like OilRig and Strider have been associated with its use.

19056.name: T1554
19056.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]T1554, known as Compromise Host Software Binary, is a Persistence technique applicable to Windows, Linux, macOS, and ESXi platforms. It involves adversaries modifying legitimate host software binaries or executables, such as SSH clients or user applications, to establish persistent access. This is achieved by replacing or infecting binaries with backdoors, patching in malicious code via methods like IAT hooking or entry point modification, or altering binaries to steal credentials. Attackers may subsequently impair defenses by preventing binary updates, for example using the `yum-versionlock` command on Linux systems.

19057.name: Mimikatz
19057.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Mimikatz is a credential access tool for Windows that implements techniques like DCSync (T1003.006) to remotely pull password hashes from Active Directory by abusing Domain Controller replication APIs. Its key technical behaviors include extracting credentials from LSASS memory (sekurlsa::pth) and facilitating attacks such as Pass-the-Hash. It is primarily associated with threat groups including APT10, APT32, Anunak, and Gallium, and is frequently integrated into other malware like Wannamine, Black Basta, and Hive for post-exploitation activities.

19058.name: Checkout
19058.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Checkout is a malware entity targeting e-commerce platforms, with observed infrastructure including domains like www.msn-microsoft.org and www.upload-microsoft.com, and callback servers such as toun.callback.red. It is associated with groups like FIN6 and Magecart, and its behavior involves scanning websites for keywords like "checkout," "cart," and "pay" to steal credit card information, which is then exfiltrated to domains like opendoorcdn[.]com. It has been deployed in regions including Central African Republic and South Africa, and its infrastructure mimics legitimate services to evade detection.

19059.name: Pillager
19059.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Pillager is a malware used by the Andariel group (also known as Silent Chollima), targeting entities in locations like the Central African Republic and South Africa. Its key technical behaviors include using malicious HTA files hosted on domains like github.githubassets.net and establishing command and control (C2) communications through domains such as toun.callback.red and msn-microsoft.org, as well as subdomains like chyedweeyaxkavyccenwjvqrsgvyj0o1y.oast.fun for callback operations. This infrastructure supports its data exfiltration and remote access activities on Windows platforms.]

19060.name: Cobalt Strike - S0154
19060.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Cobalt Strike - S0154 is a malware tool used by various threat groups including APT29, APT32, APT41, FIN6, FIN7, and Leviathan, as indicated by similar entities. It employs command and control techniques such as One-Way Communication (T1102.003) and Bidirectional Communication (T1102.002) to blend with legitimate web traffic, and uses domains (T1583.001) for operations. Its infrastructure includes C2 servers like https://medpagetoday.icu/nicheediting/trends and https://taskandpurpose.icu/hews/coast-guard-0reg0n-c0ncrete.jpg, and it has been deployed in locations including Taiwan, Ukraine, and South Africa.

19062.name: PLUSINJECT
19062.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]PLUSINJECT is a malware entity, not a family, associated with the use of Domain Generation Algorithms (DGAs) for command and control, as well as techniques like Process Hollowing (T1055.012) for defense evasion. Its infrastructure includes domains such as pubs.infinityfreeapp.com, resource.infinityfreeapp.com, word.msapp.workers.dev, cloud.msapp.workers.dev, and ways-sms-pmc-shareholders.trycloudflare.com. It has been observed targeting Taiwan. Retrieved information suggests technical overlaps with entities like Bazarnimrod, which shares a C2 POST request structure and a public key, and Coper and Shifu, which are also associated with injection capabilities.[/profile]

19063.name: PLUSDROP
19063.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]PLUSDROP, also known as MAGICHOUND.DROPIT, is associated with groups like Magic Hound, Rocket Kitten, APT33, APT35, and OilRig. It uses techniques including Process Hollowing (T1055.012) for defense evasion and Domain Generation Algorithms (T1568.002) for command and control, alongside One-Way Communication (T1102.003) and Multi-hop Proxy (T1090.003) to obscure traffic. It primarily targets Windows systems and has utilized infrastructure domains such as cloud.msapp.workers.dev, word.msapp.workers.dev, pubs.infinityfreeapp.com, resource.infinityfreeapp.com, and term-restore-satisfied-hence.trycloudflare.com.[/profile]

19064.name: ToughProgress
19064.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]ToughProgress is a malware that uses the Domain Generation Algorithms (DGA) technique for command and control, and employs Process Hollowing for defense evasion. Its infrastructure includes domains such as resource.infinityfreeapp.com, cloud.msapp.workers.dev, word.msapp.workers.dev, pubs.infinityfreeapp.com, and term-restore-satisfied-hence.trycloudflare.com. It has been observed targeting Taiwan.

19071.name: T1090.003
19071.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]T1090.003, Multi-hop Proxy, is a Command and Control technique used across Windows, Linux, macOS, Network Devices, and ESXi platforms. It involves chaining multiple proxies, such as onion routing networks like Tor, operational relay box (ORB) networks, or compromised devices, to obfuscate the original source of malicious traffic by routing it through several intermediary hops, making traceback difficult for defenders.

19072.name: Domain Generation Algorithms
19072.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Domain Generation Algorithms (DGAs) is a command and control technique under MITRE ATT&CK ID T1568.002, applicable to Windows, Linux, macOS, and ESXi platforms. It works by algorithmically generating a large number of potential domain names (e.g., random strings like 'istgmxdejdnxuyla.ru' or concatenated words like 'cityjulydish.net') for malware to contact, often using time-based seeds to create new domains periodically. This dynamic generation makes blocking or tracking C2 traffic difficult and is frequently used to establish fallback channels if primary C2 servers are lost. Groups like APT41 and TA551 have been associated with this technique.

19073.name: Multi-hop Proxy
19073.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Multi-hop Proxy, identified as MITRE ATT&CK technique T1090.003, is a Command and Control tactic applicable to Windows, Linux, macOS, Network Devices, and ESXi platforms. It involves chaining multiple proxies, such as onion routing networks like Tor, operational relay box (ORB) networks using VPS and IoT devices, or compromised network devices, to obfuscate the original source of malicious traffic. This makes forensic tracing difficult as defenders must identify each hop, and adversaries may implement this via patched router firmware or by abusing peer-to-peer and blockchain infrastructure for routing.

19085.name: T1055.012
19085.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]The entity is Process Hollowing, a sub-technique under MITRE ATT&CK ID T1055.012 within the Defense Evasion and Privilege Escalation tactics for Windows. It executes arbitrary code by creating a process in a suspended state, hollowing its memory via APIs like `CreateProcess` and `ZwUnmapViewOfSection`, then replacing it with malicious code using `VirtualAllocEx`, `WriteProcessMemory`, `SetThreadContext`, and `ResumeThread`. This evades detection by masking execution under a legitimate process, though it typically inherits the security context of the injector. It is associated with groups like Gorgon Group and Patchwork, and a related vulnerability is CVE-2023-21839.[/profile]

19086.name: Process Hollowing
19086.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Process Hollowing is a Windows-specific technique (T1055.012) used for Defense Evasion and Privilege Escalation. It works by creating a legitimate process in a suspended state, unmapping its memory using APIs like `NtUnmapViewOfSection`, and replacing it with malicious code via `WriteProcessMemory`. Execution is then resumed under the guise of the legitimate process, evading detection. It is distinct from Thread Execution Hijacking, which targets existing processes, and Process Doppelgänging, which uses transactional file operations.

19106.name: UnmarshalPwn
19106.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]UnmarshalPwn is a malware targeting Taiwan, exploiting the CVE-2018-0824 deserialization vulnerability. Its technical behaviors include using Remote Access Tools and an Application Layer Protocol for command and control, performing OS Credential Dumping, and conducting Query Registry and Remote System Discovery for reconnaissance and lateral movement. Its infrastructure involves indicators like the domains www.nss.com.tw and IPs 103.56.114.69 and 45.85.76.18, used to host payloads such as p.ps1 and calc.exe. It is related to techniques and groups associated with tools like Cobalt Strike, Lowkey, and Pebbledash.[/profile]

19125.name: T1563
19125.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]T1563, known as Remote Service Session Hijacking, is a Lateral Movement technique applicable to Windows, Linux, and macOS. It involves adversaries taking control of existing, authenticated sessions on remote services like RDP, SSH, or telnet to execute actions, rather than creating new sessions with stolen credentials. This method can be associated with vulnerabilities such as CVE-2018-0824.[/profile]

19126.name: Remote Service Session Hijacking
19126.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Remote Service Session Hijacking is a Lateral Movement technique (MITRE ATT&CK T1563) applicable to Windows, Linux, and macOS. It involves adversaries taking control of existing, authenticated sessions on remote services like RDP, SSH, or telnet to move laterally, rather than creating new sessions with stolen credentials. A specific technical method for RDP hijacking uses the native Windows command `tscon.exe` with system permissions to steal a session without triggering user alerts. This technique allows adversaries to assume the privileges and access of the hijacked user session.

19127.name: DUSTTRAP
19127.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]DUSTTRAP is a malware family attributed to APT41. Its key techniques include Defense Evasion via Binary Padding (T1027.001) and Process Hollowing, and Command & Control via Data Encoding (T1132.001), Symmetric Cryptography (T1573.001), and Web Services (T1102), including suspected use of the Google API. It uses infrastructure like trycloudflare.com domains and has been associated with a stolen code signing certificate from CCR Inc.[/profile]

19128.name: Voldemort
19128.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Voldemort is a malware loader using a DLL named CiscoSparkLauncher.dll. Its key techniques include Process Hollowing for defense evasion, Binary Padding to alter file checksums, and Symmetric Cryptography and Standard Encoding for obfuscating command and control traffic. It communicates via Web Services, using domains like ways-sms-pmc-shareholders.trycloudflare.com. It is associated with threat groups including APT29, APT32, APT41, FIN6, FIN7, Mustang Panda, and Winnti, and primarily targets Windows systems.[/profile]

19130.name: Glutton
19130.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Glutton is a PHP backdoor attributed to the Winnti APT group, delivered via web shells and exploiting vulnerabilities like CVE-2021-26857. It establishes persistence through boot/logon scripts (T1037) and executes commands via Unix shells (T1059.004). For command and control, it uses non-standard ports (T1571) and traffic signaling techniques like port knocking (T1205), communicating with domains such as v20.thinkphp1.com and v6.thinkphp1.com to evade detection.[/profile]

19136.name: Boot or Logon Initialization Scripts
19136.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Boot or Logon Initialization Scripts is MITRE ATT&CK technique T1037, used for Persistence and Privilege Escalation on platforms including Windows, Linux, macOS, and ESXi. It involves adversaries placing scripts to be automatically executed during system boot or user logon. These scripts, which vary by OS, can run other programs or establish communication, and they often execute with higher privileges, enabling both persistence and potential privilege escalation. Associated threat groups include APT29, APT41, and UNC3886.

19137.name: MS Edge password stealer
19137.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]MS Edge password stealer, also known as a component of Godrat, is a credential stealer targeting the Microsoft Edge web browser. It is attributed to APT41 and possibly The Gorgon Group. Its key technical behaviors involve stealing saved credentials by accessing the browser's SQLite database and the Local State file containing the encryption key, using the CryptUnprotectData() API, and staging collected data into a local file like edge.txt. It targets Windows platforms and employs data encoding and encrypted channels for command and control.[/profile]

19138.name: Chrome password stealer
19138.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Chrome password stealer is a malware that steals stored credentials from the Google Chrome browser. It is associated with the APT41 group through the GodRAT malware family and shares functional similarities with credential stealers like Loki and Agent Tesla. Its key behaviors include Input Capture for credential access and Data Staging for collection, and it has been deployed in regions including Lebanon, Hong Kong, Jordan, Malaysia, and the United Arab Emirates.[/profile]

19139.name: GodRAT
19139.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]The malware GodRAT is a Remote Access Trojan (RAT) based on the Gh0st RAT codebase. It is attributed to APT41 and has been deployed against financial firms via malicious .scr files on Skype. Its key behaviors include data staging (T1074), clipboard data theft (T1115), data encoding (T1132), input capture (T1056), and using encrypted channels (T1573) for command and control. It targets Windows systems and has been associated with activity in locations including Lebanon, Hong Kong, Jordan, Malaysia, and the United Arab Emirates.[/profile]

19178.name: unkown_apt_group
19178.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]This intrusion set, likely associated with the financially motivated threat group known as Alpha Spider (also known as Scattered Spider, Vanilla Tempest, and UNC3944), is a prolific operator of ransomware and infostealer malware. Its key tools include the BlackCat ransomware (also known as BlackMatter or Sphynx) and credential stealers such as Vidar Stealer, RedLine Stealer, and Stealc. Its technical behaviors involve establishing infrastructure and accounts (T1585, T1608), compromising domains (T1584.001), and harvesting unsecured credentials (T1552) to facilitate ransomware deployment and data theft. The group is attributed to a financially motivated cybercriminal nexus, primarily targeting a wide range of global sectors, with infrastructure indicators including domains like nike-support.com, corp-cox.com, and creditkarma-help.com.

19574.name: T1589.002
19574.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]T1589.002, also known as Email Addresses, is a reconnaissance technique within the MITRE ATT&CK framework, applicable to the PRE platform. It involves adversaries gathering email addresses from public data sets like social media, victim-owned websites, or via active scanning of services such as Office 365 APIs (e.g., autodiscover and GetCredentialType endpoints). This collected information enables follow-on activities like phishing, brute force attacks, or further reconnaissance. Groups including HAFNIUM, Lazarus Group, and Volt Typhoon have been observed using this method.

19957.name: T1606
19957.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]T1606, Forge Web Credentials, is a credential-access technique applicable across macOS, Linux, Windows, and cloud platforms (IaaS, SaaS, Identity Provider). It involves adversaries generating new, forged session cookies, tokens, or pre-authentication keys to access web applications and services, differing from stealing existing credentials. This process often requires secret values like passwords or private keys and can leverage specific APIs (e.g., AWS `AssumeRole`) or commands (e.g., Zimbra `zmprov gdpak`). The forged credentials can be used to bypass multi-factor authentication.

20006.name: BlackCat
20006.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]BlackCat, also known as BlackMatter, is a ransomware family attributed to groups including Alpha Spider, RansomHub, and Vanilla Tempest. It employs techniques such as disabling or modifying system firewalls (T1562.004) and creating accounts (T1136) for persistence. The malware targets both Windows and Linux platforms, with detection signatures including Ransom:Win32/Blackcat and Ransom:Linux/BlackCat. Associated infrastructure includes domains like forward-icloud.com and authenticate-bt.com.[/profile]

20007.name: RedLine Stealer
20007.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]RedLine Stealer, also known as redline stealer, is a malware family. Its key technical behaviors include credential theft via the Unsecured Credentials technique (T1552) and data exfiltration over web services (T1567). It targets credentials saved in web browsers, including those with automatic login features. Its infrastructure includes C2 servers such as 66.206.18[.]186 and domains like securian-hr.com and creditkarma-help.com.[/profile]

20008.name: BlackCat - S1068
20008.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]BlackCat - S1068 is a specific variant of the BlackCat ransomware family, which is written in Rust and operates under a Ransomware-as-a-Service (RaaS) model. It is also known as Sphynx and is associated with groups including Alpha Spider, Scattered Spider, RansomHub, and Vanilla Tempest. Key behaviors involve using tools to reset passwords and spread across networks, creating its payload, and employing techniques like Account Discovery (T1087), Brute Force (T1110), and Unsecured Credentials (T1552) for credential access, as well as Create Account (T1136) for persistence. It targets a wide range of sectors globally across Windows, Linux, and macOS platforms, utilizing infrastructure such as domains like creditkarma-help.com and login.five9-hr.com for malicious activity.[/profile]

20009.name: Raccoon Stealer
20009.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Raccoon Stealer, also known as Raccoon, is an information stealer malware family active since at least 2019, operating as a malware-as-a-service offering. It is associated with the Scattered Spider threat group. Its key behaviors include credential theft, specifically searching for unsecured credentials stored in files and system repositories. The malware has been observed in two distinct periods of activity, with a revised version emerging in June 2022. Associated infrastructure indicators include domains like gimpimageeditor.com, forward-icloud.com, and securian-hr.com.[/profile]

20010.name: Vidar Stealer
20010.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Vidar Stealer is an infostealer malware, also known simply as Vidar. It is associated with or shares infrastructure with Arkei, Megumin, and Oski Stealer. It employs DerpLoader for packing and exfiltrates stolen data via HTTP POST requests. Its primary function is credential theft, targeting browser autofill data, cookies, saved payment information, history, cryptocurrency wallets, and Telegram databases, and it can also take screenshots. It has used domains such as servicenow-help.com, creditkarma-help.com, and revolut-ticket.com for command-and-control infrastructure.[/profile]

20011.name: Stealc
20011.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Stealc is a malware family that steals data, with its version StealC V2 being packed using the Themida packer. Its technical behaviors include searching for and exfiltrating insecurely stored credentials (T1552), impairing system defenses to evade detection (T1562), and creating accounts for persistence (T1136). It has been associated with infrastructure indicators such as the domains forward-icloud.com, login.five9-hr.com, revolut-ticket.com, and authenticate-bt.com.[/profile]

20028.name: Brute Force
20028.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Brute Force, identified as T1110, is a Credential Access technique applicable across multiple platforms including Windows, Linux, and macOS. It involves systematically guessing passwords through a repetitive mechanism, either by interacting with a live service to check credential validity or offline against previously acquired password hashes. This activity is often conducted against common management services like SSH, RDP, and SMB, and may be combined with other techniques such as OS Credential Dumping or External Remote Services. Numerous threat groups, including APT28, APT29, and OilRig, have been associated with its use.[/profile]

20030.name: PolyVice
20030.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]PolyVice is a ransomware variant used by the Vice Society threat group. It is a customizable locker, with observed changes to its file extension and email contact details indicating the use of builder tools by affiliates. Its technical behaviors include Account Access Removal to hinder response, Data Encrypted for Impact for extortion, and Masquerading to evade detection. It targets Windows systems and uses Tor-based C2 infrastructure, such as the domains wjdgz3btk257obba7aekowz7ylm33zb6hu4aetxc3bypfajixzvx4iad.onion and ml3mjpuhnmse4kjij7ggupenw34755y4uj7t742qf7jg5impt5ulhkid.onion.[/profile]

20031.name: Chily
20031.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Chily is a malware variant related to the HelloKitty ransomware family, specifically targeting ESXi servers and virtual machines. It employs Defense Evasion techniques like Masquerading (T1036) and Subvert Trust Controls (T1553), and uses Impact tactics including Data Encrypted for Impact (T1486) and Account Access Removal (T1531) to lock accounts and encrypt data, often as part of ransomware operations. It conducts System Network Connections Discovery (T1049) and operates through specific onion domain infrastructure such as wjdgz3btk257obba7aekowz7ylm33zb6hu4aetxc3bypfajixzvx4iad.onion.[/profile]

20032.name: SunnyDay
20032.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]SunnyDay is a malware entity associated with the Akira ransomware group, as indicated by its use of the T1531 Account Access Removal technique to delete or lock user accounts and the T1486 Data Encrypted for Impact technique for file encryption, operating on Windows, Linux, macOS, and ESXi platforms. It utilizes command and scripting interpreters (T1059) for execution and conducts System Network Connections Discovery (T1049). Its infrastructure includes Tor domains such as wjdgz3btk257obba7aekowz7ylm33zb6hu4aetxc3bypfajixzvx4iad.onion and wmp2rvrkecyx72i3x7ejhyd3yr6fn5uqo7wfus7cz7qnwr6uzhcbrwad.onion.[profile]

20033.name: RedAlert
20033.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]RedAlert is a ransomware that demands Monero payments and uses a three-day negotiation deadline with threats to leak personal data. It employs TTPs including Data Encrypted for Impact (T1486) for encryption, Account Access Removal (T1531) to inhibit user access, and Masquerading (T1036) for defense evasion. Its infrastructure includes Tor-based C2 and leak sites such as wjdgz3btk257obba7aekowz7ylm33zb6hu4aetxc3bypfajixzvx4iad.onion and wmp2rvrkecyx72i3x7ejhyd3yr6fn5uqo7wfus7cz7qnwr6uzhcbrwad.onion.[/profile]

20035.name: unkown_apt_group
20035.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]This intrusion set is likely the ransomware-focused threat group known as Vice Society, which also operates under the alias "V-Society" as indicated by its infrastructure. Its key malware includes the custom ransomware PolyVice, and it has also been observed using tools like FIVEHANDS, Zeppelin Ransomware, and Hello Kitty. Its primary TTPs involve Account Access Removal to hinder response, OS Credential Dumping, use of Remote Services for lateral movement, and Indicator Removal for defense evasion. The group's origin is unattributed, but its operations have targeted sectors and organizations in Switzerland, Argentina, Brazil, and Israel, with a clear motivation for financial gain through ransomware extortion.[/profile]

20060.name: T1531
20060.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]The entity is the MITRE ATT&CK technique Account Access Removal, with ID T1531, categorized under the Impact tactic and applicable across Windows, Linux, macOS, ESXi, and SaaS platforms. It involves adversaries inhibiting legitimate user access by deleting, locking, or manipulating accounts, such as changing passwords or revoking permissions. Specific technical mechanics include using the Windows `Net` utility or PowerShell cmdlets like `Set-LocalUser`, the Linux `passwd` utility, and ESXi commands like `esxcli system account set`. This technique is often employed by groups like Akira and LAPSUS$ in conjunction with ransomware attacks to impede recovery, and it may be paired with actions like system reboots or precede the creation of masquerading accounts.[profile]

20062.name: Active Scanning
20062.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Active Scanning is MITRE ATT&CK technique T1595 under the Reconnaissance tactic, applicable to the PRE platform. It involves adversaries directly probing victim infrastructure with network traffic, such as ICMP pings, to gather information like active IPs, open ports, and service banners. This data enables follow-on actions like vulnerability exploitation or credential attacks, as indicated by its association with CVEs like CVE-2018-0171.

20063.name: Account Access Removal
20063.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Account Access Removal, identified as T1531, is an Impact tactic affecting Windows, Linux, macOS, ESXi, and SaaS platforms. Adversaries inhibit legitimate user access by deleting, locking, or manipulating accounts, such as by changing passwords or revoking permissions. Specific mechanics include using the Windows Net utility or PowerShell cmdlets like `Set-LocalUser`, the Linux `passwd` utility, and ESXi commands `esxcli system account set` or `remove`. This technique is often a precursor to ransomware attacks, used to impede incident response before data encryption. Associated groups include Akira and LAPSUS$.[/profile]

20064.name: T1595
20064.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Active Scanning (T1595) is a Reconnaissance tactic in the MITRE ATT&CK framework applicable to the PRE platform. It involves adversaries directly probing victim infrastructure with network traffic, such as using ICMP or other protocol features, to gather information like IP ranges or domain names. This data can enable subsequent reconnaissance, capability development, or initial access operations.

20066.name: Hello Kitty
20066.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Hello Kitty is a ransomware malware with aliases including HelloKitty and a Linux variant. It is associated with ransomware groups like Conti and LockBit, and its infrastructure includes email addresses like 876505846904@onionmail.org and domains such as 57thandnormal.com. Its key technical behaviors involve using Remote Services for lateral movement, OS Credential Dumping for credential access, and Indicator Removal (T1070) for defense evasion. It primarily targets platforms including Linux and Windows, with victim locations spanning Switzerland, Argentina, Brazil, and Israel.[/profile]

20067.name: Zeppelin Ransomware
20067.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Zeppelin Ransomware, also known as zeppelin, is attributed to the Vanilla Tempest group. It can be deployed as a .dll file. Key behaviors include OS Credential Dumping, Exploit Public-Facing Application for initial access, and use of Remote Services and Create Account for persistence and lateral movement. It also performs Indicator Removal. Its infrastructure includes domains like 57thandnormal.com and onion addresses like vsociethok6sbprvevl4dlwbqrzyhxcxaqpvcqt5belwvsuxaxsutyad.onion, and it has targeted locations including Switzerland, Argentina, Brazil, and Israel.[/profile]

20068.name: FIVEHANDS

It is associated with an unnamed group and utilizes techniques including OS Credential Dumping (T1003), Create Account (T1136), Exploit Public-Facing Application (T1190), Remote Services (T1021), and Indicator Removal (T1070). It employs an encrypted dropper variant and has been linked to infrastructure such as the onion domains vsociethok6sbprvevl4dlwbqrzyhxcxaqpvcqt5belwvsuxaxsutyad.onion and ssq4zimieeanazkzc5ld4v5hdibi2nzwzdibfh5n5w4pw5mcik76lzyd.onion, and email addresses v-society.official@onionmail.org and 316186524106@onionmail.org. Its operations have targeted locations including Switzerland, Argentina, Brazil, and Israel.[/profile]

20069.name: Virus:Win32/Neshta

It operates by prepending itself to executable files to proliferate on an infected host, creating files like %windir%\svchost.com and setting a Registry entry for persistence. Its associated infrastructure includes domains like r1.57thandnormal.com and onion addresses like vsociethok6sbprvevl4dlwbqrzyhxcxaqpvcqt5belwvsuxaxsutyad.onion. It has been deployed since its discovery in 2003 and has been observed in locations including Switzerland, Argentina, Brazil, and Israel.[/profile]

20071.name: Ransom.Win64.VICESOCIETY.A

It has been observed in locations including Switzerland, Argentina, Brazil, and Israel.[/profile]

20112.name: ScRansom
20112.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]ScRansom, also known as Spacecolon, is a ransomware variant attributed to the CosmicBeetle group. It is a file-encrypting malware (Win32/Filecoder.Spacecolon) with identified auto and static variants, such as auto.exe and New.exe. Its operations have been geolocated to Cuba, China, and the United States.[/profile]

20113.name: Grixba
20113.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Grixba, also known as Infostealer.Grixba, is a network-scanning tool used to enumerate all users and computers in a domain. It has been observed in locations including Cuba, China, and the United States of America.

20114.name: SystemBC
20114.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]SystemBC is a malware, also known as systembc, attributed to the threat group Vanilla Tempest. It is associated with Ryuk and Trickbot malware operations, as indicated by shared infrastructure paths like "www/systembc/index.html" and "www/systembc/password.php". The malware leverages proxy services such as NSOCKS and ProxyAM for traffic obfuscation, utilizing residential proxy networks to conceal command and control communications, with known targeting in the United States of America.

20115.name: EDRKillShifter
20115.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]EDRKillShifter is a tool designed to disable multiple Endpoint Detection and Response (EDR) systems, including CrowdStrike, Microsoft Defender, TrendMicro, and SentinelOne. It operates in a three-stage process to deliver, decrypt, and execute a malicious embedded resource in memory. It has been associated with the ClickFix malware family and is used by threat actors targeting locations such as Cuba, China, and the United States.

20116.name: unkown_apt_group
20116.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]The intrusion set is most likely the Mustang Panda APT group, also known as Bronze President, RedDelta, and TEMP.Hex. Its key malware includes the SocGholish (FakeUpdates) loader and the RansomHub ransomware, and it employs techniques such as DCSync for credential theft, Password Spraying for initial access, and Subvert Trust Controls for defense evasion. The group is attributed to China and primarily targets entities in the United States and Cuba, with motivations believed to be cyber espionage. Its operations show overlaps with other groups like Lotus Panda.

20134.name: SocGholish
20134.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]SocGholish, also known as FakeUpdates, is a JavaScript-based loader malware family operated by Mustard Tempest and used by groups like Indrik Spider and Gold Prelude. It achieves persistence via Boot or Logon Autostart Execution, uses Python for execution, and employs Dynamic Resolution, Encrypted Channel, and Proxy techniques for command and control. It primarily targets sectors globally via drive-by-downloads masquerading as software updates, with observed infrastructure including domains like rapiddevapi.com, codecruncher.pro, and virtual.urban-orthodontics.com.[profile]

20135.name: RansomHub
20135.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]RansomHub is a ransomware family. It is associated with the threat groups ShadowSyndicate and CosmicBeetle. Its technical behaviors include credential access via DCSync (T1003.006) and Password Spraying (T1110.003), data exfiltration over alternative protocols (T1048), discovery of local system groups (T1069.001), and subverting trust controls for defense evasion (T1553). It targets Windows, Linux, and macOS platforms. Its infrastructure has been linked to the FakeUpdates campaign.[/profile]

20138.name: Brave Prince - S0252
20138.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Brave Prince - S0252, also known as Brave Prince, is a Korean-language implant first observed in December 2017. It is attributed to the Kimsuky threat group and was deployed in operations surrounding the 2018 Pyeongchang Winter Olympics alongside related malware like Gold Dragon and RunningRAT. Its technical behaviors include Defense Evasion techniques such as System Binary Proxy Execution (T1218), Impair Defenses (T1562), Masquerading Tasks/Services (T1036.004), Subverting Trust Controls, and performing Dynamic-link Library Injection (T1055.001). The malware targets Windows platforms.[profile]

20139.name: Qilin
20139.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Qilin is a ransomware family known for its modular and customizable design. Key technical behaviors include using commands like 'net stop vss' and 'wmic service where name='vss' call ChangeStartMode Disabled' to impair defenses by disabling services, and it operates TOR-based infrastructure for communication, such as the onion domains 'kbsqoivihgdmwczmxkbovk7ss2dcynitwhhfu5yw725dboqo5kthfaad.onion' and 'ijzn3sicrcy7guixkzjkib4ukbiilwc3xhnmby4mcbccnsd7j2rekvqd.onion'. It is associated with the threat group '未知' and primarily targets Windows platforms, leveraging techniques like System Binary Proxy Execution and Impair Defenses to evade detection and disable security mechanisms.[/profile]

20140.name: Crytox
20140.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Crytox is a ransomware malware. Its key technical behaviors include self-decryption multiple times to hinder static analysis, injecting shellcode into different processes, using API hashing, and encrypting files with a unique AES key per file that is then protected with RSA. It is a 64-bit executable developed in C and often packed with UPX, with an embedded uTox client found in its payload. Its associated MITRE ATT&CK techniques include Dynamic-link Library Injection (T1055.001), Subvert Trust Controls, System Binary Proxy Execution (T1218), Impair Defenses (T1562), and User Execution (T1204).[/profile]

20141.name: Lynx
20141.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Lynx is a ransomware strain that uses the contact email martina.lestariid1898@proton[.]me and operates a leak site at lynxblog[.]net and a Tor site. Its technical behaviors involve defense evasion through techniques like Subvert Trust Controls (T1553), Disable or Modify System Firewall (T1562.004), System Binary Proxy Execution (T1218), User Execution (T1204), and Impair Defenses (T1562). No specific attributed groups or target platforms are definitively identified in the provided data.[/profile]

20143.name: BlackSuit
20143.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]BlackSuit is a ransomware targeting both Windows and Linux platforms, with known executable file hashes for each. It shares significant behavioral overlaps with the Royal ransomware, as both avoid encrypting files containing specific strings (like 'perflogs', 'tor browser', 'windows', 'windows.old') and directories (like ADMIN$ and IPC$), and both skip files with extensions such as .exe and .dll. BlackSuit specifically avoids files with extensions .BlackSuit, .blacksuit, and its ransom note README.BlackSuit.txt. Its technical behaviors align with MITRE ATT&CK techniques including Subvert Trust Controls, System Binary Proxy Execution, Impair Defenses, Dynamic-link Library Injection, and User Execution for defense evasion and execution.[/profile]

20144.name: MedusaLocker
20144.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]MedusaLocker is a ransomware entity. Its technical behaviors include defense evasion techniques such as Subvert Trust Controls, System Binary Proxy Execution, and Impair Defenses, as well as execution via User Execution and the use of Dynamic-link Library Injection for code execution. It is associated with the threat group Pinchy Spider. Target platforms include Windows, Linux, and macOS.[/profile]

20145.name: AVKiller
20145.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]AVKiller is a malware tool, not a full family, used to disable antivirus and security software on Windows systems. It is often deployed as a module within other malware like Betabot, which uses it to impair defenses and eliminate competing malware (BotKiller) by targeting persistence mechanisms. Key associated techniques include Impair Defenses (T1562) and System Binary Proxy Execution (T1218) for evasion. Its primary function is to subvert trust controls and clear the infection path for primary payloads.[/profile]

20265.name: DCSync
20265.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]DCSync is identified as MITRE ATT&CK technique T1003.006, falling under the Credential Access tactic and targeting Windows platforms. It works by abusing the Domain Controller's API to simulate replication, allowing attackers with sufficient privileges (e.g., Domain Admins) to remotely pull password hashes, including for critical accounts like KRBTGT, from Active Directory. This stolen data is often leveraged to create Golden Tickets for persistence. The technique is notably implemented in tools like Mimikatz's lsadump module and has been associated with threat groups such as Lapsus$ and Mustang Panda.

20266.name: Exfiltration Over Alternative Protocol
20266.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Exfiltration Over Alternative Protocol is technique T1048 under the Exfiltration tactic. It operates across Windows, Linux, macOS, Network Devices, IaaS, ESXi, Office Suite, and SaaS platforms. Adversaries steal data by sending it over a network protocol different from the primary command and control channel, such as FTP, SMTP, HTTP/S, DNS, or SMB, potentially to an alternate destination. Execution often leverages common OS utilities like Net/SMB, FTP, or curl. Data may be encrypted or obfuscated within these alternate channels. This technique is associated with groups like OilRig and can involve direct downloads from cloud services via web consoles or APIs.[/profile]

20267.name: T1069.001
20267.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]T1069.001, known as Local Groups, is a Discovery technique for Windows, Linux, and macOS. It involves adversaries using commands like `net localgroup` on Windows, `dscl . -list /Groups` on macOS, and `groups` on Linux to enumerate local system groups and user memberships. This reconnaissance helps identify users with elevated permissions, such as local administrators, to inform subsequent privilege escalation. Groups like Chimera, Turla, and Volt Typhoon have been associated with this technique.

20268.name: T1069.002
20268.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]T1069.002 (Domain Groups) is a Discovery technique for Windows, Linux, and macOS. It involves enumerating domain-level groups and their members to identify users with elevated permissions, such as domain administrators. Adversaries use commands like `net group /domain` on Windows, `dscacheutil -q group` on macOS, and `ldapsearch` on Linux. This technique has been associated with groups including Dragonfly, FIN7, Volt Typhoon, and Scattered Spider.

20269.name: T1003.006
20269.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]The entity is the DCSync technique, formally identified as T1003.006 under the Credential Access tactic for Windows platforms. It works by abusing the Microsoft Directory Replication Service (DRS) Remote Protocol to simulate domain controller replication, allowing an attacker with sufficient privileges (e.g., Domain Admin) to request and extract password hashes for domain accounts, including the KRBTGT account, directly from a domain controller. This stolen data is often used with tools like Mimikatz for subsequent attacks like Pass-the-Ticket.

20270.name: File and Directory Permissions Modification
20270.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]File and Directory Permissions Modification, identified as MITRE ATT&CK T1222, is a Defense Evasion technique applicable to Windows, Linux, macOS, and ESXi platforms. It involves modifying file or directory access control lists (ACLs) to bypass permissions and access protected files. On Windows, adversaries use commands like `icacls`, `cacls`, `takeown`, and `attrib` to manipulate Discretionary ACLs (DACLs), while on Linux and macOS, the `chmod` and `chown` commands are commonly used. This technique is often a prerequisite for establishing persistence or hijacking execution flow and is employed by groups like Wizard Spider and APT32.

20271.name: Domain Trust Discovery
20271.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Domain Trust Discovery is the MITRE ATT&CK technique T1482 under the Discovery tactic for Windows platforms. It involves adversaries gathering information on trust relationships between domains in multi-domain/forest environments to identify lateral movement paths. Technical mechanics include enumeration via the DSEnumerateDomainTrusts() Win32 API, .NET methods, LDAP queries, and the Windows utility Nltest. This discovered information can facilitate follow-on techniques like SID-History Injection, Pass the Ticket, and Kerberoasting.

20272.name: Local Groups
20272.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Local Groups is the MITRE ATT&CK technique T1069.001 under the Discovery tactic for Windows, Linux, and macOS platforms. It involves adversaries enumerating local system groups and permission settings to identify users with elevated privileges, such as local administrators. This is executed using specific commands: `net localgroup` on Windows, `dscl . -list /Groups` on macOS, and `groups` on Linux.

20273.name: Clear Windows Event Logs
20273.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Clear Windows Event Logs is a Defense Evasion technique (T1070.001) on Windows platforms. Adversaries with administrator privileges use commands like `wevtutil cl security` or PowerShell's `Remove-EventLog -LogName Security` to erase System, Application, and Security logs, or may directly delete log files from `C:\Windows\System32\winevt\logs\` to hide intrusion evidence.

20274.name: Domain Groups
20274.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Domain Groups is a discovery technique (T1069.002) within the MITRE ATT&CK framework, applicable to Windows, Linux, and macOS platforms. It involves adversaries enumerating domain-level groups and permissions to identify users with elevated privileges, such as domain administrators. Specific commands for this discovery include `net group /domain` on Windows, `dscacheutil -q group` on macOS, and `ldapsearch` on Linux. This technique has been associated with threat groups including Dragonfly, FIN7, and Scattered Spider.

20275.name: Password Spraying
20275.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Password Spraying, identified as T1110.003, is a Credential Access technique applicable across Windows, Linux, macOS, and cloud platforms. It involves using a single or small list of common passwords (e.g., 'Password01') against many different accounts to avoid account lockout thresholds. Adversaries typically target management services like SSH, SMB, LDAP, Kerberos, and RDP, as well as cloud applications and SSO, often throttling attempts or preferring LDAP/Kerberos to reduce detection by events like Windows logon failure 4625.

20278.name: More_eggs
20278.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]More_eggs is a JScript backdoor malware family, also known as S0284, used by groups including Cobalt Group and FIN6. It establishes persistence via Boot or Logon Autostart Execution (T1547) and uses Data Encoding (T1132) like Base64 to obfuscate its command-and-control traffic. It targets Windows systems and has been associated with infrastructure such as the domains bobbybradley.net, annalanyi.com, and edwarddhall.com, as well as specific URLs like https://6f4922f4.bobbyweisman.com/brake/. Its C2 infrastructure has also included domains like mail[.]rediffmail[.]kz and api[.]cloudservers[.]kz.[/profile]

20279.name: More_eggs - S0284

The group's infrastructure has included domains like jacknwoods.com, samsnewlooker.com, and academymusica.com. Its technical behaviors align with the MITRE ATT&CK techniques for Impair Defenses, Network Share Discovery, and Application Layer Protocol communication for command and control. 20842.name: WmRAT

20844.name: MiyaRAT

It is attributed to the Bitter APT group, also known as Hazy Tiger. Its key technical behaviors include using the Non-Application Layer Protocol (T1095) for command-and-control communications, archiving data via utilities (T1560.001) for exfiltration, performing screen capture (T1113), and discovering security software (T1063). It targets Windows, Linux, and macOS platforms, employing the T1036.006 technique on macOS to evade detection. Its known infrastructure includes domains like samsnewlooker.com, academymusica.com, and jacknwoods.com, and it has been distributed via malicious MSI files such as http://jacknwoods.com/gfxview.msi.[/profile]

20861.name: T1036.006
20861.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]T1036.006 (Space after Filename) is a Defense Evasion technique for macOS and Linux platforms. It works by appending a space to the end of a filename (excluding .app files), which causes the operating system to ignore the file extension and instead determine the true file type for execution. This tricks users into double-clicking a file that appears benign, like a .txt document, but actually runs a hidden executable binary. The technique has been used by groups like APT38.

20862.name: Space after Filename
20862.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Space after Filename is a defense evasion technique (T1036.006) used on macOS and Linux platforms. It works by appending a space character to the end of a filename, which can cause the operating system to ignore a deceptive file extension and instead correctly identify and execute the file's true binary format. This tricks users into launching malicious executables disguised as benign documents. The technique is associated with threat groups like APT38 and does not work with .app extensions.

20865.name: unkown_apt_group

It targets entities in the United Kingdom, Australia, Canada, Ukraine, and the United States, and has leveraged vulnerabilities such as CVE-2024-1709 and CVE-2023-32315. Its motivation appears to be cyber espionage, and it shows operational overlaps with other APT clusters.[/profile]

20889.name:
rule M_Hunting_GOGETTER_SystemdConfiguration_1

{

     meta:

          author = "Mandiant"

          description = "Searching for Systemd Unit Configuration Files but with some known filenames observed with GOGETTER"

          disclaimer = "This rule is for hunting purposes only and has not been tested to run in a production environment."

 

     strings:

          $a1 = "[Install]" ascii fullword

          $a2 = "[Service]" ascii fullword

          $a3 = "[Unit]" ascii fullword

          $v1 = "Description=" ascii 

          $v2 = "ExecStart=" ascii 

          $v3 = "Restart=" ascii 

          $v4 = "RestartSec=" ascii 

          $v5 = "WantedBy=" ascii 

          $f1 = "fail2ban-settings" ascii fullword

          $f2 = "system-sockets" ascii fullword

          $f3 = "oratredb" ascii fullword

          $f4 = "cloud-online" ascii fullword

 

     condition:

          filesize < 1MB and (3 of ($a*)) and (3 of ($v*)) and (1 of ($f*))

}

{

          date = "2023-02-13"

20923.name: Infamouse Chisel

This technique is used by threat groups like APT28 to obscure C2 communications and bypass security monitoring.

20958.name: T1422

20959.name: T1421

20965.name: GreyEnergy - S0342
20965.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]GreyEnergy - S0342, also known as GreyEnergy, is a backdoor malware written in C and compiled in Visual Studio, considered a successor to BlackEnergy. It is attributed to groups including Telebots and the Sandworm Team. Its key TTPs include using HTTP and HTTPS for command and control (C2) communications, modifying the Windows Registry for persistence and defense evasion, and abusing scheduled tasks for execution. Its primary target platform is Windows, with observed targeting of locations including Ukraine and Estonia.[profile]

20966.name: Kapeka
20966.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Kapeka is a backdoor malware family attributed to the Sandworm group, used in destructive attacks against targets in Estonia and Ukraine. It establishes persistence via scheduled tasks (T1053) and employs command and control (TA0011) and persistence (TA0003) tactics. Its technical behaviors include using a custom algorithm implementing CRC32 and a pseudo-random number generator (PRNG) to generate a unique GUID, with versions defaulting to a hardcoded GUID value like "0CA1BE92-FB73-BB74-".

20972.name: TA0011
20972.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]TA0011 is the Command and Control tactic within the MITRE ATT&CK framework, representing the adversary's objective to communicate with and control compromised systems. This tactic encompasses various techniques for establishing and maintaining covert channels. Specific techniques include using custom command and control protocols (T1094) to mimic legitimate traffic or create unique channels, and employing data obfuscation methods like adding junk data (T1001.001) to protocol traffic to evade detection. Adversaries may also leverage compromised or legitimate infrastructure, such as databases (T1213.006), to facilitate these communications or host command and control servers.

20973.name: TA0003
20973.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]TA0003 is the MITRE ATT&CK Persistence tactic, applicable across multiple platforms. It encompasses techniques adversaries use to maintain access to systems after initial compromise, such as modifying macOS plist files to auto-run malicious apps on login, scheduling tasks via cron for recurring execution, and obfuscating C2 traffic with junk data to hinder detection.

21031.name: ShadowLink
21031.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]ShadowLink is a malware attributed to the Silent Chollima group. It leverages techniques including Account Manipulation (T1098) for persistence and privilege escalation, Account Discovery (T1087) to enumerate valid accounts, and Remote Services (T1021) like SSH and RDP for lateral movement. It also utilizes Service Execution (T1035) via the Windows Service Control Manager. Its infrastructure includes domains like support.csolve.net, hwupdates.com, lt.tech-keys.com, and cloud-sync.org, and it has been associated with vulnerabilities CVE-2024-1709, CVE-2023-32315, CVE-2023-23397, CVE-2022-41352, and CVE-2021-34473. Targets have been located in the United Kingdom, Australia, Canada, Ukraine, and the United States.[/profile]

21032.name: LocalOlive

21060.name: OM.vbs

21065.name: OMClientService.exe

Its technical behaviors involve credential theft from the Windows Registry (T1552.002), system location discovery (T1614), and enumeration of local and domain groups (T1069.001, T1069.002) for privilege escalation and lateral movement. The group's command-and-control infrastructure has used domains such as questdisar.com, pikchayola.pics, and trentonkaizerfak.com. Analysis shows overlaps with other APT clusters, including Lotus Panda (also known as Lotus Blossom, Red Salamander). Its primary motivation appears to be financial gain through ransomware deployment.

21977.name: Office Template Macros
21977.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Office Template Macros is a persistence technique with MITRE ATT&CK ID T1137.001, operating on Windows and Office Suite platforms. It involves inserting malicious Visual Basic for Applications (VBA) macros into base Office templates like Word's Normal.dotm or Excel's Personal.xlsb, which execute code each time the respective application starts. Adversaries can also modify the GlobalDotName registry key to redirect the template load location to a remote or custom file for persistence.

21981.name: Nokoyawa
21981.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Nokoyawa is a ransomware strain with known versions 1.0, 1.1, and 2.0. Its technical behaviors include credential theft via the Windows Registry (T1552.002), discovery of system location (T1614), and enumeration of local and domain groups (T1069.001, T1069.002) to identify high-privilege users for lateral movement. It also performs Domain Trust Discovery (T1482) to map network trust relationships. It communicates with command-and-control infrastructure using domains such as pikchayola.pics, questdisar.com, and trentonkaizerfak.com.

22008.name: Credentials in Registry
22008.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Credentials in Registry, identified as MITRE ATT&CK technique T1552.002, is a Credential Access tactic executed on Windows platforms. Adversaries query the Windows Registry to locate passwords and credentials stored insecurely by the system or other programs, often for automatic logons. Specific technical mechanics include using commands like `reg query HKLM /f password /t REG_SZ /s` to search the Local Machine hive and `reg query HKCU /f password /t REG_SZ /s` for the Current User hive. This technique is associated with threat groups such as RedCurl and APT32.

22009.name: T1552.002
22009.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]T1552.002, known as Credentials in Registry, is a Credential Access technique for Windows. Adversaries search the Windows Registry for insecurely stored credentials and passwords used by programs or services, sometimes for automatic logons. This is performed using commands like `reg query HKLM /f password /t REG_SZ /s` for the Local Machine hive or `reg query HKCU /f password /t REG_SZ /s` for the Current User hive. Groups such as RedCurl and APT32 have been associated with this technique.

22010.name: System Location Discovery
22010.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]System Location Discovery, identified as MITRE ATT&CK T1614, is a Discovery technique used on Windows, Linux, macOS, and IaaS platforms. It involves gathering information to infer a host's geographical location by checking system settings like time zone, keyboard layout, and language, using Windows API functions such as GetLocaleInfoW. In cloud environments, adversaries may query the instance metadata service to discover the availability zone. Additionally, they may use the host's IP address with online geolocation lookup services.

22014.name: Charon
22014.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Charon is a ransomware malware targeting Middle Eastern public institutions and the aviation industry. Its key techniques include inhibiting system recovery by deleting Volume Shadow Copies and disabling automatic recovery, encrypting data for impact, moving laterally using SMB/Windows Admin Shares, and exploiting vulnerabilities for privilege escalation. It is associated with the Andariel group, which is linked to Silent Chollima.[/profile]

22015.name: unkown_apt_group

22017.name: Dridex

For command and control, it utilizes web services (T1102), encrypted channels, and dynamic resolution techniques (T1568). Its infrastructure involves domains like docs.nynovation.com and cpanel.santechplumbing.com, and it primarily targets systems in the United States, Canada, and the Russian Federation.[/profile]

22018.name: WastedLocker - S0612

Its key behaviors include establishing persistence via Boot or Logon Autostart Execution, using Dynamic Resolution and Encrypted Channels for command and control, and communicating over Application Layer Protocols like HTTP. It primarily targets Windows systems and has been deployed against sectors including manufacturing, IT, and media, with infrastructure involving domains such as docs.nynovation.com and blacksaltys.com. Technical analysis indicates code obfuscation and similarities to the Dridex and BitPaymer malware families.[/profile]

It primarily targets financial institutions across platforms like Windows, using techniques such as Boot or Logon Autostart Execution (T1547) for persistence, Encrypted Channel (T1573) and Application Layer Protocol (T1071) like HTTP for command and control, and Dynamic Resolution (T1568) for infrastructure evasion. Initial access is often via Drive-by Compromise (T1189). Its infrastructure includes domains like blacksaltys.com and publication.garyjobeferguson.com, with infections reported in countries including the United States, Canada, and the Russian Federation.[profile]

22086.name: T1550
22086.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]T1550, known as "Use Alternate Authentication Material," is a Defense Evasion and Lateral Movement technique applicable to Windows, Linux, and cloud platforms. It involves adversaries using stolen legitimate authentication artifacts like password hashes, Kerberos tickets, or application access tokens to authenticate to systems without needing plaintext credentials, thereby bypassing normal access controls. This material is often cached by systems after successful user login and can be acquired through Credential Access methods.

22087.name: Use Alternate Authentication Material
22087.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Use Alternate Authentication Material (T1550) is a Defense Evasion and Lateral Movement technique applicable to Windows, Linux, and cloud platforms. It involves adversaries using stolen, cached authentication material like password hashes (e.g., NTLM), Kerberos tickets (including Golden Tickets), or application access tokens to authenticate to systems without needing plaintext credentials, thereby bypassing normal access controls and multi-factor authentication. This material is typically obtained via Credential Access techniques and can be forged, as seen with web credentials or authentication certificates, to enable persistent lateral movement.

22301.name: T1208
22301.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]The entity T1208 is a technique known as Kerberoasting. It is a credential access technique within the MITRE ATT&CK framework, targeting Windows platforms. Adversaries with a valid Kerberos Ticket-Granting Ticket (TGT) can request Ticket-Granting Service (TGS) tickets for Service Principal Names (SPNs). Portions of these tickets, encrypted with the RC4 algorithm, contain the service account's Kerberos hash, which can be extracted and subjected to offline brute-force attacks to recover plaintext credentials, enabling persistence, privilege escalation, and lateral movement.

This method is used by groups like FIN7, APT41, and Lazarus Group. It can be implemented as backup callbacks in multi-stage channels (T1104) or through dynamic resolution (T1568) to re-establish lost connections.

For credential access, it uses Steal Web Session Cookie (T1539), and for command and control, it utilizes Standard Encoding (T1132.001) to obfuscate traffic. 22723.name: PteroX

22724.name: PteroDash

For command and control, it uses Standard Encoding to obfuscate traffic and has been associated with infrastructure domains such as hulortad.ru, nododru.ru, dfgqdsd.ru, hakold.ru, and marginisbi.ru.[/profile]

22726.name: PteroSand
22726.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]PteroSand is a downloader malware used by the Gamaredon threat group. It is employed in spearphishing campaigns, often delivered via heavily obfuscated HTA files containing blank lines, unused string variables, and fake C2 servers. Its primary function is to acquire additional payloads. Its technical behaviors include data collection from removable media, stealing web session cookies, using standard encoding for C2 obfuscation, local data staging, and screen capture. It primarily targets systems in Latvia, Lithuania, Bulgaria, Poland, and Ukraine, and has been associated with domains like fritopa.ru, lokalut.ru, loturam.ru, www.toorisugita.ru, and rieturc.ru.[/profile]

22771.name: GammaSteel
22771.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]GammaSteel is a malware variant attributed to the Gamaredon APT group (also known as Operation Armageddon). Associated command and control infrastructure includes domains such as nav-ni-furnished-handy.trycloudflare.com and des-cinema-democrat-san.trycloudflare.com.[/profile]

22866.name: Indicator Blocking
22866.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Indicator Blocking, also known as T1054, is a Defense Evasion technique applicable to Windows, Linux, macOS, and ESXi platforms. It involves adversaries blocking the collection and analysis of security indicators by tampering with host-based sensor settings, such as Event Tracing for Windows (ETW) via PowerShell's Set-EtwTraceProvider cmdlet or direct registry manipulation, or by creating host firewall rules to block network traffic to central reporting systems like SIEMs. This action aims to prevent event telemetry from reaching defenders and can be complemented by spoofing security alerts to falsely indicate normal system operation.

22867.name: T1054
22867.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]T1054, known as Indicator Blocking, is a Defense Evasion technique where adversaries block or tamper with event telemetry collection to avoid detection. This is achieved by disabling or reconfiguring host-based sensors like Event Tracing for Windows (ETW) through PowerShell cmdlets such as Set-EtwTraceProvider or by directly modifying Windows Registry settings. Adversaries may also block network traffic to security monitoring systems, such as SIEMs, using host-based firewall rules or by stopping local telemetry-forwarding processes.

22869.name: unkown_apt_group

Its tactics involve spearphishing links for initial access, discovery of security software and internet connectivity, and symmetric cryptography for command and control, as seen in its operational infrastructure (e.g., cast.voxcdn.kz). The group has targeted the United States. Its primary motivation is financial gain, consistent with the Cobalt Group's activities. The retrieved data indicates potential overlaps with other clusters like Backdoordiplomacy and Lotus Panda, but the core attribution remains to the Cobalt Group.[profile]

22909.name: T1016.001
22909.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]T1016.001, Internet Connection Discovery, is a Discovery technique for Windows, Linux, macOS, and ESXi platforms. Adversaries check for Internet connectivity on compromised systems to determine if they can communicate with command and control servers before attempting to connect. This can be accomplished using tools like Ping, tracert, or GET requests to websites, and the results may also be used to identify network routes, redirectors, or proxy servers. Groups such as FIN13, Volt Typhoon, and APT29 have been associated with this technique.

22910.name: Internet Connection Discovery
22910.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Internet Connection Discovery, identified as T1016.001, is a Discovery tactic technique used on Windows, Linux, macOS, and ESXi platforms. It involves checking for Internet connectivity on compromised systems using tools like Ping, tracert, and GET requests to websites. Adversaries perform this to determine if a system can communicate with their command and control servers and to identify network routes, redirectors, or proxy servers before attempting a connection.

22912.name: unkown_apt_group

Its primary motivation is believed to be espionage, focusing on sectors and regions of strategic interest in East and Southeast Asia.

22955.name: K4Spreader
22955.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]K4Spreader is a malware known for dropping hidden files in the `/dev/` and `/dev/shm/` directories, a behavior it shares with the Kaiji and Gsocket malware families. Its key technical behaviors include Brute Force credential attacks, the use of SSH and External Remote Services for access and lateral movement, Remote System Discovery, and Masquerading for defense evasion. It has been observed exploiting vulnerabilities including CVE-2017-10271, CVE-2020-14883, and CVE-2023-46604. Associated infrastructure includes the domains run.on-demand.pw and http://154.213.192.44, and it has been linked to activity in Brazil and China.[/profile]

22956.name: PwnRig

Its key behaviors include leveraging external remote services like SSH for initial access and lateral movement, performing remote system discovery, and using masquerading for defense evasion. It exploits vulnerabilities including CVE-2020-14883, CVE-2017-10271, and CVE-2023-46604. Its infrastructure involves indicators such as irc.bashgo.pw and 154.213.192.44, and it has been observed targeting systems in Brazil and China.[/profile]

22957.name: Hadooken
22957.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Hadooken, also known as hadooken, is a Linux malware that targets Oracle WebLogic servers via vulnerabilities like CVE-2017-10271, CVE-2020-14883, and CVE-2023-46604. It is deployed via Python scripts that download and execute it, often into temporary directories. Its key behaviors include dropping two ELF files: a packed cryptocurrency miner (using names like '/usr/bin/crondr') and the Tsunami malware for DDoS attacks. It also performs defense evasion by clearing logs and can enable lateral movement via SSH brute force and remote system discovery. Associated infrastructure includes IP addresses like 154.213.192.44.[/profile]

22959.name: unkown_apt_group

Its key malware includes Hadooken, PwnRig, and XMRig for cryptocurrency mining, and it leverages the Tsunami backdoor for DDoS capabilities and command and control. Common TTPs include SSH brute force for lateral movement, clearing logs for defense evasion, and using data obfuscation in C2 traffic. 23088.name: Hidden Window
23088.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Hidden Window is the MITRE ATT&CK technique T1143 under the Defense-Evasion tactic, applicable to Windows, macOS, and Linux platforms. It conceals malicious activity by hiding application windows from the user interface. On Windows, adversaries use scripting features like PowerShell with the `-WindowStyle Hidden` parameter. On macOS, they can abuse the `apple.awt.UIElement` tag in property list files to hide Java application windows from the Dock.

23090.name: DarkNights

Its toolkit includes the Spellbinder lateral movement tool, which performs adversary-in-the-middle attacks via IPv6 SLAAC spoofing. It uses infrastructure like mkdmcdn.com, vv.ssl-dns.com, ssl-dns.com, plugin-audiofirstpiece.ml, and assetsqq.com. Its technical behaviors involve symmetric cryptography for C2, direct Native API calls for execution, and Windows Registry modification for persistence and defense evasion.[/profile]

23091.name: WizardNet

Its technical behaviors involve process injection (T1055), modifying the Windows Registry (T1112), using native APIs for execution (T1106), and employing symmetric cryptography for command and control (T1573.001). It primarily targets individuals and the gambling sector in specific regions including the Philippines, Hong Kong, China, and the United Arab Emirates. Its infrastructure has used domains such as assetsqq.com, ssl-dns.com, and mkdmcdn.com.[/profile]

23092.name: Spellbinder

Its technical behaviors include using the Native API (T1106) for execution, employing symmetric cryptography (T1573.001) for command-and-control traffic, and modifying the Windows Registry (T1112) for persistence and defense evasion. It has been deployed against targets in Cambodia, Hong Kong, the United Arab Emirates, the Philippines, and China, utilizing infrastructure domains such as plugin-audiofirstpiece.ml, ssl-dns.com, assetsqq.com, mkdmcdn.com, and vv.ssl-dns.com.[profile]

23262.name:
This artifact is a cross platform full featured FRP that is written in GO language (Golang) and packed using Ultimate Packer for Executables (UPX). This utility can be used to locate servers behind a network firewall or obscured through NAT. It includes the KCP (no acronym) network protocol that allows for error-checked and anonymous delivery of data streams using the User Datagram Protocol (UDP) with packet level encryption support.

The program contains two different multiplexer libraries that can bi-directionally stream data over a NAT’d network. It also contains a command line interface (CLI) library that can leverage command shells such as PowerShell, Windows Management Instrumentation (WMI), and Z Shell (zsh). In addition, the utility features a unique capability that detects if the utility is executed from the command line or by double-clicking. 

By default it is configured to connect to the Internet Protocol (IP) address, 203.95.8.98 on Transmission Control Protocol (TCP) port 1080. It must receive a specially formed packet from the C2 for the utility to deploy on the system.

Specific technical mechanics include using commands like `bcdedit.exe -set TESTSIGNING ON` on Windows or `csrutil disable` on macOS, often requiring elevated permissions and potentially a system reboot. This technique has been associated with groups like APT39 and Turla, and can be facilitated by exploiting vulnerabilities such as CVE-2025-22457 to alter kernel memory variables like `g_CiOptions` and disable security features like Driver Signature Enforcement.[/profile]

23434.name: Code Signing Policy Modification

Specific methods include using commands like `bcdedit.exe -set TESTSIGNING ON` on Windows or `csrutil disable` on macOS, modifying the registry, booting into recovery mode, or altering kernel memory variables such as `g_CiOptions`, often requiring a system reboot and sometimes leaving visible artifacts like a "Test Mode" watermark.[/profile]
